Infinity-corrected, coverslip-free (inf/0) metallurgical objective - the odd one out in this set. Needs a tube lens; will NOT focus on a 160 mm finite stand. Best pick in this batch for a bench relay/imaging arm. VERIFY tube-lens focal length before computing magnification.

OBJ-011

Infinity-corrected plan apochromat objective, 10x, long working distance

Mitutoyo
Engraved 'M Plan Apo 10X / 0.28 / infinity / 0 / f = 200'; YELLOW band. Catalogue P/N 378-803-3 (Thorlabs MY10X-803).
Wavelength
436-656 nm - VISIBLE ONLY. This objective is NOT usable on your 1550 nm PL bench: it is not merely uncorrected there, the coatings are visible-optimised and transmission collapses in the SWIR.
Size
NA 0.28; M26 x 0.706 thread (26 mm x 36 TPI, JIS B-7141) - NOT RMS. Parfocal length 95 mm. Designed for a 200 mm tube lens. No cover glass ('infinity / 0'). Exit pupil 11.2 mm; supports up to a 2/3 in sensor.
Key spec
f = 20.0 mm (200 mm tube / 10x). WORKING DISTANCE 34.0 mm - the longest of any objective in this catalogue by a wide margin. Resolving power 1.0 um; depth of focus +/-3.5 um; field of view O0.48 mm at FN24.

THE LONG-WORKING-DISTANCE ONE. 34 mm of clearance is what lets you put a cryostat window, a vacuum flange, a sample cell or a beam-steering mirror between the objective and the sample. Compare OBJ-017 (Zeiss Achroplan 40x) at about 0.6 mm - that objective essentially touches the coverslip. This one gives you room to build. PAIRS WITH YOUR CAMERAS: at 10x the O0.48 mm field maps to 4.8 mm on the sensor, which fits comfortably inside the 8.9 mm diagonal of CAM-001/002/003. With 2.4 um pixels you sample at 0.24 um per pixel at the sample - comfortably finer than the 1.0 um resolving power, so this pairing is OPTICS-limited, not pixel-limited, which is the right way round. THREAD AND PARFOCAL WARNING: M26 x 0.706 is NOT RMS. RMS is 20.32 mm major diameter with the SAME 0.706 mm pitch, which is exactly why the two get confused - they will start to engage and then jam. Your OBJ-001 to OBJ-010 are all RMS, and the Zeiss (OBJ-017) is RMS too. Mitutoyo parfocal is 95 mm against 45 mm for the biological standard, so these cannot share a turret with the RMS objectives without refocusing on every change.

'SL' MEANS SUPER LONG WORKING DISTANCE, and that is the whole point of this lens: 13 mm of clearance at 100x. The standard Mitutoyo 100x gives you 6 mm at NA 0.70. YOU ARE TRADING NA FOR SPACE - 0.55 against 0.70 costs you resolution (0.5 um against 0.4 um) and about 40% of the collected solid angle. Take that trade only when you actually need the clearance. HIGHEST RESOLUTION IN YOUR COLLECTION at 0.5 um - and note that TGT-001, your USAF target, tops out at 2.19 um bar width, so it CANNOT characterise this objective. You would need a Group 9-11 target for that. DEPTH OF FOCUS IS +/-0.9 um: at this magnification focus drift from thermal expansion is a real experimental problem, not a theoretical one. Mitutoyo
Engraved 'M PLAN APO / NIR 20X / 0.40 / infinity / 0 / f = 200'; black barrel with a GREEN band. Catalogue P/N 378-824-16 (Thorlabs MY20X-824).

ONE OF ONLY TWO OBJECTIVES YOU OWN THAT WORKS AT 1550 nm - the other is OBJ-016. Everything else in this catalogue, including the Mitutoyo visible apos and the Zeiss, is visible-only. THIS IS THE ONE FOR THE 1550 NIR PL BENCH. It gives 20 mm working distance at NA 0.40, so you can get a filter, a cryostat window or a dichroic between it and the sample. COLLECTION EFFICIENCY IS WHAT MATTERS FOR PL, and it scales roughly as NA squared: NA 0.40 collects about 4% of the full sphere. If your signal is weak, OBJ-016 at NA 0.42 buys you only about 10% more - a real upgrade would be the M Plan Apo NIR HR 50X/0.65 (378-863-5, 10 mm WD), which collects roughly 2.6x more than this one. Worth knowing before you spend time optimising elsewhere. NEARLY IDENTICAL TO OBJ-012 ON THE SHELF: same 20x, same 20 mm working distance, NA 0.40 against 0.42. The difference is the word NIR on the barrel and about 1100 nm of usable range. READ THE BARREL. THREAD AND PARFOCAL WARNING: M26 x 0.706 is NOT RMS. RMS is 20.32 mm major diameter with the SAME 0.706 mm pitch, which is exactly why the two get confused - they will start to engage and then jam. Your OBJ-001 to OBJ-010 are all RMS, and the Zeiss (OBJ-017) is RMS too. Mitutoyo parfocal is 95 mm against 45 mm for the biological standard, so these cannot share a turret with the RMS objectives without refocusing on every change.

Engraved 'M Plan NIR 50 / 0.42 / infinity / 0 / f = 200'; black barrel with a teal/blue band. NOTE: current Mitutoyo catalogues list no series called plain 'M Plan NIR' - only 'M Plan Apo NIR'. The 50X / NA 0.42 combination matches M Plan Apo NIR 50X (P/N 378-825-16/-17) exactly, so this is most likely the same optical design under an older engraving. NOT CONFIRMED from a Mitutoyo document.

THE SECOND OF YOUR TWO 1550 nm-CAPABLE OBJECTIVES, and the higher magnification one. 17 mm working distance at 50x is excellent. WHY THE NA MATTERS MORE THAN THE MAGNIFICATION FOR PL: magnification only sets image scale - you can change it with the tube lens. NA sets how much light you actually collect, and it is fixed in the glass. At NA 0.42 this collects marginally more than OBJ-015 (NA 0.40), so choose between them on working distance and field, not on brightness. ONE THING TO VERIFY: check the barrel really does read NIR. A Mitutoyo 50X/0.42 marked NIR and a visible M Plan Apo 50X/0.55 are different lenses, and the visible one would be useless on your 1550 bench. The NA is the tell: 0.42 at 50x is the NIR series; 0.55 at 50x is the visible one. THREAD AND PARFOCAL WARNING: M26 x 0.706 is NOT RMS. RMS is 20.32 mm major diameter with the SAME 0.706 mm pitch, which is exactly why the two get confused - they will start to engage and then jam. Your OBJ-001 to OBJ-010 are all RMS, and the Zeiss (OBJ-017) is RMS too. Mitutoyo parfocal is 95 mm against 45 mm for the biological standard, so these cannot share a turret with the RMS objectives without refocusing on every change.

OBJ-017

Infinity-corrected achromat objective, 40x, cover-glass corrected

Carl Zeiss
Engraved 'ZEISS ACHROPLAN 40x / 0,65 / infinity / 0,17'; BLUE band.
Wavelength
ACHROMAT - VISIBLE ONLY. Corrected at two wavelengths (typically 486 and 656 nm) with the focus in the green. No NIR correction and no SWIR specification. NOT usable at 1550 nm.
Size
NA 0.65 (dry). RMS thread (0.8 in x 36 TPI) - the ORIGINAL Achroplan; the later N-Achroplan is M27 x 0.75, so check yours. Parfocal 45 mm. Field number about 25.
Key spec
Designed for a 164.5 mm ZEISS tube lens, NOT 200 mm. f = 164.5 / 40 = 4.11 mm. Working distance about 0.55-0.60 mm. REQUIRES A 0.17 mm COVER GLASS.

THE ODD ONE OUT IN THIS BATCH, in three ways that all matter. FIRST, THE TUBE LENS: Zeiss infinity optics are designed around 164.5 mm, Mitutoyo around 200 mm. Put this on a 200 mm tube lens and you get 40 x (200/164.5) = 48.6x, not 40x. Put a Mitutoyo 20x on a Zeiss 164.5 mm tube lens and you get 16.45x. The formula is M_actual = M_design x (f_tube_actual / f_tube_design). NA never changes - only the image scale. SECOND, THE COVER GLASS: the '0,17' means it REQUIRES a 0.17 mm coverslip. At NA 0.65 that is not advisory - imaging a bare sample with this objective visibly degrades the image through spherical aberration, and there is no correction collar to compensate. Every Mitutoyo in this batch is the opposite ('infinity / 0', no cover glass), so the two families are not interchangeable on the same sample. THIRD, THE WORKING DISTANCE: about 0.6 mm. It practically touches the coverslip. Nothing fits in between - no filter, no window, no cryostat. Compare OBJ-011 at 34 mm. ALSO NOTE it is 'Achroplan', not 'Plan-Achroplan': field flatness is only partial, so expect the edges to go soft. WHAT IT IS GOOD FOR: conventional coverslipped biological or thin-sample imaging in the visible, at the highest dry NA you own (0.65 beats every Mitutoyo here). It is the wrong tool for anything on an optical bench.

Infinity-corrected plan apochromat objective, 20x, ELWD - MAKER NOT CONFIRMED

Motic (LEADING CANDIDATE - not confirmed; no maker name on the photographed face)
Engraved 'PLAN APO / ELWD 20X/0.42 / infinity / 0 / WD=20'; GREEN band. No manufacturer name visible.
Wavelength
NOT MARKED. If it is the Motic ELWD PLAN APO, Motic does not publish a wavelength range; a visible-band apochromat is the safe assumption. DO NOT USE IT AT 1550 nm without testing - only OBJ-015 and OBJ-016 are confirmed NIR.
Size
NA 0.42. Motic's version uses M26 x 0.706 and no cover glass, matching the engraving. Parfocal length and design tube-lens focal length NOT PUBLISHED by Motic - MEASURE THEM.
Key spec
Working distance 20 mm (engraved). Design tube-lens focal length NOT ENGRAVED - which is itself the point (see notes). Two knurled rings on the barrel.

SAME NA AND WORKING DISTANCE AS THE MITUTOYO 20x (OBJ-012/013), DIFFERENT MAKER. The engraving style gives it away: Mitutoyo always engraves the series name and 'f = 200'; this one says 'ELWD' and 'WD=', which Mitutoyo never uses. LEADING CANDIDATE IS MOTIC: they sell, for the PA53MET and PSM1000, an objective whose official name is literally 'ELWD PLAN APO 20X/0.420 (WD=20mm)', P/N 1101001700042, with M26 x 0.706 and no cover glass. The engraving matches character for character, including the unusual 'WD=' form. Their whole ELWD ladder shadows Mitutoyo's: 2X/0.055 WD=34, 5X/0.14 WD=34, 10X/0.28 WD=33.5, 20X/0.42 WD=20, 50X/0.55 WD=13, 100X/0.80 WD=3. NOT CONFIRMED - no maker's name is visible on your unit. RULED OUT: Nikon (their ELWD 20x is 0.45 NA at 8.2 mm WD, and CFI Plan Apo 20x is 0.75/1.0 mm); Olympus (LMPLFLN 20x is 0.40/12 mm, a fluorite not an apo, and Olympus designs for a 180 mm tube lens); Mitutoyo (wrong engraving convention). STILL POSSIBLE: Edmund's house-brand EO M Plan Apo 20X, or one of several Chinese OEMs building to the same M26 / 95 mm ladder. THE ONE MEASUREMENT THAT SETTLES THE FAMILY: parfocal length, shoulder to focal plane. 95 mm means it belongs with the Mitutoyos and expects a 200 mm tube lens. 45 mm means it is a biological objective on a completely different design. Then measure the thread major diameter: about 26 mm is M26, about 20.3 mm is RMS. Thirty seconds with calipers. ON THE TWO KNURLED RINGS: probably NOT a correction collar. An objective engraved 'infinity / 0' is specified for zero cover glass, so a cover-glass collar would be pointless, and a real one carries a graduated range like '0-2' or '0.17-1.1'. More likely a grip knurl, a retaining ring, or an iris diaphragm - some metallurgical apos have one.

OBJ-019Confocal / fibre-coupling stage (with STG-022)

Finite achromat objective, 10x, mounted in a fibre-coupling jig

Unbranded (no maker's mark visible)
Engraved '10 / 0.25' with a YELLOW band. Held in a black V-clamp by a rubber band, with a yellow-jacketed fibre running into the back.
Wavelength
~400-700 nm (VIS achromat) - assumed from the class; not marked.
Size
NA 0.25; RMS thread assumed. Currently clamped in the alignment mount recorded as STG-022.
Key spec
EFL ~16 mm. Working distance not marked.

POSSIBLE DUPLICATE - CHECK BEFORE COUNTING IT TWICE. OBJ-005 in this catalogue is also a 10x / NA 0.25 with a yellow band ('DIN 10 0.25'), and OBJ-009 is another 10x / 0.25 with a blue-grey band. This one may simply be OBJ-005 taken out of the drawer and put into the jig. Compare the exact engraving - 'DIN 10 0.25' versus '10 / 0.25' - and merge the rows if they match. WHAT IT IS DOING HERE MATTERS MORE THAN WHICH ONE IT IS: it is set up as a FIBRE COUPLER. A yellow-jacketed fibre goes into the back and the objective focuses onto or collects from it, on a micrometer-driven alignment mount. NA 0.25 is a sensible match to standard single-mode fibre (NA about 0.14) with margin to spare. IT IS HELD BY A RUBBER BAND. That is fine for a bench test and hopeless for anything you want to reproduce - the band creeps, relaxes with temperature and lets the objective rotate. If this coupling is worth keeping, replace it with a proper clamp or an RMS-threaded adapter. CONFOCAL CAPABILITY - NOTED BY THE LAB: a PINHOLE can be mounted in FRONT of this stage, which turns the assembly into a CONFOCAL detection arm. That is the point of the setup: the pinhole sits at the image plane conjugate to the focal spot, so light from the focal plane passes through it and light from above or below the focus is blocked. You get optical sectioning, much better background rejection, and a real depth resolution instead of collecting the whole column. The pinholes are already in this catalogue: PIN-001 (2 um) and PIN-003 (10 um). SIZING RULE: the right pinhole diameter is roughly the Airy disc at the image plane, i.e. about 1.22 x lambda x M / NA. For this 10x / NA 0.25 at 633 nm that is around 31 um, so BOTH stocked pinholes are considerably TIGHTER than one Airy unit - they will sharpen the sectioning further but cost signal. Open up (or use the fibre core itself as the pinhole) if you are photon-starved. NOTE THE FIBRE ALTERNATIVE: a single-mode fibre core IS a pinhole. If the yellow fibre already in the back of this jig is single mode, you have a confocal arm without needing a separate pinhole at all - which is how most fibre-coupled confocal setups are built.

THE COLLECTION OBJECTIVE OF THE BAND-STRUCTURE SETUP. In Fourier-plane imaging, the angle of light leaving the sample maps to position in the objective's back focal plane: r = f sin(theta), so NA 0.26 means you see emission angles out to about 15 deg. That is the k-space window of the measurement - a larger-NA objective shows more of the band structure. HOW TO TELL IT IS A COPY: genuine Mitutoyo M Plan Apo objectives are white/grey with Mitutoyo engraving; this one is red with no maker name. It is built to the Mitutoyo 10x NIR prescription (Mitutoyo 378-823-5: WD 30.5 mm, parfocal 95 mm, M26 x 0.706 thread), but working distance, transmission and correction of the copy are NOT CONFIRMED - measure the WD before relying on it. f = 200 mm means it is designed for a Mitutoyo/Thorlabs 200 mm tube lens: with a Nikon 200 mm tube lens magnification is correct, with Olympus 180 mm it becomes 9x. Not a duplicate of OBJ-016: that is a genuine Mitutoyo 50x / 0.42 NIR objective; the automatic part-number check matched only the words Plan Apo NIR in its notes.

THE LARGEST SINGLE HOLDING IN THIS CATALOGUE, and the most broadly useful coating you own. Protected silver spans 450 nm to 20 um at >97% through the near-IR - it beats your E02 dielectric cube (MIR-003, 400-750 nm) everywhere above 750 nm, and beats gold everywhere below 800 nm. Use these for alignment and rough beam steering; pull fresh ones from MIR-005 for anything where throughput or stray light is being measured. Square and rectangular mirrors are not just round ones with the corners cut off - the shape is the point. A rectangle is what you want when the beam itself is elliptical (a bare diode output, or anything after a single cylindrical lens), because it accepts the long axis without wasting aperture on the short one. Squares also tile and clamp along a flat edge, which lets you fold a beam much closer to a neighbouring component than a round mount allows. Both of these look clean and unscratched. FLAG: dimensions here are photo-estimated - measure before you design or order a mount, since square mirror mounts are far less forgiving about size than Ø1 in holders.

TBD, set by SUBSTRATE not coating (it is uncoated). If N-BK7: ~350-2000 nm. If UV fused silica: ~200-2500 nm. Confirm the glass before assuming UV or IR capability.

TIR turning prism: at 45 deg internal incidence any glass with n > 1.414 totally internally reflects, which N-BK7 (n~1.52) does across the whole VIS-NIR - so the reflecting face is effectively lossless and broadband with no coating to damage or degrade. The loss lives on the two entry/exit faces instead: ~4% Fresnel each, ~8% round trip, unless they are AR coated (these look uncoated - no coloured bloom). IMPORTANT: TIR imposes a polarisation-dependent s-vs-p phase shift, so this is NOT a polarisation-neutral fold the way a metal mirror is - linear input at 45 deg to the plane of incidence comes out elliptical. Use a coated mirror if polarisation state must be preserved. FLAG: a chip is visible on the lower edge - inspect before use in a beam path.

WEDGE PRISMS, 0.5 degree beam deviation, VIS-NIR coated - TWO UNITS, sealed

Edmund Optics (TECHSPEC)
PN 49437 (stock #49-437); "PRISM WEDGE 0.5 DEG VIS-NIR TS"; PO P00000153683 0-241008; Made in Singapore
Wavelength
VIS-NIR AR coated, 400-1000 nm
Size
O25.0 mm (+0.00 / -0.10), centre thickness 3.00 mm; N-BK7
Key spec
BEAM DEVIATION 0.5 degrees at 633 nm (0.87 dioptres). NOTE the physical WEDGE ANGLE is 0 deg 58 min (about 0.967 deg) - Edmund names these parts by DEVIATION, not by apex angle. Surface quality 20-10 scratch-dig; flatness 0.50/0.20 fringes at 632.8 nm

READ THE PART NAME CAREFULLY - "0.5 DEG" IS THE BEAM DEVIATION, NOT THE WEDGE ANGLE. The glass is actually wedged by about 0.967 degrees; the deviation follows from delta = (n-1) x alpha, and with N-BK7 at n = 1.5151 that gives 0.5151 x 0.967 = 0.498 degrees. Getting this backwards is a common and expensive mistake in a design. Because n is dispersive, the deviation drifts slightly with wavelength (about 0.499 deg at 588 nm, 0.491 deg at 1064 nm) - a wedge is mildly chromatic, which matters for broadband use. WHAT WEDGES ARE FOR HERE - three jobs: (1) FINE BEAM STEERING. One wedge tilts a beam 0.5 degrees. TWO counter-rotating wedges (a Risley pair) give continuously variable deviation from 0 to 1.0 degrees in ANY azimuth - which is exactly why there are two of these. That is a far finer and more stable adjustment than walking a kinematic mirror. (2) BEAM SAMPLING. The Fresnel reflection off a face gives a low-power monitor pick-off that is ANGULARLY SEPARATED from the ghost off the second face, so the two do not overlap. (3) KILLING ETALON FRINGES - and this is the one worth understanding. In a PLANE-PARALLEL plate the two surface reflections are collinear and recombine coherently, making a low-finesse Fabry-Perot whose transmission ripples with wavelength and with temperature. Those periodic fringes are what wreck absorption and cavity spectroscopy. A WEDGE makes the two reflections non-parallel, so the second-surface ghost simply walks out of the beam and never interferes. Same reason laser windows, etalon substrates and beam samplers are wedged. Both units still sealed in their Edmund bags. "TS" = TECHSPEC, Edmund in-house designed line. SECOND PHOTO, PROBABLY THE SAME PAIR: two unmounted ~25 mm discs on lens tissue, with a printed lab label reading "widge plate" (wedge plate). Same quantity, same size class. I have NOT created a second row for them, on the assumption these are the Edmund 49437 pair unpacked and labelled. IF THAT IS WRONG AND YOU HAVE A SECOND, SEPARATE PAIR OF WEDGES, TELL ME and I will add them - the count matters here, because two wedges is exactly a Risley pair and four would be two pairs.

Inserting a glass block of thickness t into a converging beam pushes the focus back by t(1 - 1/n); for N-BK7 (n = 1.517) that is 0.341 t, so df = 500 um corresponds to a glass path of about 1.5 mm, and for UV fused silica (n = 1.458) about 1.6 mm. A numbered SET of such elements, each giving a different df, is exactly how MULTIFOCAL or REMOTE-FOCUSING imaging is built - you put different glass thicknesses in different parts of the pupil or in different arms so several object planes land on one camera simultaneously. That reading is consistent with a set labelled PRISM1/2/3 with individual df values. READ THE ANGLE SPEC BEFORE USING THIS. Unlike every other filter in this catalogue, a DMLP is designed to work at 45 degrees, not straight on. Put it at normal incidence and the cut-on shifts substantially (dielectric edges move blue as angle increases, so the reverse also applies) and the blocking degrades. Used correctly it does something none of the others can: it SPLITS rather than absorbs, giving you both the short-wavelength arm (reflected) and the long-wavelength arm (transmitted) simultaneously. That is the standard way to separate a pump from a longer-wavelength signal while keeping both. It is also unmounted, so it needs a filter mount or a dichroic holder and should only be handled by the edge.

Filed under Dichroics at your instruction - the coating is wavelength-selective, reflecting two narrow bands and passing the rest. BUT READ THIS BEFORE USING IT, BECAUSE IT DOES NOT DO WHAT MOST DICHROICS DO: it reflects BOTH bands at once. Rs is >99.9% at 385-415 nm AND >99.9% at 770-830 nm. It STEERS the 800 nm fundamental together with its 400 nm second harmonic on a single optic - it does NOT split them apart. If you want to SEPARATE 400 from 800, that is a different part: FDM-002 (the Ti:Sapphire harmonic isolator) or FDM-004 (the CVI 90:10 at 800 nm). Between the two reflection bands - roughly 450-750 nm - this mirror transmits, which is the sense in which it is dichroic, but that region is not where you would use it. WHY IT EXISTS: in an SHG setup the fundamental and the harmonic have to travel the same path after the crystal. An ordinary broadband mirror either will not reflect both efficiently or will add dispersion; this one does both at once with GDD under 35 fs2 at 400 nm and under 20 fs2 at 800 nm, so it does not stretch the pulses. IBS coating on fused silica with a stress-compensating back layer. DESIGNED FOR 45 DEGREES - do not use it at normal incidence, the bands shift.

Between the two you can route a fundamental and its harmonic independently. If it came out of one of the Ti:Sapphire lasers, that laser may be missing a part - worth confirming before someone spends a day debugging stray blue light on the Vitesse or Chameleon. HANDLING: the coating is exposed and the aperture is large; hold the flange only, blow dust off with the bulb blower (TLS-046), and store it face-protected. THE PUMP-PROBE SPLITTER FOR THE Ti:SAPPHIRE BENCH. A 90:10 at 800 nm is the classic pump-probe element - 90% into the pump arm, 10% into the probe - or a 10% diagnostic tap to an autocorrelator (INS-015), spectrometer or power meter while 90% goes to the experiment. Pairs with the Vitesse (LSR-008) and Chameleon (LSR-009). THE "P" IS NOT DECORATION - READ IT BEFORE USING IT. At 45 degrees, p-polarization sits toward Brewster (56.6 deg for fused silica), so bare-surface p-reflectance is only about 0.6% versus about 9% for s. Every layer pair in the stack has weaker index contrast in p, which makes 90% R in p genuinely harder to achieve than in s. CONSEQUENCE: this coating is specified and guaranteed ONLY for p-polarised light at 45 degrees. Feed it s-polarised light and it will reflect FAR MORE than 90% and your split ratio is simply wrong. Check your polarisation before you trust the ratio. WHY GDD MATTERS HERE, and how much: a 100 fs pulse at 800 nm carries about 10 nm of bandwidth. Broadening goes as sqrt(1 + (4 ln2 x GDD / tau^2)^2), and with tau^2 = 1e4 fs^2 a few hundred fs^2 only stretches it a few percent - tolerable. At 20 fs (tau^2 = 400 fs^2) the same 300 fs^2 MORE THAN DOUBLES the pulse. So low-GDD matters mildly at 100 fs and is essential below about 30 fs. Also note the substrate itself: fused silica adds about +36 fs^2/mm at 800 nm, so a 1.75 mm plate puts about 60 fs^2 into the TRANSMITTED arm only - the two arms of a pump-probe are dispersion-mismatched unless you add a compensating plate. That is a real and commonly overlooked error. AND IT SHOULD BE WEDGED: an unwedged plate gives a back-surface reflection delayed by 2nd cos(theta)/c - a satellite pulse a few picoseconds behind the main one, which shows up as a spurious feature in a pump-probe trace. Check for a wedge when you open it. THE HANDWRITTEN LABEL SAYS "90/20", WHICH CANNOT BE RIGHT - 90 + 20 = 110%. The part number itself carries the 90, so read it as 90:10 (minus a few percent coating loss). Most likely a slip of the pen, possibly confusing it with the adjacent 80:20 part in the same catalogue. PROVENANCE: shipped to UNIV OF CALIF BERKELEY - another item on the Berkeley trail alongside the Bandwidth9 EDFA (MAJ-005), the OZ Optics tapered fibres (ACC-043), the HP 70951A OSA (MAJ-014), stages STG-002/009/010 and wafers WFR-006. FLAG: the "UT" prefix is NOT CONFIRMED against any published CVI series (their documented prefixes are BS1, BS2, FABS, TLM, PR1, W1/W2, LWP/SWP) - it is most likely a legacy Melles Griot or custom number. The 800-90-45P fields are decoded with confidence. Substrate, thickness, diameter, wedge and GDD spec are unknown until you open it.

At 45 degrees any dielectric plate has Rs not equal to Rp, and the quoted 10:90 is the average of the two. For a linearly polarised beam the real ratio shifts with the input polarisation angle. If the split ratio matters to your measurement, fix the polarisation and calibrate at that setting with the power meter (MTR-008). Thorlabs naming, for reference: BSN = 10:90, BSX = 90:10, BSS = 30:70, BST = 70:30, BSW = 50:50; the trailing number is the coating band (10 = 400-700 nm).

A cube also has a LOWER DAMAGE THRESHOLD because the cement at the hypotenuse absorbs and fails first.

BiBO has the highest effective nonlinearity of the common borates: roughly 1.5-2x BBO and 3.5-4x LBO, which is why it is the usual pick for efficient SHG into the blue and for OPO/OPA pumping. It also resists moisture, unlike LBO. The trade-off is damage threshold: ~0.3 GW/cm2 at 1064 nm / 10 ns versus BBO's ~5 GW/cm2, so it is the wrong crystal for high-peak-power nanosecond work. CRITICAL: a cut crystal only phase-matches near its design wavelength, so without theta you cannot predict what this doubles. THE LABEL IS THE IMPORTANT PART: "in Ar" means it is stored under ARGON, and that is not fussiness. BETA-BBO IS HYGROSCOPIC - atmospheric moisture attacks the polished faces and produces a permanent hazy, etched surface that scatters and cannot be polished out in a normal lab. A degraded BBO face is a dead crystal. So: keep it sealed, keep it dry, and if it has been out in room air for a long period, inspect the faces under magnification before assuming it still works. Some groups keep BBO in a desiccator or under a slow argon purge for exactly this reason - the vacuum desiccator (MAJ-020) is available if you want a dry store. THE ROTATION MOUNT MATTERS TOO: BBO is birefringent and angle-phase-matched, so the conversion efficiency depends steeply on the crystal angle. Being in a graduated rotation mount means the phase-matching angle is settable and readable - but note a rotation mount rotates about the BEAM axis, which sets the polarisation orientation, while phase matching also needs TILT. Check what degree of freedom you actually have before assuming you can tune it. POSSIBLE DUPLICATE - CHECK BEFORE COUNTING IT TWICE. This catalogue already has NLC-002 ("BBO", gold-ring mounted on a 3D-printed holder) and NLC-003 (a fully specified beta-BBO SHG crystal, NLC07, 3.00 mm, theta = 19.8 deg, in a O1 inch housing). This one may be NLC-003 taken out of its box and put into a rotation mount. Compare the housing engraving - NLC-003 has everything engraved on it, so if this housing carries "NLC07" they are the same crystal and the rows should be merged. FLAG: if it is NOT NLC-003, then nothing about this crystal is specified and it cannot be designed with - only experimented with. Worth pulling it out and reading the housing.

CALCITE CRYSTAL BLANK, 10 x 10 x 8 mm - ONE PIECE, sealed

Not marked (Chinese supplier)
No part number. Hand-written label reads 方解石 (calcite), 10x10x8, 1pc
Wavelength
Calcite transmits roughly 350 nm to 2.3 um
Size
10 x 10 x 8 mm rectangular block, in a small clear clamshell
Key spec
Cut angle and orientation NOT MARKED. Calcite is strongly birefringent: no = 1.658, ne = 1.486 at 589 nm, so delta-n is about -0.17

A BIRDFRINGENT CRYSTAL BLANK, not a nonlinear crystal in the frequency-conversion sense - filed here because that is where the other bulk crystals live. Calcite is THE workhorse birefringent material: the Glan-Taylor polarizers in this catalogue (POL-001/002/003) and the Glan-Laser (POL-008) are all calcite prisms. WHAT A 10 x 10 x 8 mm BLOCK IS FOR: most likely a BEAM DISPLACER or a walk-off plate. With delta-n about 0.17 and the optic axis cut at 45 degrees, calcite separates the ordinary and extraordinary rays by roughly 0.1 x the thickness - so an 8 mm block gives about 0.8 mm of lateral separation between the two orthogonal polarisations, both exiting parallel. That is the standard way to build a polarisation-analysing detection arm where you want BOTH polarisations, side by side, rather than throwing one away as a polarizer does. FLAG - THE CUT IS EVERYTHING AND IT IS NOT MARKED: a beam displacer needs the optic axis at about 45 degrees to the faces; a waveplate blank needs it parallel; a polarizer prism needs a specific wedge. Without knowing the cut you cannot predict what it will do. Look for a scribed axis mark on an edge, or test it: shine an unpolarised beam through and look for TWO output spots (displacer) versus one (axis normal or parallel to the faces). CALCITE HANDLING - IT IS FRAGILE IN A WAY GLASS IS NOT: it is soft (Mohs 3), it CLEAVES readily along rhombohedral planes, and it is damaged by water and dilute acid. Do not drop it, do not clamp it hard, do not clean it with anything aqueous, and keep it in its box. Thermal shock cracks it too.

Wavelength
SAFETY LABEL SAYS 300-2700 nm; the WhiteLase datasheet band is 400-2400 nm. Both are right - the safety label states the widest possible emission envelope including residual pump and weak spectral wings. THIS IS THE ONLY SOURCE YOU OWN THAT COVERS EVERY WAVELENGTH IN THIS CATALOGUE AT ONCE: 405, 488, 532, 633, 810, 1064 and 1550 nm are all inside it simultaneously.

THE NUMBERS THAT MATTER: 4 W / 40 MHz = 100 nJ per pulse; 100 nJ / 6 ps = about 17 kW PEAK POWER. The '<10 uJ' on the safety label is a loose bounding figure, roughly 100x the real per-pulse energy - do not use it as a spec.

READ THIS BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE: NO EYEWEAR YOU OWN PROTECTS AGAINST THIS LASER ACROSS ITS BAND. SAF-007, your best pair, covers 180-534 nm and 740-1095 nm - so a supercontinuum passes straight through it in the 534-740 nm window AND everywhere above 1095 nm, out to 2400 nm. Same gaps on SAF-009. The green NIR pairs and the FreeMascot reds are worse. A BROADBAND SOURCE DEFEATS BAND-SPECIFIC GOGGLES BY CONSTRUCTION - that is the whole problem with supercontinuum safety. The correct answer is eyewear rated continuously across 400-2400 nm, or an enclosed beam path with interlocks, not a better notch filter. AND MOST OF THE OUTPUT IS INVISIBLE: everything above about 700 nm gives you no blink reflex at all, while carrying most of the average power. THE DELIVERY FIBRE IS THE OTHER HAZARD. 'DO NOT BEND or PULL' is not advisory - a broken armoured delivery fibre emits a diverging CLASS IV beam from the break, and at 4 W that is an immediate skin and eye hazard anywhere in the room. Route it once and leave it alone. WHAT IT IS ACTUALLY FOR, AND WHY IT CHANGES YOUR LAB: a supercontinuum is a white-light laser - spatially coherent like a laser, spectrally broad like a lamp. Combined with GRT-001 (600 l/mm, 1600 nm blaze) and SLT-001 (the micrometer slit), it becomes a TUNABLE SOURCE: disperse it, slit it, and you can pick any wavelength from 400 to 2400 nm. That is a far more capable instrument than any of your fixed lasers, and it is the natural excitation source for the 1550 nm PL bench - it can pump at 1064 and probe at 1550, or sweep the whole band in one measurement. YOUR FILTER COLLECTION IS THE OTHER HALF OF THIS. Sixteen longpass, eleven bandpass and two shortpass filters are close to useless with single-line lasers and exactly right for carving up a supercontinuum. SUPPORT: NKT Photonics acquired Fianium on 31 March 2016, retired the WhiteLase name into the SuperK FIANIUM family, and still services legacy units. Contact NKT, not Fianium. CONFIRM THE MODEL by finding the plate on the rear or underside - SC400 cuts in near 410 nm, SC450 at 450, SC480 at 480, and that lower edge decides whether your 405 nm-band optics are usable with it.

FLAG - CLASS 4, AND THE MOST DANGEROUS THING IN THIS CATALOGUE AFTER THE CHLOROFORM. The yellow label says 1.3 W max in the green band out of a BARE FIBRE END ('LASER APERTURE AT FIBER END'). A watt of visible light coming out of a diverging fibre cone will damage an eye instantly, will burn skin, and will ignite dark plastic or paper at close range. NEVER look into the connector, powered or not, and NEVER put a fibre inspection scope on a fibre that might be live. READING THE THREE-WAVELENGTH LABEL, which confuses everyone: only ONE of those bands comes out. Sapphire is an OPSL - optically pumped semiconductor laser - so an 808 nm diode (the 0.79-0.82 um line) pumps a semiconductor chip which lases around 1.04-1.16 um inside the cavity, and an intracavity doubling crystal halves that to the 0.52-0.57 um green you actually use. The 20 mW and 200 mW figures are leakage ratings for the internal fields, not outputs. PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE: green-only laser goggles are NOT sufficient if a fibre or splice ever fails - you need eyewear that also blocks ~808 nm and ~1100 nm, both invisible. WAVELENGTH: the '548' tab is almost certainly 548 nm. That is NOT a Coherent catalogue wavelength (the published Sapphire list is 458, 488, 514, 532, 552, 561, 568, 588, 594), so this is a CUSTOM OEM build - OPSL lets Coherent pick any wavelength. Be careful: the 532nm patch cords lying with them are NOT matched to the heads. PROVENANCE - NOT CONFIRMED: 'Titan' appears in no Coherent literature at all; it reads as a customer programme name. A published teardown of a visually identical assembly (two Sapphire heads, OEM LPX-class controllers, common baseplate, PM fibre spliced to a Diamond E-2000 shuttered pigtail) identifies it as coming from a PacBio Sequel DNA sequencer, and that unit was marked 'Sapphire 548-300 FPT FT' - 548 nm, 300 mW. SO THE 1.3 W ON THE LABEL MAY BE A FAMILY CEILING RATHER THAN THIS UNIT'S POWER. Treat it as 1.3 W until measured. TO RUN ONE ON THE BENCH: +10.8-15 VDC (12 V nominal) at >60 W, low ripple; RS-232 at 19200 8N1; 10-pin Molex Micro-Fit carrying supply, interlock and keyswitch. The gold heatsink block is NOT optional - the baseplate must stay below 50 C. The driver boards ARE the controllers, so no separate Coherent controller is needed, but the teardown found the head will talk serial and still emit NOTHING with the programme-specific daughter board removed. Fibre minimum bend radius 50 mm - a tight bend on a watt-class fibre is a burn and fire point, not just a loss. NOT RECORDED: measured output power, whether both heads work, the exact daughter-board revision, and whether a suitable 12 V supply exists in the lab.

IT NEEDS A DRIVER YOU DO NOT APPEAR TO OWN. This is a bare LED head with a Binder M8 lead - there is no driver in the case. It must run from a Thorlabs constant-current LED driver (LEDD1B, DC2200, DC4104 or similar) at 1000 mA. DO NOT connect it to a bench supply in voltage mode: an LED's forward voltage varies with temperature, so a fixed-voltage source lets the current run away and the emitter dies in seconds. Constant current, always. WHAT IT IS ACTUALLY FOR: this is the standard Koehler illumination / epi-fluorescence excitation source for a microscope. It replaces an HBO/XBO arc lamp - no warm-up, no alignment drift, no mercury, instant on/off and clean electronic modulation. Worth checking the thread on ACC-005 with this in hand. THE 1 x 1 mm EMITTER IS THE NUMBER THAT SETS EVERYTHING: it is an extended source, not a point, so you cannot collimate it tightly - etendue forbids it. Through a lens of focal length f the beam divergence is roughly 1 mm / f. It is excellent for flooding a field uniformly and poor for anything needing a small spot. PAIRING NOTES FOR YOUR FILTERS: at 6500 K it drives FBP-002 (FBH400-40) only weakly - the blue pump peak sits near 450 nm, above that filter's band. FBP-003 (10LF01 488) sits right on the phosphor dip, so expect low throughput. FLP-001/002 (FEL0450) will pass the phosphor and cut the blue pump, which is a clean way to get a warm broadband source. CASE CONDITION: the head and its cable are in the foam; the second foam cutout in the lid area is empty, so check whether a collimation adapter or a driver originally shipped with it.

Measures the DIFFERENCE between its two ports (P1 - P2), not an absolute pressure. Leave one port open and it reads gauge pressure, i.e. relative to the room - which means its zero moves with the weather and the altitude. Real uses here: pressure drop across a filter or a restriction, gas line and manifold pressure, fume-hood or room pressurisation checks, and leak/decay tests on a sealed volume. Tee one port into each side of whatever you are measuring across. DO NOT REACH FOR THIS FOR VACUUM WORK. 1 mbar is one display count, and a meter of this class is typically +/-0.3-0.5% of full scale, i.e. +/-6-10 mbar - several times its own resolution. It cannot tell 1 mbar from 1e-3 mbar from hard vacuum. The vacuum work in this lab is covered by the Edwards AIM-S gauge on the pumping station (MAJ-017), which reads 1e-8 to 1e-2 mbar. FLAG: no manufacturer or model marked anywhere; accuracy NOT CONFIRMED.

Key spec

Instant non-contact surface temperature - good for a quick check on a hot plate, a chiller line, a laser head or a power supply that feels warm. TWO THINGS THAT WILL GIVE YOU WRONG NUMBERS IF YOU DO NOT KNOW THEM: (1) IT LIES ON SHINY METAL. Polished aluminium and steel have very low emissivity (0.05-0.2) and reflect strongly, so most of what the sensor sees is infrared REFLECTED off the surface from the surroundings, not emitted by it. Left at the default emissivity of 0.95 the reading can be tens to hundreds of degrees LOW, and it drifts with whatever hot or cold object happens to be nearby. Fix: stick a piece of matte tape or paint a flat-black spot on the target, let it equilibrate, and read that - or use the contact thermocouple meter (MTR-010), which is the right tool for bare metal. (2) DISTANCE-TO-SPOT 16:1 means the measured circle is about one sixteenth of your distance - at 400 mm you are averaging over a 25 mm spot. The reading is the AVERAGE over that whole circle, so to measure something small you have to get close. The two lasers bracket the spot edges to help you judge it. The laser is Class 2 - do not point it at anyone eyes. FLAG: whether this particular unit has ADJUSTABLE emissivity (0.10-1.00) or is fixed at 0.95 is NOT CONFIRMED - check for an emissivity menu.

DET-001High-speed / optical communications

HIGH-SPEED NIR photoreceiver, 22 GHz - for optical communications - LINEAR, NOT a photon counter

New Focus (now a Newport brand within MKS Instruments)
Front panel: 'Model 1484-A-50 / 22-GHz NIR Photoreceiver', PWR LED, Optical Input, 'Bias Monitor 1mV/uA', Made in USA. Powered from the New Focus 0901 supply (INS-003).
Wavelength
800-865 nm - a NARROW NIR WINDOW, limited by the input lens dispersion, not by the detector material. THIS COVERS YOUR 810 nm SPDC LINE (FBP-009, HQ810/20) AND ESSENTIALLY NOTHING ELSE YOU OWN. It does NOT reach 1064 nm and it does NOT reach 1550 nm.
Size
Optical input is FC/PC on 50 um core GRADED-INDEX MULTIMODE fibre - that is what the '-50' means (50 um core), NOT 50 ohms. The single-mode sibling is the 1474-A on 9 um fibre. Output is an Anritsu K connector, 50 ohms.
Key spec
22 GHz typical, 20 GHz minimum 3 dB bandwidth. Conversion gain -75 V/W typical (the minus sign means the amplifier inverts). Max safe input 8 mW CW; saturation around 2 mW. Bias monitor 1 V/mA, 15 kHz bandwidth. Needs +/-12 to 15 V at 100 mA.

IMPORTANT CORRECTION - THIS IS NOT A SINGLE-PHOTON DETECTOR. You recorded it as one, and it is worth being precise because the difference is about eight orders of magnitude in sensitivity. This is a LINEAR analog photoreceiver: a PIN photodiode with no internal gain, giving a continuous voltage proportional to instantaneous optical power, read on a scope or spectrum analyser. There is no discriminator, no TTL click output and no Geiger-mode bias. A REAL SINGLE-PHOTON DETECTOR (a Si SPAD like the Excelitas SPCM-AQRH, an InGaAs SPAD like the ID Quantique id230, or an SNSPD) has internal gain of 10^6 or more, so one absorbed photon makes a macroscopic digital pulse. You measure a COUNT RATE and the noise figure is dark counts per second, not NEP. WHY A PIN DIODE PHYSICALLY CANNOT DO IT: one 1550 nm photon liberates one electron, 1.6e-19 C. Even dumped into 50 ohms in 1 ns that is about 8 nV. Johnson noise in 50 ohms over 1 GHz is about 29 uV rms - the single-photon signal sits three to four orders of magnitude UNDER the thermal noise floor. You need roughly 10^3 to 10^5 simultaneous photons before a PIN diode produces anything above noise. FOR SCALE: 1 nW at 1550 nm is about 8 BILLION photons per second. A nanowatt is an enormous amount of light in photon-counting terms. WHAT IT IS ACTUALLY EXCELLENT AT: measuring the TIME STRUCTURE of a bright optical signal. At 22 GHz it resolves features down to about 15 ps, which is fast enough to see the individual 6 ps pulses from your supercontinuum (LSR-005) if you can get them into the 800-865 nm window. THE PRICE OF THAT SPEED IS SENSITIVITY: noise scales as the square root of bandwidth, so a 22 GHz receiver has a noise floor in the MICROWATT range. Compare DET-003 (Thorlabs DET110) at about 50 nW over 17.5 MHz. Fast and sensitive are opposites; pick one. MULTIMODE INPUT IS A REAL CONSTRAINT: 50 um graded-index fibre is telecom-datacom fibre, not the single-mode fibre your 1550 nm bench uses. You cannot simply plug an SMF-28 patch cord into it and expect the specified performance. IT NEEDS THE 0901 SUPPLY (INS-003) - it will not run on a battery like DET-002 or DET-003. WHICH DETECTOR DO I USE? THE SPEED LADDER IN THIS LAB, fastest first: DET-002 (New Focus 1011, 40 GHz) and DET-001 (New Focus 1484-A-50, 22 GHz) are THE HIGH-SPEED PAIR - these are the only detectors here fast enough for OPTICAL COMMUNICATIONS work: modulated data streams, eye diagrams, RF beat notes, heterodyne detection, and resolving the mode spacing of the femtosecond lasers. Everything else in the catalogue is orders of magnitude slower. DET-003 (Thorlabs DET110, Si) is a general-purpose biased photodiode - nanosecond class, fine for alignment, pulse detection and slow signals, useless above a few tens of MHz. The power-meter heads (MTR-002, MTR-006, MTR-007) are AVERAGE POWER sensors, not signal detectors - the thermopile MTR-007 has a thermal time constant of seconds. DET-004 and DET-005 (MPD SPADs) are the opposite extreme: single-photon sensitive but photon-COUNTING, giving TTL clicks with dead time, not a linear waveform. THE READOUT IS USUALLY WHAT LIMITS YOU, NOT THE DETECTOR: the only oscilloscopes in this catalogue are two LeCroy WaveAce 102 at 60 MHz (ELE-010). They cannot show anything these two fast detectors can resolve. To actually use 22 or 40 GHz of bandwidth you need a sampling scope, a real-time scope of comparable bandwidth, or an RF spectrum analyser - and matched 50 ohm coax with proper connectors throughout, since at these frequencies cable and connector quality dominates. ALSO NOTE THE BAND MISMATCH: DET-001 only covers 800-865 nm, so despite being the "comms-speed" pair it is DET-002 (if it is indeed InGaAs) that would reach the 1550 nm telecom bench. Confirm DET-002 detector material before planning a 1550 nm high-speed measurement around it. POWER: needs the current-limited New Focus 0901 supply (INS-003) - see that entry, it exists specifically to stop a wiring fault destroying this receiver front end.

DET-003

Biased silicon photodiode detector, 350-1100 nm - LINEAR, NOT a photon counter

Thorlabs
Round silver housing marked 'THORLABS DET110', CE. ON/OFF switch, BAT compartment, BNC output. DISCONTINUED - Thorlabs' current equivalent line is the DET-A2 series, and the DET36A2 matches this one's 13 mm2 active area and speed most closely.
Wavelength
350-1100 nm (silicon), peak 960 +/- 50 nm. Covers 405, 532, 633 and 810 nm. Does NOT reach 1064 nm usefully and does NOT reach 1550 nm.
Size
Active area 3.6 x 3.6 mm = 13 mm2 - a large target, which makes free-space alignment forgiving. BNC output, DC coupled. 12 V bias from an A23 battery.
Key spec
Rise time 20 ns; catalogue bandwidth 17.5 MHz. NEP 1.2e-14 W/sqrt(Hz). Dark current 10 nA. Junction capacitance 20 pF. Damage threshold 100 mW CW; linearity limit about 1 mW.

IMPORTANT CORRECTION - THIS IS NOT A SINGLE-PHOTON DETECTOR. You recorded it as one, and it is worth being precise because the difference is about eight orders of magnitude in sensitivity. This is a LINEAR analog photoreceiver: a PIN photodiode with no internal gain, giving a continuous voltage proportional to instantaneous optical power, read on a scope or spectrum analyser. There is no discriminator, no TTL click output and no Geiger-mode bias. A REAL SINGLE-PHOTON DETECTOR (a Si SPAD like the Excelitas SPCM-AQRH, an InGaAs SPAD like the ID Quantique id230, or an SNSPD) has internal gain of 10^6 or more, so one absorbed photon makes a macroscopic digital pulse. You measure a COUNT RATE and the noise figure is dark counts per second, not NEP. WHY A PIN DIODE PHYSICALLY CANNOT DO IT: one 1550 nm photon liberates one electron, 1.6e-19 C. Even dumped into 50 ohms in 1 ns that is about 8 nV. Johnson noise in 50 ohms over 1 GHz is about 29 uV rms - the single-photon signal sits three to four orders of magnitude UNDER the thermal noise floor. You need roughly 10^3 to 10^5 simultaneous photons before a PIN diode produces anything above noise. FOR SCALE: 1 nW at 1550 nm is about 8 BILLION photons per second. A nanowatt is an enormous amount of light in photon-counting terms. THE TERMINATION YOU CHOOSE CHANGES THIS DETECTOR BY A FACTOR OF TWENTY THOUSAND, and it is the single most misunderstood thing about it. Output voltage is V = I_photo x R_load, while bandwidth is 1/(2*pi*R_load*C_j) with C_j = 20 pF. Gain and bandwidth trade exactly inversely. INTO 50 OHMS: the RC limit is about 159 MHz, so the diode's own 20 ns rise time dominates and you get the catalogue 17.5 MHz - but the signal is tiny (microamps times 50 ohms is microvolts). Use this for pulses, modulation and nanosecond timing. INTO 1 MEGOHM (a scope's high-Z input): bandwidth collapses to roughly 8 kHz, but the signal is 20,000 times larger. Use this ONLY for DC or slow measurements. THE TRAP: people plug it into a high-Z scope input, see a beautiful large signal, and conclude the detector is slow or the laser is not pulsing. Terminate at 50 ohms and keep the cable short for anything fast; if the signal is then too small, add an amplifier rather than raising the load. WHY THE BATTERY: the A23 cell provides REVERSE BIAS. Without it the diode runs photovoltaic - much higher junction capacitance, far slower, and poor linearity. As the battery drains, capacitance rises and you lose bandwidth silently. Check it when results stop making sense. THIS IS THE RIGHT DETECTOR FOR MOST OF YOUR VISIBLE WORK - large area, forgiving alignment, 350-1100 nm, and a simple BNC out.

DET-004needs check

SINGLE-PHOTON counting module, Si SPAD, 100 um, cooled, fibre-coupled

Micro Photon Devices (MPD), Bolzano, Italy
Plate: 'PDM / $PD-100-CTC-FC / MPD / SN: 02463 / input: 5-12V 1.2A / CE'. Mounting plate tapped 1/4-20 UNC and M6. Hand labels: '#12' and 'ch8'.
Wavelength
375-1000 nm (silicon). Peak detection efficiency about 49% at 550 nm; 37% at 650 nm; falling steeply through the red. ZERO response at 1550 nm.
Size
100 um active area. FC/PC fibre receptacle on the underside (over 80% coupling for SM or MM up to 105 um core). Two 50 ohm outputs on top: TTL counting and NIM timing.
Key spec
Dark count rate UNDER 100 counts per second (grade C). Timing jitter under 50 ps FWHM on the NIM output. Dead time 77 ns. Saturated count rate about 13 Mcps.

THIS TIME YOU ARE RIGHT - THESE REALLY ARE SINGLE-PHOTON DETECTORS, unlike the New Focus and Thorlabs units in the previous batch. A PDM is a Geiger-mode silicon SPAD with an active quench-and-reset circuit, a TEC cooler and temperature control in the box. One absorbed photon produces one digital pulse. That is a genuinely different device class from DET-001, DET-002 and DET-003, which are linear analog photoreceivers. WHY THIS MATTERS FOR YOUR SPDC WORK: you now have TWO photon counters plus a PicoQuant TimeHarp 260 (INS-001) - that is a complete coincidence-counting setup. Two SPADs plus a TCSPC card with independent timing channels is exactly the hardware for measuring g2 correlations, heralded single photons, or coincidence rates from the 405 nm -> BBO -> 810 nm chain you already own (LSR-003, NLC-002, FBP-009, FLP-001/002). THE PDM'S DISTINCTIVE STRENGTH IS TIMING, NOT EFFICIENCY. Under 50 ps jitter is best-in-class - an Excelitas SPCM-AQRH is about 350 ps and an ID Quantique id120 is 200-1000 ps. You pay for it in detection efficiency (49% peak against over 70% for the SPCM) and in count rate. For lifetime and correlation measurements that is the right trade. AT 810 nm YOU ARE ON THE FALLING EDGE. Efficiency is about 37% at 650 nm and drops steeply through the red; at 810 nm expect meaningfully less. The detectors still work there, but if photon-starved SPDC counting is the goal, that loss is worth knowing about before you blame the alignment. AND AT 1550 nm THEY ARE COMPLETELY BLIND - silicon stops around 1000 nm. For the 1550 PL bench you would need MPD's PDM-IR (InGaAs/InP) or an SNSPD. PROTECT THEM FROM ROOM LIGHT. A SPAD in Geiger mode is destroyed or badly degraded by bright light while biased. Cap the FC input when not in use - both units have their dust caps on chains, which is why. 'TD 50ns' IS NOT AN MPD SETTING - NOT CONFIRMED what it means. There is no user-settable dead time on a PDM; it is fixed at 77 ns by the quench circuit. The most likely reading is a lab note that this channel carries 50 ns of cable or delay-box delay - MPD sell a Picosecond Delayer for exactly that - or a downstream gate setting. The paired '#12 / ch8' label looks like an inventory number plus a TCSPC channel assignment, which supports the wiring-note reading. WORTH WRITING DOWN PROPERLY: which physical detector is on which TimeHarp channel, and what delay is in each arm. Coincidence measurements fail silently when that bookkeeping is wrong. PART NUMBER DECODED: PD = photon detector module; 100 = 100 um ACTIVE AREA (the largest of the 020/050/100 options, and the only one rated for 105 um multimode fibre); C = COOLED (Peltier plus closed-loop temperature control); T = fast TIMING BOARD fitted, which is what gives the NIM output and the sub-50 ps jitter; the third letter C = DARK COUNT GRADE C, under 100 counts per second (MPD grades run A <500 down to F <5 cps); FC = FC/PC fibre receptacle, over 80% coupling for single-mode or multimode up to 105 um core. SPECS: 375-1000 nm; peak photon detection efficiency about 49% at 550 nm, 24% at 400 nm, 37% at 650 nm, ZERO at 1550 nm (silicon bandgap); timing jitter UNDER 50 ps FWHM on the NIM output (about 250 ps on the TTL counting output); dead time 77 ns typical; saturated count rate about 13 Mcps, but keep it under roughly 3 Mcps for linear counting; afterpulsing 0.1% typical. THE TWO BNCs ARE NOT THE SAME SIGNAL: one is a TTL counting pulse (3.4 V, 20 ns wide, 50 ohms) for a counter, the other is a NIM timing pulse (-700 mV, 17 ns, 450 ps edges, 50 ohms) for TCSPC. Use the NIM output for anything where timing matters - that is where the 50 ps lives. POWER: unregulated DC anywhere from 5 to 12 V at about 1.2 A, matching the plate. Case 15-40 C. MPD (Micro Photon Devices S.r.l., Bolzano, Italy, founded 2004) is independent and still trading; the PDM is a CURRENT catalogue product. PicoQuant also resells these under their own PDM Series badge - relevant to you because INS-001 is a PicoQuant TimeHarp 260.

'TD 50ns' IS NOT AN MPD SETTING - NOT CONFIRMED what it means. There is no user-settable dead time on a PDM; it is fixed at 77 ns by the quench circuit. The most likely reading is a lab note that this channel carries 50 ns of cable or delay-box delay - MPD sell a Picosecond Delayer for exactly that - or a downstream gate setting. The paired '#12 / ch8' label looks like an inventory number plus a TCSPC channel assignment, which supports the wiring-note reading. WORTH WRITING DOWN PROPERLY: which physical detector is on which TimeHarp channel, and what delay is in each arm. Coincidence measurements fail silently when that bookkeeping is wrong. PART NUMBER DECODED: PD = photon detector module; 100 = 100 um ACTIVE AREA (the largest of the 020/050/100 options, and the only one rated for 105 um multimode fibre); C = COOLED (Peltier plus closed-loop temperature control); T = fast TIMING BOARD fitted, which is what gives the NIM output and the sub-50 ps jitter; the third letter C = DARK COUNT GRADE C, under 100 counts per second (MPD grades run A <500 down to F <5 cps); FC = FC/PC fibre receptacle, over 80% coupling for single-mode or multimode up to 105 um core. SPECS: 375-1000 nm; peak photon detection efficiency about 49% at 550 nm, 24% at 400 nm, 37% at 650 nm, ZERO at 1550 nm (silicon bandgap); timing jitter UNDER 50 ps FWHM on the NIM output (about 250 ps on the TTL counting output); dead time 77 ns typical; saturated count rate about 13 Mcps, but keep it under roughly 3 Mcps for linear counting; afterpulsing 0.1% typical. THE TWO BNCs ARE NOT THE SAME SIGNAL: one is a TTL counting pulse (3.4 V, 20 ns wide, 50 ohms) for a counter, the other is a NIM timing pulse (-700 mV, 17 ns, 450 ps edges, 50 ohms) for TCSPC. Use the NIM output for anything where timing matters - that is where the 50 ps lives. POWER: unregulated DC anywhere from 5 to 12 V at about 1.2 A, matching the plate. Case 15-40 C. MPD (Micro Photon Devices S.r.l., Bolzano, Italy, founded 2004) is independent and still trading; the PDM is a CURRENT catalogue product. PicoQuant also resells these under their own PDM Series badge - relevant to you because INS-001 is a PicoQuant TimeHarp 260.

POL-001

Glan-Taylor calcite polarizer, 5 mm aperture, in SM05PM5 mount on a graduated rotation mount

Thorlabs
GT5 (no coating suffix on the label - i.e. UNCOATED calcite) | mount: SM05PM5
Wavelength
Uncoated calcite Glan-Taylor: Thorlabs quotes roughly 350-2300 nm for the uncoated GT series - the widest band of any polarizer in this collection. Uncoated also means ~4% Fresnel loss per surface. VERIFY the exact range on the Thorlabs datasheet before relying on the edges.
Size
5.0 mm clear aperture (the '5' in GT5); SM05-threaded housing seated in a 360 deg graduated rotation mount
Key spec
Extinction ratio typically >100,000:1 (Thorlabs GT-series spec). Air-spaced calcite prism pair.

A Glan-Taylor is an air-spaced calcite prism pair: the p-polarised beam passes straight through, while the s-polarised (ordinary) ray strikes the internal air gap beyond its critical angle and is rejected out the SIDE of the housing. Two consequences matter. FIRST, extinction of order 100,000:1 - orders of magnitude beyond any film polarizer here. This is what you use when the polarisation state has to be genuinely clean: defining the input state for an SPDC source, or analysing one in a Bell-type measurement, where a leaky polarizer shows up directly as reduced visibility. SECOND, the rejected beam is dumped INSIDE the housing rather than exiting as a usable port, so it turns into heat. Damage thresholds are low compared with a beamsplitter cube - do not use one as a variable attenuator on a high-power beam, and never on the 532 nm module at full output without checking the rating. MOUNT DETAIL WORTH USING: the SM05PM5 barrel is engraved 'TRANS AXIS' with an index line, and that line marks the TRANSMISSION axis. Zero the rotation dial against it once and write the offset down - otherwise every angle you record later is relative to nothing. Unit A of a matched pair (see the other GT5 row); two high-extinction polarizers is exactly what a two-arm polarisation measurement needs.

In a polarisation experiment those two behave completely differently, and mistaking one for the other produces results that look plausible and are wrong. RESOLVED - this was the "UNIDENTIFIED copper-coloured optic, ON HOLD" row. The printed label identifies it as a Thorlabs LPIREA100-C. MY EARLIER GUESS WAS WRONG IN THE DETAIL: I proposed a wire-grid polarizer. It is not. It is an ABSORPTIVE DICHROIC POLYMER FILM laminated between two AR-coated N-BK7 windows (Thorlabs "Economy Film Polarizers with Windows"). The polarisation function was the right call; the mechanism was not. WHY IT LOOKS COPPER: the AR coating is optimised for 1050-1700 nm, so in the visible it is far off-band and reflects a few percent with the residual peaking toward the red - the same reason 1064 and 1550 nm AR-coated optics look purple-to-copper while visible AR looks blue-magenta. The IR film underneath absorbs most of the visible, so there is no white backscatter to wash the colour out. That coppery flash is a reliable visual tell for an IR-coated optic. NAMING: "LPIREA" = film polarizer, IR, with AR-coated windows (LPIRE without the A has uncoated windows and a narrower 1100-1630 nm spec). The "-C" is the Thorlabs coating band code for 1050-1700 nm. FOUR HANDLING POINTS THAT MATTER: (1) IT IS ABSORPTIVE, NOT REFLECTIVE - the rejected polarisation becomes HEAT IN THE FILM. The damage threshold is only 1 W/cm CW, which is low. Do not put it in front of an EDFA output (MAJ-005, MAJ-010) or any amplified 1550 nm beam without attenuating first. (2) Set the TRANSMISSION AXIS by the mark on the edge of the optic, not by which face points at the beam - the construction is symmetric. (3) COLLIMATED LIGHT ONLY. Do not put it in a converging beam: 3.7 mm of glass plus an angle-dependent film adds aberration and degrades extinction. Designed for near-normal incidence. (4) DO NOT MOUNT IT WITH SETSCREWS OR OVERTIGHTEN THE RETAINING RING - stress-induced birefringence in the epoxy and film wrecks the extinction ratio. A stress-free retaining ring is the right fix. IN CONTEXT: this is the ONLY polarizer in the catalogue that works at 1550 nm. POL-001/002/003 are Glan-Taylor calcite and POL-005 is a visible film polarizer (500-720 nm), so for the telecom bench this is the one.

THE HIGHEST-PERFORMANCE POLARIZER IN THE CATALOGUE, and the one to use where extinction actually matters. PART NUMBER DECODED: M = mounted, GL = Glan-Laser, B = calcite quality grade B (>1 wave wavefront deformation from striae; KLCC A grade is 1/4 to 1 wave, S and E are tighter), 10 = 10 mm clear aperture. AN IMPORTANT CAVEAT ABOUT THE NAME - DO NOT ASSUME "LASER" MEANS HIGH POWER. KLCC "MGLB" is the variant with NO ESCAPE WINDOW. In any Glan-type prism the rejected ordinary ray is totally internally reflected at the air gap; with no escape window it is absorbed inside the prism, in the blackened side wall, where it heats the calcite and the paint. The high-power members of the family are the MGLA-SW / MGLA-DW / MGLS-SW / MGLS-DW parts, which have one or two polished side windows to let that beam out - those are the ones rated to the ~500 W/cm2 CW / 500 MW/cm2 pulsed class. THIS ONE IS NOT. Treat it as a low-to-moderate-power part and keep it out of the Ti:Sapphire and amplified beams (LSR-008, LSR-009, MAJ-005, MAJ-010). HOW IT COMPARES WITH WHAT YOU ALREADY HAVE: POL-001/002 are Glan-Taylor GT5 (5 mm aperture) and POL-003 is a GT10 (10 mm, unmounted). Glan-Laser is geometrically the same air-spaced design as Glan-Taylor but built from laser-grade low-striae calcite with a better polish, so it scatters less and has a cleaner wavefront - which is why it is worth more than the GT10 despite the same aperture. All of these beat a cemented Glan-Thompson for power handling, because there is no optical cement to absorb. PRACTICAL: calcite is SOFT and CLEAVES - do not touch the faces, do not overtighten the mount, and do not drop it. The acceptance angle is only about 8-10 degrees in the visible and narrows badly in the infrared, so it needs a well-collimated beam. Already in a graduated rotation mount, so the angle is directly readable. FLAG: the specific damage threshold for the no-escape-window MGLB variant is not published - NOT CONFIRMED.

THE FIRST WAVEPLATE IN THIS CATALOGUE - everything polarisation-related so far has been an ANALYSER (the GT5s, the GT10, the LPVIS films). Those only SELECT a polarisation and throw the rest away. A half-wave plate ROTATES it without loss, which is the difference between attenuating your beam and steering its polarisation. THE STANDARD PAIRING: put this waveplate in front of one of your Glan-Taylors (POL-001 / POL-002 / POL-003) and you have a continuously variable, polarisation-clean attenuator - rotate the plate, and the analyser converts the rotation into a smooth intensity change with no change in beam pointing. That is a far better attenuator than an ND wheel for a 1550 nm bench. THE CATCH AT 1550 nm: your Glan-Taylors are UNCOATED calcite quoted to about 2300 nm, so they do work at 1550, but at roughly 4% Fresnel loss per surface. THE MOUNT IS THE OTHER HALF OF THE VALUE: the CRM1 gives a lockable, graduated 360 deg rotation inside a 30 mm cage, so this can go straight onto the same cage rods as ACC-002 and LEN-010 on the 1550 NIR PL bench. CONFIRM which WPH it is before ordering a spare - the O1/2 in and O1 in versions are different part numbers and different money.

WVP-002needs check

FRESNEL RHOMB HALF-WAVE RETARDER, MOUNTED, 10 mm CA - SEALED, NEW

Thorlabs
FR600HM | TP04154180 | Made in USA
Wavelength
400-1550 nm IN A SINGLE PART - visible right through to telecom
Size
Clear aperture Ø10.0 mm (+0.0/-0.1); N-BK7; surface quality 20-10 on both faces; cylindrical mount, SM1-threaded (NOT CONFIRMED)
Key spec
Retardance lambda/2 (180 deg). Accuracy about 2% over 600-1550 nm, 5% max at 400 nm

THE ACHROMATIC HALF-WAVE PLATE - and it is the most broadband retarder in this catalogue by a very wide margin. One part covers 400-1550 nm, which spans essentially every source in the lab from the 405 nm violet line through 800 nm Ti:Sapphire to the 1550 nm telecom bench. WHY IT WORKS WHERE A WAVEPLATE DOES NOT: a birefringent waveplate gets its retardance from delta-n x d / lambda, so the retardance is EXPLICITLY wavelength-dependent - a zero-order quartz half-wave plate is only half-wave at one wavelength and drifts away quickly either side. A Fresnel rhomb instead gets its retardance from the PHASE SHIFT BETWEEN S AND P ON TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION, which depends only on the incidence angle and the refractive index. Since n varies very slowly with wavelength in glass, the retardance is nearly achromatic. Two TIRs at the right angle contribute 90 degrees each, summing to 180. THREE TRADE-OFFS, and the second one bites people: (1) IT IS BIG AND HEAVY - a solid glass block tens of mm long, not a thin plate. It dominates the space in a beam path and does not fit tidily in a cage system. (2) THE OUTPUT BEAM IS LATERALLY OFFSET from the input (parallel, but displaced), because the beam makes two internal reflections. So it is NOT a drop-in replacement for a waveplate in an aligned system - and if you ROTATE it to change the polarisation angle, THE OFFSET BEAM SWEEPS AROUND A CIRCLE. That is the single biggest practical annoyance. Plan the downstream alignment around it. (3) IT IS ANGLE SENSITIVE - the retardance depends on the internal incidence angle, so it needs a well-collimated beam near normal incidence on the entrance face. BEHAVIOUR: exactly like a half-wave plate - linear input at angle theta to the fast axis comes out linear at minus theta, i.e. rotated by 2 theta. Rotate the rhomb 45 degrees and the polarisation flips 90 degrees. Pairs naturally with the isolator (MSC-005) for setting input polarisation, and with the Glan polarizers for a broadband variable attenuator.

Cylindrical lenses focus in ONE axis only and leave the perpendicular axis untouched. That makes them the tool for anamorphic work: circularising the elliptical output of a laser diode, generating a line focus, or magnifying one axis of a beam independently of the other. A spherical lens cannot do any of those. The positive half of the most useful beam-shaping pair you own. Combined with LEN-006 (LK1816L1-A, f = -13.7 mm) as a Galilean cylindrical telescope it gives 40 / 13.7 = 2.9x magnification in one axis, with the two lenses separated by 40 - 13.7 = 26.3 mm. A typical edge-emitting laser diode has roughly 3:1 beam ellipticity, so a 2.9x anamorphic expansion is very close to exactly what circularising one requires. Both are A-coated, so the pair works across the whole visible including your 405 nm CUBE.

THE ODD ONE OUT OF THE THREE, and worth knowing why before you reach for it. It is the only B-coated lens of the new trio, and that leaves it without a useful partner: the only other B-coated element you own is LEN-002 (LJ1821L1-B, f = +50 mm), and +50 paired with -50 gives 1x magnification - a zero-power relay, useless as an expander. COATING EDGE: at 632.8 nm the HeNe falls just outside the 650 nm lower limit. AR coatings degrade gradually rather than cliff, so it will still pass light, but expect noticeably more Fresnel reflection than the specification promises. The 'RM' suffix is the practical difference from LEN-001 to LEN-006: ROUND MOUNTED. The element is a round cylindrical lens already seated in a Ø1 in SM1-threaded ring, so it screws straight into a lens tube, cage plate or SM1 mount. The six earlier cylindrical lenses are bare rectangular H x L elements that need a clamping mount and manual clocking. Same optics, far less mounting work - but you give up the ability to rotate the cylinder axis freely once it is threaded in, so decide the axis orientation before you tighten it.

FLAG - THE COATING DOES NOT MATCH THIS BENCH, and it is the only optic on the 1550 setup that has this problem. The 'A' coating runs 400-700 nm, so at 1550 nm it provides no anti-reflection at all: you get roughly 4% Fresnel at each of the four glass-air surfaces instead of well under 1%, and those reflections do not simply vanish - they travel back up the beam, which is the last thing you want anywhere near a narrow-linewidth source. TWO MORE CONSEQUENCES people forget. First, an achromat is corrected at two wavelengths inside its design band; at 1550 nm that correction simply does not apply, so it behaves as an ordinary uncorrected doublet there. Second, the refractive indices drop toward the infrared, so the actual focal length at 1550 nm is a few percent LONGER than the 80 mm printed on it - enough to matter if you set a conjugate distance from the catalogue number. It will still pass light: N-BK7 and N-SF5 both transmit fine at 1550. It is just lossy and off-spec. THE FIX YOU ALREADY OWN: AC254-080-C is the same lens with 1050-1700 nm coating. Note also that LEN-013 (AC508-300-C) and LEN-015 (the Edmund NIR-II achromats) ARE correctly coated for this band - so the rest of the 1550 optics are right and this one is the outlier.

Uncoated 2 in singlet. WORTH KNOWING FOR A SINGLE-WAVELENGTH BENCH: people reach for achromats reflexively, but chromatic correction buys you nothing with a monochromatic 1550 nm source. What an achromat actually gives you at one wavelength is better SPHERICAL aberration correction, because the extra surface is a design degree of freedom. So the real trade here is 8% Fresnel loss and more spherical aberration versus an AR-coated doublet - not 'colour'. DIRECT COMPARISON: LEN-015, the Edmund NIR-II achromats, are the same 150 mm focal length and effectively the same diameter, but AR-coated for 750-1550 nm and achromatised. HOW TO RECOVER THE FOCAL LENGTH IN TWO MINUTES, using kit already in this catalogue: point the lens at a distant object - a light fixture across the room works - and catch the image on a card. The card-to-lens distance at sharpest focus IS the focal length to within a few percent, because a far object is effectively at infinity. That single number plus a caliper measurement of the diameter is enough to make these usable rather than mystery stock. Being uncoated they cost about 4% per surface at any wavelength, so treat them as alignment and scratch optics regardless of what the focal length turns out to be.

Thorlabs coating codes: A = 400-700 nm, B = 650-1050 nm, C = 1050-1620 nm, AB = 400-1100 nm. Outside its coated band a lens still transmits, it just costs ~4% Fresnel per surface instead of well under 1%, and the achromatic correction no longer applies. THE SPECTROMETER CAMERA LENS. C-coated at 150 mm is exactly what pairs with the GR25-0616 grating (GRT-001): at 1550 nm in Littrow the grating's angular dispersion is about 6.8e-4 rad/nm, so a 150 mm focal length gives roughly 100 um/nm at the detector - about 0.1 nm per 10 um pixel. That is a well-sampled NIR spectrometer built from parts you already own. Do not confuse it with LEN-028, the A-coated 150 mm.

A singlet rather than a doublet - one element, so no achromatic correction and more spherical aberration than an AC254 of the same focal length. Two things it is genuinely better at: it is cheaper to risk in a rough setup, and with only two surfaces instead of four it has fewer reflections to bounce back up the beam. ORIENTATION MATTERS MORE THAN PEOPLE THINK for a plano-convex: put the CURVED side toward the collimated beam and the flat side toward the focus, and you roughly halve the spherical aberration compared with the reverse.

LEN-037

Laser-diode objective, f = 4.5 mm, NA 0.47

Newport
F-L40B (engraved 'F-L40B 4.5mm/0.47 CG 0.3')
Wavelength
Not marked on the barrel. Newport's F-L series laser-diode objectives are multi-element and AR-coated; confirm the band before assuming.
Size
f = 4.5 mm, NA 0.47 - the highest NA of any lens in this catalogue; multi-element design
Key spec
f = 4.5 mm; NA 0.47; corrected for a 0.3 mm cover glass ('CG 0.3')

THE 'CG' NUMBER IS THE WHOLE POINT, and it is what separates this from LEN-038. These are laser-diode objectives: they are designed to focus THROUGH the window of a diode package, and 'CG 0.3' means the design assumes 0.3 mm of glass in the path. Its twin, the F-LA40, assumes 1.2 mm. Swap them and you introduce real spherical aberration - the beam will not focus to the spot the NA promises, and on a fibre-coupling stage that shows up directly as lost coupling efficiency you will spend an afternoon chasing. At NA 0.47 the working distance is very short; treat the front element as crash-prone.

The 1.2 mm cover-glass variant of the pair - see LEN-037 for why that number decides which one you should be using. Essentially the same focal length and NA; the difference is entirely in what thickness of window it expects to focus through. A 1.2 mm correction suits a thicker diode window, a sealed package, or focusing through a chamber window. Keep the two labelled and stored apart; they are visually near-identical and the engraving is the only tell.

Edmund Optics

TEN UNITS IN ONE SEALED BAG - the bag has not been opened, so the count comes from the Edmund label, not from a physical count. THE USEFUL PROPERTY: at O6 mm these drop straight into SM05 hardware with an adapter, or into a 3D-printed cell, and they are cheap enough to risk in a tight or dirty spot where you would not put an AC254. WHY UNCOATED MATTERS HERE: 8% loss through a single element is tolerable in an illumination or alignment path and unacceptable in a low-signal detection path. Use them upstream of the sample, not downstream of it. WATCH THE ORIENTATION: plano-convex lenses are minimum-spherical-aberration with the CURVED side facing the collimated beam. At f/6 the penalty for getting it backwards is small but real.

LEN-060×5needs check

Five AR-COATED but UNLABELLED lenses - part numbers unknown

Unbranded / unmarked
None - no part number on any of the five. One is seated in a black anodised ring mount.
Wavelength
COATED, band UNKNOWN. The faces throw strong coloured reflections - green/yellow on two, magenta/blue on the others - so every one of these carries a real AR coating. The colour is the residual reflection, so a GREEN residual means the coating is suppressing red and blue and is likely a visible-band design, while a MAGENTA/BLUE residual usually points to a NIR design. That is a hint, not a measurement.
Size
MEASURE - five lenses, roughly O25 mm down to O12 mm; the smallest is fitted in a black ring
Key spec
UNKNOWN - focal lengths not determined.

THE ONE GROUP HERE THAT IS WORTH IDENTIFYING. Unlike the uncoated unknowns, these are good optics - somebody paid for the coating - and they are being wasted as anonymous glass. TELLING THEM APART BY EYE: photograph each face under a white LED at a shallow angle and compare the residual colour against a lens whose coating you DO know (LEN-053 is an A coating, LEN-018 is a C coating, LEN-016 is AB). A match narrows the band immediately. THE RISK OF GUESSING: putting a visible-coated lens into the 1550 nm bench costs you a few percent per surface and adds a ghost; that is survivable. Putting one into a high-power beam because you assumed the wrong damage threshold is not.

Barrel reads roughly 'P(45)/DGT/1.3R' - the leading characters are cut off in the photo and the middle group is not certainly resolved. RE-READ IT under a lamp.

UNKNOWN. The marking style - a slash-separated coating code rather than a catalogue part number - is how coating shops label a run, so the string probably encodes the coating spec, not the lens.
Size

UNKNOWN. The faces look nearly flat, so this may be a WINDOW or a beamsplitter substrate rather than a lens.

READ THE FULL MARKING BEFORE DOING ANYTHING ELSE - a coating-run code usually names the angle of incidence and the design wavelength, which is exactly what you need. The '(45)' is suggestive: coating codes that quote 45 belong to optics designed for 45 degree incidence, i.e. beamsplitters and turning optics, and those behave completely differently at normal incidence. Photographed alongside MSC-002 (the '#23.10 B20' disc) and LEN-062.

THE FUSED-SILICA TWIN OF LEN-054. SPX016 and KPX082 are the same geometry - O1 in, f = 50.2 mm, plano-convex - built on different glass. That gives you a genuinely useful pair: identical optics, one N-BK7 and one fused silica, so you can swap them to test whether a background you are seeing is SUBSTRATE FLUORESCENCE. If the background drops when the fused-silica lens goes in, the N-BK7 was glowing. Photographed with LEN-061 and MSC-002.

PLANO-CONVEX: orient the CURVED face toward the collimated side to minimise spherical aberration. Getting it backwards is the single most common avoidable error with this form. IN THE KIT: this lens lives in the Newport 20LKT-1 master lens kit (wooden 3-tray case), which holds a graded ladder of O2 inch uncoated N-BK7 singlets so you can try a focal length before buying a coated one. NOTE ALSO that the KPX193 slot currently holds a KBX145 - a bi-convex lens filed in a plano-convex slot - so do not trust slot position alone when you pull one out; read the engraving.

Wavelength
UNCOATED N-BK7 - substrate-limited, roughly 380-2100 nm, about 4% Fresnel loss per surface. The plain Newport part number with no -AR suffix is itself the proof: coated versions of this kit carry -AR.14 / -AR.16 / -AR.18 in the number.

f = -500.00 mm plano-concave (DIVERGING - negative focal length)

PLANO-CONCAVE, so the focal length is NEGATIVE and it diverges. Pair it with a positive lens for a Galilean expander: magnification M = |f+ / f-|, and the separation is f+ plus f- (algebraically, so the lenses sit CLOSER together than a Keplerian pair of the same power, with no internal focus to ionise the air). IN THE KIT: this lens lives in the Newport 20LKT-1 master lens kit (wooden 3-tray case), which holds a graded ladder of O2 inch uncoated N-BK7 singlets so you can try a focal length before buying a coated one. LEN-090Thorlabs LSA01-A lens kit (black hard case)

Bi-concave singlet, O1/2 in, f = -15.0 mm (mounted)

Thorlabs
LD2060-A (engraved on the mount)
Wavelength
350-700 nm (Thorlabs singlet BBAR "A"). Covers 405, 488, 532 and 633 nm - every visible source you own.
Size
O1/2 in (12.7 mm); N-BK7; SM05-threaded ring mount, engraved with the part number and focal length
Key spec
f = -15.0 mm bi-concave (DIVERGING - negative focal length)

BI-CONCAVE and DIVERGING. Symmetric, so orientation does not matter. Same Galilean-expander use as the plano-concave lenses, and slightly better corrected when both conjugates are finite. IN THE KIT: this lens lives in the Thorlabs LSA01-A lens kit (black hard case) - Thorlabs' 22-piece O1/2 inch plano/bi convex/concave set. THREE SLOTS ARE EMPTY, all of them in the plano-convex row: LA1540 (f = 15.0 mm), LA1289 (f = 30.0 mm) and LA1207 (f = 100.0 mm) are missing and are not catalogued anywhere else - either they are in a setup or they are lost. Every bi-convex, plano-concave and bi-concave slot is full. WATCH THE COATING SUFFIX: LEN-041 (LA1560-C), LEN-045 (LA1304-C) and LEN-046 (LB1450-C) are the SAME GEOMETRY in the 1050-1700 nm coating. Once these are out of their slots the engraved suffix is the only thing telling a visible lens from a telecom one.

IN THE KIT: this lens lives in the Thorlabs LSA01-A lens kit (black hard case) - Thorlabs' 22-piece O1/2 inch plano/bi convex/concave set. THREE SLOTS ARE EMPTY, all of them in the plano-convex row: LA1540 (f = 15.0 mm), LA1289 (f = 30.0 mm) and LA1207 (f = 100.0 mm) are missing and are not catalogued anywhere else - either they are in a setup or they are lost. Every bi-convex, plano-concave and bi-concave slot is full. WATCH THE COATING SUFFIX: LEN-041 (LA1560-C), LEN-045 (LA1304-C) and LEN-046 (LB1450-C) are the SAME GEOMETRY in the 1050-1700 nm coating. Once these are out of their slots the engraved suffix is the only thing telling a visible lens from a telecom one.

Fibre collimator / lens assembly in a black lens tube - UNIDENTIFIED

Unbranded / unmarked (mount looks like Thorlabs SM-series)
No part number and no engraving anywhere on the barrel.
Wavelength
UNKNOWN. The element inside shows a clear specular reflection but no strongly coloured AR residual in this photo, so whether it is coated is NOT determined.
Size
MEASURE - a black anodised tube roughly O12-15 mm and 25-30 mm long, externally threaded, with a small lens recessed at one end and an open bore at the other.
Key spec
UNKNOWN - focal length and NA not determined.

PROBABLY A COLLIMATOR OR A FOCUSER, from the form: a small, deeply recessed element at one end of a threaded tube is what a fibre collimation package looks like. But it carries no marking at all, and that is unusual for a Thorlabs collimator - the F-series (see LEN-109) engrave the part number right on the barrel. THE MOST LIKELY EXPLANATION is that this is a lens tube with a lens screwed into it rather than a factory collimation package. HOW TO MEASURE THE FOCAL LENGTH WITHOUT DISASSEMBLING IT: shine a collimated beam in and find the focus on the far side with a card - the distance from the tube face is the back focal length, close enough to the focal length for a first cut.
