LEN-109needs check

Fixed-focus fibre collimation package, f = 6.29 mm, FC/PC, 980 nm

Thorlabs
F110FC-980 (engraved on the stainless barrel)
Wavelength
Design wavelength 980 nm. AR band NOT CONFIRMED on the datasheet, but the F110 series uses an A110 moulded aspheric, and the 980 nm build corresponds to Thorlabs' B coating, roughly 600-1050 nm. TREAT THE COATING AS 600-1050 nm UNTIL VERIFIED - which means it does NOT belong on the 1550 nm bench.
Size
Stainless steel barrel roughly O11 mm and 15 mm long, externally threaded at both ends; FC receptacle at the input face. The element inside shows a strong BLUE AR residual.
Key spec
f = 6.29 mm; NA 0.37 - the highest NA of any optic in this catalogue except the F-L40B laser-diode objective (LEN-037, NA 0.47). Design wavelength 980 nm.

READ THE CONNECTOR TYPE CAREFULLY: this is FC/PC - a FLAT-POLISH ferrule. Your ACC-002 (SM1FCA2) is FC/APC - an 8 DEGREE ANGLED ferrule. THEY ARE NOT INTERCHANGEABLE. Mate an APC fibre into a PC receptacle and the two ferrule faces touch only at one edge: you lose a large fraction of the light, you get an unstable coupling that changes when the connector is nudged, and you can chip the ferrite. The FC/APC sibling of this part is F110APC-980, same f and same NA. WHY 980 nm IS THE ODD ONE OUT HERE: 980 nm is the standard pump wavelength for erbium-doped fibre amplifiers, which sits alongside a 1550 nm bench but is not part of the signal path. If this came off an EDFA pump, it belongs with that, not with your 1550 nm PL detection. THE NA IS THE USEFUL NUMBER: at NA 0.37 it will take the full output of a standard single-mode fibre (NA ~0.14) with plenty of margin, so alignment is forgiving.

LEN-111needs check

Mounted laser collimator, 25 mm output aperture

Melles Griot
09 LCM 011 (box: 'COLLIMATOR, MOUNTED / 25mm MAX BEAM DIA / ORIGIN USA / 80004A 001046 79'). Barrel engraved 'COLLIMATOR 25mm' and 'MELLES GRIOT'.
Wavelength
NOT CONFIRMED. No datasheet for the -011 suffix survives online. The sibling 09LCM001 is the 450-750 nm visible version, so the suffix most likely encodes a DIFFERENT coating band on this unit - possibly 632.8 nm or 1064 nm. DO NOT ASSUME IT IS VISIBLE-COATED until you check the residual reflection colour off the front element.
Size
25 mm maximum beam diameter (the box label), which is the output clear aperture. Black anodised barrel, two knurled sections, a focus / adjustment ring, and a threaded receptacle at the narrow input end.
Key spec
Focal length NOT CONFIRMED. Input thread NOT CONFIRMED, but the sibling 09 LBM beam expanders use 1 inch - 32 TPI, which is the Melles Griot laser-accessory standard - try that first. '80004A 001046 79' reads as a lot / serial with a 1979 date code, not a spec.

WHAT '09 LCM' MEANS: Melles Griot's 09 Lxx block is laser beam-conditioning assemblies - 09 LBX / 09 LBM fixed beam expanders, 09 LBV variable beam expander, 09 LSF spatial filter, 09 LCM Laser Collimator, Mounted. That reading is inferred from the part-number pattern across surviving catalogue entries, not lifted from a catalogue page; the family and the number 09LCM011 are both real and confirmable, the specs are not. WHAT IT ACTUALLY DOES, AND WHY IT IS NOT JUST A LENS: it takes a small, strongly divergent input at the threaded end and delivers a large collimated output - functionally a beam expander, but sold on OUTPUT DIVERGENCE rather than expansion ratio. Melles Griot quoted 0.015 milliradians for the 50 mm member of this family with the aperture filled. At 25 mm expect a few times that, still far better than anything you can assemble from your singles. WHY YOU MIGHT CARE: 0.05 mrad over 10 m is a half-millimetre of growth. Nothing else in this catalogue collimates that well - LEN-109 (F110FC-980) is a fibre collimator at NA 0.37 with a 6.29 mm focal length, an entirely different job. THE 25 mm APERTURE IS THE OTHER HALF OF THE VALUE: it is bigger than every O1 in optic you own can pass cleanly, and it comes pre-aligned in a barrel. BEFORE USING IT: it is a 1979-vintage part, so inspect the front element for coating degradation and haze - old AR stacks do age. And the threaded input end is what constrains the pairing, so measure that thread before ordering anything to mate with it.

LEN-112needs checkMelles Griot FL lens set (hinged hardwood case)

Mounted lens, f = 10 mm (Melles Griot FL set)

Melles Griot
Engraved 'FL 10' in white on the barrel; MELLES GRIOT wordmark. NO catalogue number on the lens.
Wavelength
NOT CONFIRMED - no coating band is marked on any lens in this set and no catalogue page for it survives online. The faces should be checked for a coloured AR residual before assuming they are coated at all.
Size
Short black anodised ring mount with the yellow MELLES GRIOT wordmark; engraved in large white text with the FL value. MEASURE THE MOUNT THREAD - it is the one number that decides what this set can bolt into, and it is not marked.
Key spec
f = 10 mm, per the engraving. Element form (singlet, doublet, plano-convex) NOT determined - look at the edge profile.

PART OF A BOXED SET, CATALOGUE NUMBER UNKNOWN. I could not find any Melles Griot product - catalogue page, datasheet or surplus listing - matching a hardwood-cased set of ring-mounted lenses engraved 'FL nn'. Ruled out along the way: the 06 GLC collimating/focusing lenses (single-digit mm focal lengths, far too short), the 09 LBX / 09 LBM beam expanders (sealed assemblies, not sets) and the 09 LSF spatial filters (one objective, not six). One partial lead worth chasing: Melles Griot 14 KLS 001, a cased 'Laser Lens Kit', though every listing of it describes a hard carrying case with about 40 lenses, not a six-slot wooden box. 'FL' ALMOST CERTAINLY MEANS FOCAL LENGTH IN MILLIMETRES - the ladder 10 / 25 / 50 / 65 / 120 / 200 reads that way and Melles Griot used 'FL' for focal length in its own copy - but I could not source a document showing lenses engraved in this form, so it is inference, not confirmation. THE 65 IS THE TELL: a pure catalogue ladder would go 10 / 25 / 50 / 100 / 200. A 65 mm rung in the middle says this was assembled as a FUNCTIONAL kit for a particular instrument or experiment, not sold as a geometric series. That, plus the empty slots and the non-optical clamp sharing the tray, points at a system kit rather than a lens set. WHERE TO FIND THE CATALOGUE NUMBER: Melles Griot cased sets normally carry it stamped inside the lid or on the underside of the foam tray, not on the optics. Look there before searching further. SEVERAL SLOTS ARE EMPTY - the tray is milled for more lenses than are present, so this set is incomplete and the missing focal lengths are not recorded anywhere.

Size

Key spec
UNKNOWN. One face is strongly curved and the other appears much flatter, so plano-convex or a steep meniscus - but the photo is taken from too shallow an angle to be sure. Focal length not determined.

RECORDED AS 'NO INFORMATION' AT YOUR INSTRUCTION, alongside LEN-055 to LEN-059 and LEN-014. TWO MEASUREMENTS TURN THIS FROM SCRAP INTO A USABLE OPTIC, and both take a minute. FOCAL LENGTH: point it at a window or a distant lamp and focus the image onto a card - the card-to-lens distance is the focal length to within a few percent. SHAPE: hold a straight edge behind it and look through; if the image flips as you move it away, the lens is positive. WHAT THE THICK RIM AND HIGH SAG SUGGEST: this is the profile of a CONDENSER or a collector lens - high numerical aperture, short focal length for its diameter, made to gather light from a source rather than to image well. Condensers are usually single elements with heavy spherical aberration, which is fine for illumination and poor for anything else. IF IT IS A CONDENSER IT PAIRS WITH LED-001, your 6500 K mounted LED, which has a 1 x 1 mm emitter and an 80 degree output cone. Collecting that cone efficiently is exactly what a big fast condenser is for, and nothing else in your collection does that job - your fastest lenses are the two Newport laser-diode objectives (LEN-037/038) at O5 mm, far too small to catch it. IT IS SITTING BARE ON A WOODEN BENCH IN THE PHOTO. Whatever it turns out to be, put it in a case - a large unmounted lens with polished faces picks up scratches from the first thing that slides across it.

LEN-122needs check

Ø1 inch N-BK7 lens, hand-marked "LB1596A f=2.5m" - THE MARKING IS SELF-CONTRADICTORY

Thorlabs (per the marking)
Hand-written on the edge: "LB1596A f=2.5m"
Wavelength
If it is genuinely an LB1596-A: broadband AR coated 350-700 nm
Size
Ø1 inch (25.4 mm), unmounted
Key spec
THE TWO HALVES OF THE MARKING DISAGREE - see notes

READ THIS BEFORE PUTTING IT IN A LAYOUT. Thorlabs LB1596-A is a Ø1 inch N-BK7 BI-CONVEX lens of f = 60.0 mm (R1 = +61.0, R2 = -61.0 mm, centre thickness 4.7 mm, edge 2.0 mm). It is NOT a 2.5 m lens. The Thorlabs Ø1 inch N-BK7 f = 2500 mm part is LA1259 (plano-convex). So either this is an LB1596-A that was mis-annotated with the wrong focal length, or it is an LA1259 that was written up under the wrong part number. THE TWO-SECOND TEST, and they are easy to tell apart: an f = 60 mm lens is OBVIOUSLY CURVED with a thin 2 mm edge and a fat middle; an f = 2.5 m lens looks essentially FLAT, with near-uniform thickness and a sagitta of a few microns - it is easy to mistake for a window. Better still, image a distant ceiling light onto a card: at 60 mm you will find the focus by hand in seconds; at 2.5 m you will not find it on the bench at all. IF IT TURNS OUT TO BE THE f = 2.5 m LENS, that is the more interesting outcome - a very weak positive element is what you use for MODE MATCHING TO A CAVITY (cavity waists are large and far away, so matching almost always needs one or two long-focal-length lenses), as the long element of a high-magnification beam expander, or to add a controlled small amount of wavefront curvature without changing beam size. The practical difficulty is that the focus is 2.5 m away, so characterising it needs a folded path or a long rail, and the depth of focus is metres so the waist POSITION is very poorly defined by inspection. FLAG: identify it physically and re-label it. Right now this row cannot be designed with.

Loss —Setup —
LEN-123

ACHROMATIC DOUBLET, Ø9 mm, f = 22.5 mm, MgF2 coated - SEALED

Edmund Optics (TECHSPEC), Made in Japan
Stock #49-927 | bag P000001329546-21076
Wavelength
MgF2 single-layer AR, R average <=1.75% over 400-700 nm
Size
Ø9.00 mm (+0/-0.025); centre thickness 4.50 mm, edge 3.58 mm; glasses N-SSK8 / N-SF56; surface quality 40-20
Key spec
EFL 22.50 mm, BFL 20.21 mm; f/2.5; NA 0.20. Radii R1 +14.79, R2 -12.09, R3 -45.72 mm

A FAST LITTLE DOUBLET - f/2.5 at only 9 mm across. NA 0.20 is a good match to 0.22 NA multimode fibre, so the obvious uses here are fibre collimation and launch, collimating a small source, or focusing a few-millimetre beam to a tight spot. WHY A DOUBLET RATHER THAN A SINGLET, and at f/2.5 the usual answer is only half the story: yes the crown/flint pair corrects axial colour, but the extra design freedom is also used to cancel most of the third-order SPHERICAL aberration - and at f/2.5 that is the effect that dominates. A plano-convex singlet this fast is spherical-aberration-limited by a large factor; this doublet gets within a few times the diffraction limit on axis. ORIENTATION MATTERS AND IS EASY TO GET WRONG: for a collimated input, the CROWN element (the more strongly curved convex face, R1) faces the COLLIMATED side and the cemented/flint side faces the focus. Reversed, spherical aberration and coma blow up at f/2.5. For finite-to-finite conjugates near 1:1, use two doublets back to back with the crowns outward. TWO PRACTICAL LIMITS: (1) Ø9 mm does not seat cleanly in a Ø1/2 inch lens tube - it needs a custom cell or a spacer. (2) THE COATING IS A 400-700 nm DESIGN. At 800 nm it is well off its quarter-wave point and reflectance rises, so THIS IS NOT THE RIGHT LENS FOR THE Ti:SAPPHIRE WORK - use a -B coated optic there. On MgF2 generally: a single layer gives about 1.3% per surface at design and 2-3% at the band edges, versus under 0.5% for a good broadband AR and 0.1-0.2% for a V-coat. That is fine for a single element in a throughput-insensitive path, and it matters when you have many surfaces (1.3% over 20 surfaces is 24% loss versus 8%), when ghosts matter (ghost brightness scales as R squared, so about 10x worse than a BBAR), or when launching into a diode - 1.3% back-reflection is only -19 dB return loss.

LEN-124needs check

Plano-convex lens, hand-marked "UV f=50mm" - PART NUMBER UNKNOWN

Unmarked
No part number. Hand-written on the edge: "UV f=50mm"
Wavelength
Hand label says UV. The element shows no strong coloured bloom in the photo, consistent with either an uncoated UV-grade substrate or a UV AR coating - NOT CONFIRMED
Size
MEASURE - roughly Ø25 mm class, plano-convex, thick centre with a clearly curved front face
Key spec
f = 50 mm per the hand marking. Substrate NOT MARKED - a genuine UV lens would be UV fused silica or CaF2, not N-BK7 (which cuts off below about 350 nm)

Somebody recorded the focal length and the band and then stopped - which is more than most unmarked optics in this catalogue carry. THE SUBSTRATE IS THE OPEN QUESTION AND IT IS THE WHOLE POINT OF THE "UV" LABEL. N-BK7 absorbs below roughly 350 nm, so a real UV lens has to be UV FUSED SILICA (good to about 185 nm) or CaF2 (to about 170 nm). If this is actually an N-BK7 lens that someone labelled "UV" because it had a UV AR coating, it will still not transmit in the deep UV. Worth settling before anyone builds a UV path around it. HOW TO CHECK: fused silica and N-BK7 are hard to tell apart by eye, but fused silica is noticeably less dense (2.20 vs 2.51 g/cm3) - weigh it and compute. Or run it in front of the Ocean Optics USB4000 (INS-016) with a deuterium or broadband source and look for the cutoff. CaF2 is softer and slightly hygroscopic, and cleaves - handle with care if it turns out to be that. RELATED: LEN-034 in this catalogue is another optic hand-labelled only "uv coating", also with no part number. Same problem, same fix.

Working through them with the digital caliper (TLS-003) and a tape measure would convert a drawer of anonymous glass into usable stock, and is probably the single highest-value tidying job left.

LEN-126needs checkFibre / free-space coupling

HIGH-NA ACHROMATIC COLLIMATOR FOR MULTIMODE FIBRE, SMA905 - UNOPENED, still in the factory clamshell

Thorlabs
F950SMA-B. Box label: "Fiber Collimator, High NA, MM, achromat 650 - 1050nm, SMA", TP03329877, INSP 1256. Barrel engraved "THORLABS MULTIMODE COLLIMATOR F950SMA-B 650-1050 nm"
Wavelength
AR coated 650-1050 nm (the -B band). Sister parts: -A = 350-700 nm, -C = 1050-1700 nm
Size
Housing OD 15.0 mm, clear aperture 11.0 mm, overall length 31.5 mm, ~28 g. SMA905 receptacle with bulkhead dust cap. NOT CONFIRMED for the -B specifically - these mechanical figures come from the official Thorlabs drawing for the -A, and the family shares one housing
Key spec
EFL = 10.1 mm; NA 0.54

THIS IS NOT A SINGLE-MODE COLLIMATOR AND SHOULD NOT BE USED AS ONE. It is built for MULTIMODE fibre: NA 0.54 acceptance, so it captures essentially everything a 0.22 or 0.39 NA multimode fibre throws at it. The optical design is a MENISCUS LENS PLUS A CEMENTED ACHROMATIC DOUBLET - two elements, not a single moulded asphere - which is why it stays collimated across the whole 650-1050 nm band instead of only at one design wavelength. That achromatic behaviour is the entire point of the part: a plain aspheric collimator refocuses as you change colour, so a broadband source (supercontinuum, LED, lamp) coming out of a multimode fibre comes out of an asphere with a wavelength-dependent beam size. This one does not. FOCUS IS FIXED - Thorlabs aligns it at the factory (the -A drawing states 473 nm) and there is no adjustment ring, unlike C40APC-B (LEN-119) which is adjustable. BEAM SIZE: with the 200 um core / 0.39 NA test fibre Thorlabs quotes 10.0 mm output with an LED source and 4.5 mm with a laser source, full-angle divergence 0.5 deg typ. The difference is not a typo - a laser only fills part of the multimode fibre NA, an LED fills all of it, so the same collimator gives you a very different beam depending on what you launch. Rule of thumb: beam diameter ~ 2 x EFL x (fibre NA actually filled). MOUNTING: the barrel is 15 mm OD, so it takes an AD15F adapter to reach SM1 threads - NOT AD11F, which is for the 11 mm collimator family and will not fit. The lab does not appear to own an AD15F; check before building it into a cage or lens-tube setup. WHAT IT IS FOR HERE: collecting or delivering broadband light down multimode fibre - fibre-coupled photoluminescence and Raman collection, fibre-fed spectrometer input, or launching a lamp or LED into fibre. Pairs naturally with the multimode patch cords and the spectrometers. STILL SEALED - the clamshell has not been opened, so the optic is clean.

A STANDARD FOURIER / TUBE LENS. In the band-structure setup a 200 mm achromat is typically the tube lens after the objective, or one of the relay lenses that images the objective back focal plane onto the camera. THE ARROW MATTERS: "f = 200 mm -> infinity" means the side the arrow points to faces the COLLIMATED beam. Mounted backwards it adds spherical aberration, which blurs the k-space image. COATING WARNING: -A is a visible coating (400-700 nm). At 1550 nm with the SWIR camera each surface reflects several percent and you get ghosts; for SWIR use -C (1050-1700 nm) achromats. POSSIBLE DUPLICATE OF LEN-025 (AC254-200-A, recorded as unmounted): this one is the -ML version, factory-mounted in an SM1 tube, so they are probably two lenses, unless LEN-025 was later put into a tube. Test: find LEN-025 on the shelf; if it is not there, check whether this is it and correct the quantity.

CMA-25PP | S/N 012028

Key spec
2-phase stepper (UE10PP, 20 steps/rev). Resolution 0.0488 um - the finest nominal figure in the set; min. incremental motion 0.2 um; speed 0-400 um/s; load 90 N. LIMIT SENSORS ONLY - NO ENCODER.

THE ODD ONE OUT, and the one most likely to catch someone out. It has the finest nominal resolution here (0.049 um, twice as fine as the CCCL units) which makes it look like the best actuator in the drawer - but it is OPEN LOOP. A stepper with no encoder means the controller counts the steps it commanded and reports those as position. If the actuator stalls against a load, binds, or drops a step, nothing detects it: the readout stays confident and wrong. The four CMA-12CCCL units physically cannot fail that way. Use this where a lost step is harmless, or re-home it often. It also needs a STEPPER-capable controller channel - you cannot swap it onto a DC-servo axis without reconfiguring, and mixing it up with a CCCL unit is an easy mistake given the identical bodies. Note it also gives 25 mm of travel, double the CCCL units. Needs a Newport controller - ESP301, XPS, SMC100CC or CONEX-CC. The actuator is inert on its own, and the controller must be told which motor type it is driving.

Unbranded / unmarked
No maker's name or model number anywhere. Micrometer is a Starrett.
Wavelength

Size
MEASURE - bare aluminium body roughly 50 x 75 mm, drilled with a dense array of tapped and clearance holes on both faces; mounted on an angle bracket.
Key spec
Travel and resolution NOT DETERMINED - read them off the micrometer barrel.

SHOP-BUILT OR HEAVILY REWORKED. The giveaway is the hole pattern: a catalogue stage carries a regular grid on a published spacing, and this one has holes of several sizes at irregular positions - somebody drilled it for a specific job. THAT IS NOT A CRITICISM - a stage drilled to match your fixture is more useful than a generic one - but it means there is no datasheet and no spare parts. TO CHARACTERISE IT IN FIVE MINUTES: wind the micrometer end to end and count turns for the travel; read the thimble graduation for the resolution; then push sideways on the platform and feel for play, which tells you whether the ways are ball-race or plain sliding. PAIRED WITH STG-005 in the photo, and the two look like they were built to stack.

Unbranded / unmarked

THE MORE USEFUL OF THE PAIR - two axes already stacked and squared, with a central through-bore that lets a beam or a post pass through the platform. THE CENTRAL BORE IS THE FEATURE WORTH NOTING: most stages are solid, so you mount things on top. A bored platform lets you put the stage AROUND a beam path - which is what you want for a sample holder that must move transverse to a beam without occluding it. The black knurled knob is most likely a lock rather than a third axis; confirm by turning it and watching whether anything moves. SAME CAVEAT AS STG-004: unmarked, so no datasheet. Measure the travel before designing anything around it.

STG-006

Two-axis micropositioner, Model A LH

Line Tool Company
Green-and-white label: 'Line Tool Co. / 943 Kurtz St / Allentown, PA'. Model plate reads 'Model A LH'. Starrett micrometer heads.
Wavelength
N/A - mechanical positioner, no optical passband.
Size
Model A: 1/2 in (0.500 in) travel per axis. Mounting slide about 1-3/4 x 1-5/8 in with four 6-32 tapped holes; counterbored holes in the base.
Key spec
0.500 in travel per axis; Starrett heads with .001 in divisions - so roughly 25 um per division.

Line Tool Company, 943 Kurtz St, Allentown PA - family-owned since 1954 and STILL IN BUSINESS, making micropositioners and nothing else. WAYS ARE BALL-RACE, NOT DOVETAIL: hardened tool-steel slides and ball races at 60-62 Rc, nickel plated, in a cast aluminium body with enamel finish. These are the classic semiconductor probe-station positioners - probe-station vendors still list a 'Line Tool Series'. 'LH' MEANS LEFT-HAND - a mirror-image build, so the micrometer barrels come out on the opposite side from an RH unit. THAT IS NOT COSMETIC. Matched LH and RH pairs are how you work a sample from both sides without the knobs colliding, and how you keep both operators' controls facing outward. If you ever buy a partner for this one, buy the RH. HOW THEY COMPARE WITH YOUR NEWPORT 462s (STG-001/002/003): the Newports are crossed-roller, individually tested to under 100 urad, and take a 191 N load. Line Tool publishes no straightness or angular figures at all, and a ball-race slide of this vintage will show more stick-slip, more angular wander and less stiffness. Resolution is limited by the micrometer graduation, not by a fine drive. USE THEM FOR WHAT THEY ARE GOOD AT: coarse-to-medium positioning of a probe, a fibre or a detector where a few microns is fine and you want a knob you can turn by feel. Use the Newports where angular deviation matters - anything in a beam path where tilt turns into pointing error.

THIS AND STG-010 ARE THE BEST MANUAL POSITIONERS YOU OWN: three full axes, an inch of travel each, and .0001 in graduations. Compare the Model A (STG-006) at half an inch and .001 in - ten times coarser. THEY ARE A MATCHED LH/RH PAIR - see STG-010. Keep them together; a mirrored pair is worth more than two of the same hand, and they are hard to reunite once separated. HOW THEY COMPARE WITH YOUR NEWPORT 462s (STG-001/002/003): the Newports are crossed-roller, individually tested to under 100 urad, and take a 191 N load. Line Tool publishes no straightness or angular figures at all, and a ball-race slide of this vintage will show more stick-slip, more angular wander and less stiffness. Resolution is limited by the micrometer graduation, not by a fine drive. USE THEM FOR WHAT THEY ARE GOOD AT: coarse-to-medium positioning of a probe, a fibre or a detector where a few microns is fine and you want a knob you can turn by feel. Use the Newports where angular deviation matters - anything in a beam path where tilt turns into pointing error.

'-250' MEANS 250 mm OF TRAVEL - confirmed against Newmark's own ordering list. The '-A' suffix is NOT decoded in any Newmark table; every current NLE carries it, so treat it as a series designator, not an option. 250 mm IS AN ENORMOUS TRAVEL BY THE STANDARDS OF THIS CATALOGUE. Your next longest is 25 mm (the Newport 462s, STG-001/002/003) and most of the manual stages are 12.5 mm. This is a different class of motion - it is for scanning a sample or walking a detector across a whole field, not for aligning an optic. THE LEADSCREW IS THE THING TO KNOW: a 5 mm-pitch leadscrew with an acetal nut is quiet, self-compensating for wear and cheap, but it is not a ballscrew - expect more friction, lower duty cycle and more heat at continuous high speed. Fine for scanning, not for a machine running all day. OPEN-LOOP vs CLOSED-LOOP IS A FACTOR OF TEN: +/-10 um open-loop against +/-0.5 um closed-loop. The encoder is fitted, so make sure the controller is actually configured to use it - this is the single most common way people leave 20x of performance on the table. ONE OF A PAIR - see STG-017, serials 0107 and 0108, both manufactured 05/2018. Two 250 mm axes at right angles gives you a 250 x 250 mm motorised XY scanning field, which is by far the largest addressable area in this lab.

Wavelength
N/A - mechanical positioner, no optical passband.
Size
5 inch series table; 54 mm profile height; about 5 lb. TABLE DIAMETER AND CLEAR APERTURE ARE NOT PUBLISHED in the datasheet text - the RT-5 is generally a SOLID-table stage, so CHECK THE CAD DRAWING BEFORE ASSUMING YOU CAN PUT A BEAM THROUGH IT.
Key spec
360 degrees continuous; 72:1 preloaded worm drive; resolution 0.36 arc-sec at 250 microsteps; accuracy +/-108 arc-sec; unidirectional repeatability 18 arc-sec; max speed 25 deg/s; axial runout 0.038 mm TIR; max load 25 kg; moment load 10.8 Nm.

THE ONLY MOTORISED ROTATION AXIS YOU OWN. STG-011 (the Micro-Controle) is manual, and every other rotary mount in the catalogue is a hand-turned dial. WHERE THE REAL PERFORMANCE IS: resolution 0.36 arc-sec sounds spectacular but ACCURACY IS +/-108 arc-sec - a factor of 300 worse. That gap is normal on a worm-driven stage and it matters: the stage can RESOLVE a step far finer than it can PLACE the table absolutely. Use it for relative scans and differential measurements, not for absolute angle setting, unless you calibrate it against something. REPEATABILITY 18 ARC-SEC IS THE NUMBER TO DESIGN AROUND - return-to-the-same-place is ten times better than go-to-the-right-place. AXIAL RUNOUT 0.038 mm TIR is what will bite you optically: a mirror on this table walks the beam as it turns. Compare against the manual STG-011 before choosing which one carries an optic. COMPLEMENTS STG-016 AND STG-017 PERFECTLY - two 250 mm linear axes plus a rotary is a full scanning XY-theta stack, which is what you would build for angle-resolved measurements or for mapping a sample while rotating polarisation.

CTL-001

SINGLE-AXIS stepper motor controller, USB

Newmark Systems, Inc.
Front panel: 'newmark systems, inc / NSC-A1 Stepper Motor Controller'. USB socket on the top face; DB-9 female = Motor, DB-9 male = Signals. Cables tagged 'X Motor' and 'Y Signal'.
Wavelength
N/A - mechanical positioner, no optical passband.
Size
Compact grey desktop box. +12 to +24 VDC input; 3.0 A peak, run and idle current independently settable 100 mA to 3 A. Opto-isolated limit and home inputs, digital I/O, analog joystick inputs.
Key spec
ONE AXIS. USB 2.0 and RS-485 ASCII (9600-115200 baud). Microstepping 2 to 500. Standalone program storage for 1785 lines.

THE THING YOU NEED TO KNOW: ONE NSC-A1 DRIVES ONE AXIS. You have THREE motorised axes - STG-016 and STG-017 (the two NLE-250-A linear stages) and STG-018 (the RT-5 rotary) - and this is a single-axis controller. SO YOU ARE SHORT BY TWO. Three options: (a) buy two more NSC-A1s and daisy-chain all three over RS-485 with addresses SDE01/02/03, one USB host connection for the lot; (b) an NSC-A2L two-axis unit plus this one; (c) an NSC-G3 or NSC-G4 multi-axis controller, which Newmark explicitly lists as compatible with both the NLE and the RT-5 - the cleanest answer for a three-axis build. CHECK WHETHER MORE CONTROLLERS EXIST BEFORE BUYING. The cable tags read 'X Motor' and 'Y Signal', which implies somebody once ran at least two axes here. Look for a second and third box. SOFTWARE: Newmark's own ASCII command language - it does NOT emulate Newport or Parker, so existing scripts will not port. Ships with a Windows GUI, a program editor and a DLL API; drivable from Python, MATLAB or LabVIEW. An RS-485-to-USB adapter is a separate purchase. AND MAKE SURE THE ENCODERS ARE ENABLED: your NLE stages and the RT-5 all have encoders fitted. Base NSC-A1 units are open-loop; closed-loop needs the '-E' variant with differential encoder input. Open-loop costs you a factor of ten on repeatability (+/-10 um instead of +/-0.5 um), so confirm which variant this is before assuming you have the performance the stages can deliver.

MOTORISED linear stage, stainless steel with protective bellows - MTM series LIKELY

Micro-Controle (Newport) - Made in France
White factory label: 'Z18873A / MADE IN FRANCE' plus 'MICRO-CONTROLE Made in France - Experience | Solutions' and 'Do not connect or disconnect while power is applied'. 'ESP COMPATIBLE' sticker. 'Z18873A' IS ALMOST CERTAINLY NOT A CATALOGUE MODEL - Newport/Micro-Controle series prefixes are letter groups (ILS, IMS, UTS, MTM, VP, URS), never a bare Z. A Z-number on a white 'Made in France' tag reads as an internal build or works-order number. No public cross-reference exists; Newport's Evry factory can pull the build record from it.
Wavelength
N/A - mechanical positioner, no optical passband.
Size
Stainless steel body with BLACK ACCORDION BELLOWS over the rails and a removable square black carriage plate on a tapped grid. Still in its pink antistatic wrap. MEASURE THE OVERALL LENGTH - that identifies the model.
Key spec
IDENTIFICATION: stainless construction PLUS bellows way covers as standard is the MTM series signature, and no other Newport/Micro-Controle ESP family has both. MTM comes in 100/150/200/250 mm travel with CC1 (DC servo, 40 mm/s), PP1 (mini-step) or PE1 (full-step) drives. MTM SERIES SPECS: 1 um and 0.1 um resolution versions; accuracy +/-5 um guaranteed (3 um typical); unidirectional repeatability 1.5 um guaranteed; NORMAL LOAD CAPACITY 1000 N. NOT CONFIRMED which MTM this is.

THE HIGHEST LOAD CAPACITY OF ANY STAGE IN THIS CATALOGUE, if it is an MTM - 1000 N normal against 250 N for an ILS, 191 N for a Newport 462 and 22.6 kg (222 N) for the Newmark NLE. THE BELLOWS ARE THE OTHER REASON TO CARE: they keep dust and debris off the ways, which is why this family gets used in dirty or industrial environments. They also mean you should never let anything foul them - a torn bellows lets in exactly what it was there to exclude. IT IS STILL WRAPPED, so it has probably never been commissioned here. Before unwrapping, decide whether you have a controller for it - see below. WHAT THE 'ESP COMPATIBLE' STICKER MEANS: ESP is Newport's plug-and-play stage-recognition scheme (documented as 'Enhanced System Performance', later marketed as 'Embedded Stage Parameters'). On power-up the controller reads the stage's identity down the cable and auto-loads travel limits, encoder resolution, max velocity and acceleration, servo gains and home-search parameters. You plug it in and it works. CONTROLLERS THAT CAN READ IT: XPS-D and XPS-RLD (current), ESP302 (current), SMC100CC for DC or SMC100PP for stepper (current), ESP301 (DISCONTINUED September 2020), ESP300 (long obsolete). AND HERE IS THE PROBLEM: THERE IS NO NEWPORT CONTROLLER ANYWHERE IN THIS CATALOGUE. Your only motion controller is CTL-001, a Newmark NSC-A1, and it cannot read ESP and is a single-axis stepper unit. SO THESE STAGES ARE CURRENTLY UNUSABLE AS DELIVERED. Two ways out: buy an ESP302 (three axes, mixes DC and stepper) or an SMC100CC per axis; or drive them from a generic servo drive - they are ordinary brush DC servo motors with quadrature encoders, so a Galil, Copley or similar will move them once you build a DB-25 breakout. WHAT YOU LOSE GOING GENERIC: the auto-configuration, Newport's factory-tuned servo gains, and you must derive counts-per-mm and work out limit-switch polarity and supply voltage yourself. Get the limits wrong and the carriage drives into a hard stop. THE WARNING ON THE LABEL IS REAL: 'Do not connect or disconnect while power is applied.' Hot-plugging the DB-25 can destroy the driver output stage. THE DB-25 CARRIES EVERYTHING on one connector - motor phases or DC motor leads, encoder A/B/index differential pairs, positive and negative limit inputs, home signal, and the stage-ID lines. Pin mapping is in Appendix C of the ESP300 / ESP301 manual - pull it and buzz the connector out before wiring anything yourself. MIXING THESE WITH YOUR NEWMARK STAGES: no single controller runs both plug-and-play. The Newport CC stages are BRUSH DC SERVO; STG-016, STG-017 and STG-018 are NEMA-17 two-phase STEPPERS. SMC100CC is DC-only and SMC100PP is stepper-only. An ESP302 or an XPS-D with mixed driver modules is the only single box that can do both - and even then the Newmark axes get no ESP identification and must be configured by hand, with a custom adapter harness because Newmark splits motor and signals across separate connectors. THE SENSIBLE SPLIT: Newport stages on an ESP302, Newmark stages on the NSC-A1 family, coordinated in software (Python, LabVIEW or MATLAB) rather than forcing one controller. HISTORY: Newport bought Micro-Controle's micro-positioning division in 1991 for $43 million. The French operation continued as Micro-Controle Spectra-Physics S.A. in Evry and still builds the ILS, IMS, UTS and MTM lines - which is why current Newport stages say 'Made in France'.

AND HERE IS THE PROBLEM: THERE IS NO NEWPORT CONTROLLER ANYWHERE IN THIS CATALOGUE. Your only motion controller is CTL-001, a Newmark NSC-A1, and it cannot read ESP and is a single-axis stepper unit. SO THESE STAGES ARE CURRENTLY UNUSABLE AS DELIVERED. Two ways out: buy an ESP302 (three axes, mixes DC and stepper) or an SMC100CC per axis; or drive them from a generic servo drive - they are ordinary brush DC servo motors with quadrature encoders, so a Galil, Copley or similar will move them once you build a DB-25 breakout. WHAT YOU LOSE GOING GENERIC: the auto-configuration, Newport's factory-tuned servo gains, and you must derive counts-per-mm and work out limit-switch polarity and supply voltage yourself. Get the limits wrong and the carriage drives into a hard stop. THE WARNING ON THE LABEL IS REAL: 'Do not connect or disconnect while power is applied.' Hot-plugging the DB-25 can destroy the driver output stage. THE DB-25 CARRIES EVERYTHING on one connector - motor phases or DC motor leads, encoder A/B/index differential pairs, positive and negative limit inputs, home signal, and the stage-ID lines. Pin mapping is in Appendix C of the ESP300 / ESP301 manual - pull it and buzz the connector out before wiring anything yourself. MIXING THESE WITH YOUR NEWMARK STAGES: no single controller runs both plug-and-play. The Newport CC stages are BRUSH DC SERVO; STG-016, STG-017 and STG-018 are NEMA-17 two-phase STEPPERS. SMC100CC is DC-only and SMC100PP is stepper-only. An ESP302 or an XPS-D with mixed driver modules is the only single box that can do both - and even then the Newmark axes get no ESP identification and must be configured by hand, with a custom adapter harness because Newmark splits motor and signals across separate connectors. THE SENSIBLE SPLIT: Newport stages on an ESP302, Newmark stages on the NSC-A1 family, coordinated in software (Python, LabVIEW or MATLAB) rather than forcing one controller.

YOU DESCRIBED THIS AS A GOOD ALIGNMENT STAGE AND THE GEOMETRY AGREES: a micrometer on one axis, a large coarse knob on another, and a clamp positioned to hold an objective directly over a fibre. That is purpose-built fibre-coupling geometry, not a general-purpose translation stage. WHY THIS KIND OF MOUNT IS WORTH KEEPING TOGETHER WITH ITS OPTIC: coupling into single-mode fibre needs sub-micron lateral placement, because the mode field diameter at 1550 nm is only about 10 um and coupling efficiency falls off as a Gaussian overlap - half a mode field of error costs you most of the light. A mount that gets you there and HOLDS is worth more than its travel specification suggests. READ THE MODEL NUMBER off the side or the base and I can identify it properly. The logo on the adjuster knob is the best clue - photograph that knob face-on if you want me to chase it. IT IS STILL BAGGED, so it has probably not been in service here. CONFOCAL USE - NOTED BY THE LAB: there is a mounting position in FRONT of this stage for a PINHOLE, so the stage plus objective (OBJ-019) plus pinhole forms a CONFOCAL detection arm. The micrometer drive is what makes it work - confocal alignment is unforgiving, and you need fine, repeatable travel to walk the pinhole onto the focal spot. Stocked pinholes: PIN-001 (2 um) and PIN-003 (10 um). For the 10x / NA 0.25 objective at 633 nm one Airy unit at the image plane is about 31 um, so both are tighter than one Airy unit - sharper sectioning, less signal. A single-mode fibre core also acts as a pinhole, so the fibre already fitted to OBJ-019 may make a separate pinhole unnecessary.

THIS IS THE MISSING HALF OF AN AUTOMATED SCANNING MICROSCOPE. A ProScan controller plus a motorised XY stage plus a Z focus motor is exactly the hardware behind wafer-scale flake hunting: Micro-Manager rasters the wafer with the Grid/Slide-Explorer plugin, captures a tile at each position, stitches them, and you run contrast-based detection to pick out monolayer flakes against a calibrated 285 nm SiO2 background. The TTL I/O can trigger the camera or a shutter to keep exposures synchronous, and the encoded stages repeat to sub-micron so you can come back to a catalogued flake later for transfer or lithography. GENERATION: the three front LEDs (RUNNING for correct operation, TX flashing on transmit, RX on receive) and the front-panel rocker match the PROSCAN II manual. ProScan III uses a different, darker chassis. SOFTWARE: Micro-Manager has a first-class Prior device adapter exposing XYStage, Stage (Z), FilterWheel, Shutter and TTL - that is the free and easiest route, and it brings ImageJ with it. Prior also ship a Windows DLL/ActiveX SDK for LabVIEW, MATLAB and C#. Python control is straightforward with pyserial since the protocol is plain ASCII. IMPORTANT - IT CANNOT DRIVE THE LUDL HARDWARE YOU ALREADY HAVE. The flake-finder microscope (MAJ-001) carries a LUDL 99S-series motorised Z drive, which belongs on a Ludl MAC5000/MAC6000 controller. Prior and Ludl are unrelated vendors with incompatible connectors, drive electronics and serial protocols - DO NOT CROSS-WIRE THEM, you risk the drive. TWO WAYS FORWARD: (a) cheapest - keep the Ludl Z on a Ludl controller and let MICRO-MANAGER TALK TO BOTH BOXES on separate COM ports; it will happily compose a Ludl Z stage with a Prior XY stage in one configuration. (b) buy the matching Prior parts - a ProScan XY stage (H101 series, or H117 for larger travel) with the correct Olympus adapter plate, plus a Prior focus motor. THIS IS THE MISSING CONTEXT FOR PRI-014. That prism is hand-labelled "PRISM3" and I flagged that PRISM1 and PRISM2 must exist somewhere - here is PRISM1, and it is a MOTORISED ROTATION AXIS, not just a prism. So the set is a bank of prisms each on its own computer-controlled rotation stage. Someone built a multi-element, individually-addressable dispersion or beam-steering assembly. FIND OUT WHOSE IT IS AND WHAT S2 MEANS BEFORE ANYTHING IS DISASSEMBLED - the angles are almost certainly calibrated, and the "PRISM1/PRISM3" labels on the units AND on their USB cables are how the software tells them apart. If the cables get swapped, the calibration is silently wrong. Integrated stepper rotation mount - the controller is INSIDE the unit, so it needs no K-Cube or benchtop controller, only a USB cable. SPECS from the Thorlabs user guide HA0338T Rev Dk: 360 degrees CONTINUOUS rotation; 120:1 worm gear driven by a 2-phase stepper at 2048 microsteps per full step (409,600 microsteps per motor revolution); MINIMUM REPEATABLE INCREMENTAL MOVE 0.03 degrees - use this number, not the 0.0000073 degree theoretical resolution, which is meaningless in practice; unidirectional repeatability +/-0.0034 deg (12 arcsec); BACKLASH +/-0.0115 deg (41 arcsec) - so ALWAYS APPROACH AN ANGLE FROM THE SAME DIRECTION if you care about repeatability; absolute accuracy +/-0.14 deg; home accuracy +/-0.0057 deg against a precision limit switch; max velocity 10 deg/s, max acceleration 20 deg/s2; load capacity 22 N; 107 x 66 x 21.5 mm, 0.22 kg. POWER: USB BUS POWERED, no external PSU - the port is USB Micro-B and the cable must be under 3 m or you need a powered hub. FRONT PANEL: Reverse jogs clockwise, Forward jogs counter-clockwise, HOLD BOTH FOR ~2 SECONDS TO HOME; the yellow Active LED is lit while moving and flashes when you press Ident in the Kinesis GUI (that is how you tell two identical units apart on one PC). SOFTWARE: Thorlabs Kinesis (GUI plus .NET libraries). There is NO official Thorlabs Python API; the working community routes are pylablib (Thorlabs.KinesisMotor), qpit/thorlabs_apt, and pymodaq_plugins_thorlabs - all of them speak the underlying APT serial protocol. MULTI-UNIT: no daisy chain - each unit is an independent USB device, so two of them means two USB ports (use a powered hub). FLAG - DISCONTINUED: Thorlabs has moved the K10CR1 to its obsolete catalogue and the current part is K10CR2. The accessory plates (K10CR1A1 horizontal mounting plate, K10CR1A2 tongue-and-groove plate, K10CR1A3 60 mm cage adapter, K6A1 platform for prisms) are now listed for the K10CR2. DO NOT ASSUME A REPLACEMENT DROPS IN - check the K10CR2 spec table before ordering. NOT RECORDED: whether the K10CR1A1 mounting plate came with these units; without it, flat worksurface mounting is awkward (the tapped holes are 8-32 in the SIDE faces, meant for post mounting).

THE ONLY GLOBAL-SHUTTER CAMERA YOU HAVE, and that is the reason to keep track of it. Every other camera here is rolling shutter, which exposes the sensor row by row - anything that moves or flashes during the frame comes out sheared or partially captured. For pulsed sources, gated or triggered acquisition, or any beam that changes on the frame timescale, this is the correct camera and the others are not. Its 5.3 um pixels are also more than twice the area of the IMX178 cameras, so it collects more light per pixel at the cost of resolution. Two limitations to plan around: USB 2.0 caps the throughput, and 1.3 MP is modest. NIR-enhanced response makes it the best silicon camera here for 800-1000 nm work.

THE LONG-EXPOSURE CAMERA. The whole point of the finned body and the vents is the thermoelectric cooler inside: dropping the sensor tens of degrees below ambient cuts dark current roughly in half for every 6-7 C, which is what makes multi-second and multi-minute integrations usable. For faint SPDC or fluorescence signals this beats every other camera here, and mono means no Bayer losses on top. TWO PRACTICAL POINTS. First, a TEC needs its own 12 V supply - USB alone will not run the cooling, so find that power brick before planning around it. Second, cooling below the dew point condenses moisture on the window or sensor unless the chamber is sealed or purged; ramp the setpoint rather than slamming it cold. FLAG: only a serial number is marked, so resolution and pixel size are unrecorded - identify the model before you can compute a field of view.

AUTOFOCUS CAMERA - confirmed by the lab. HOW THE AUTOFOCUS ACTUALLY WORKS, because it is not what most people assume: on ToupTeks C-mount AF cameras the camera MOVES ITS OWN SENSOR along the optical axis over a few millimetres and maximises contrast in a selectable region. It does NOT drive the microscope focus stage and there is no lens motor. THREE CONSEQUENCES WORTH KNOWING: (1) Sensor-shift focusing slightly CHANGES THE MAGNIFICATION as it moves, so the image scale drifts with focus position. For any calibrated measurement, either recalibrate at the focus position you are using or switch to manual focus. (2) It only has a few mm of travel, so it corrects RESIDUAL focus error - you still have to get the microscope roughly parfocal first with the C-mount adapter collar. That is exactly why it is useful on a stereo zoom scope, where focus shifts as you zoom. (3) DO NOT BOLT AN INFINITY-CORRECTED OBJECTIVE STRAIGHT ONTO IT. An infinity objective forms no image without a tube lens - the AF will simply hunt forever. It needs a trinocular head or a tube lens in front of it. THE RED RING INSIDE THE C-MOUNT is almost certainly the 5 mm C-to-CS spacer that ToupTek ships with these (C flange 17.526 mm, CS 12.5 mm). If you unscrew it you shift the back focus by exactly 5 mm and lose focus and parfocality - so leave it in unless you know why you are removing it. FLAG: NOT CONFIRMED for this unit; if the ring rotates and moves the sensor it is a back-focus preset instead. SOFTWARE: these run standalone off HDMI with the built-in XCamView menu system driven by a USB mouse - no PC needed - as well as through ToupView or ToupLite on a PC. ToupTek publish an SDK for Windows/Linux/macOS plus DirectShow, TWAIN, LabVIEW and MATLAB drivers and their own Micro-Manager plugin. There is no official Python binding; the community `NMGRL/toupcam` ctypes wrapper works for standard USB models. FLAG: SDK control of the AUTOFOCUS specifically is NOT CONFIRMED - autofocus is normally driven from the on-screen menu. TO PIN DOWN THE MODEL: read the string on the base plate, and note which ports it has - a 12 V DC barrel jack plus HDMI and an SD slot indicates the XFCAM autofocus family; USB only would indicate a non-AF body. IN USE HERE: paired with the 0.7x-4.5x C-mount zoom lens and focus rack (LEN-121) to form the improvised inspection microscope. Kept in its own aluminium flight case.

12-bit ADC (10-bit selectable for speed); full well 20 ke-; read noise ~3.5 e- at gain 0 falling to ~1.2 e- at gain 300; exposure 32 us to 2000 s; rolling shutter; 23 fps full frame at 10-bit, 14.7 fps at 12-bit over USB 3.0; REGULATED TWO-STAGE TEC cooling to 40-45 C BELOW AMBIENT; needs DC 12 V 3 A for the cooler

THIS DISPLACES CAM-001 AS THE LOW-LIGHT CAMERA IN THIS CATALOGUE. Under CAM-001 (ASI178MM) I called that one "the one to use for photon-starved work" - that was true of the six cameras then recorded. This one is better for long exposures, and the reason is the cooling. WHY COOLING ACTUALLY MATTERS, and it is not a small effect: dark current roughly HALVES EVERY 6-7 C. Taking the sensor from +25 C ambient down to -15 C is about six halvings - roughly 1/64 of the thermal signal. The point is not the dark level itself (you subtract that) but the SHOT NOISE ON IT, which goes as the square root of the dark electrons and CANNOT be calibrated away. For a 300 s exposure that is the difference between being dark-noise-limited and being read-noise or signal limited. REGULATED set-point cooling has a second benefit: a dark library taken once at a fixed sensor temperature stays valid across sessions. An uncooled camera drifts with ambient and with self-heating, so its darks never quite match. AND IT IS MONO. No Bayer filter array, so every pixel sees every photon in the passband - roughly 2-3x the effective per-pixel QE of a colour sensor, full spatial resolution with no demosaic interpolation, and it lets you put a NARROW BANDPASS in front and integrate for hours on one line. Paired with the EFW mini filter wheel (ACC-050) that is exactly a multi-band photoluminescence imaging setup for 2D flakes. THE TWO USB 2.0 OUT PORTS ARE A POWERED HUB - they exist so the filter wheel, a focuser or a guide camera plugs into the camera head rather than running its own cable back to the PC. Note ZWO caution that heavy hub traffic can slow main-sensor readout on the non-Pro bodies. BACKFOCUS DISCIPLINE: 6.5 mm from the front face to the sensor, and the ZWO ecosystem is built around a 55 mm total flange distance (camera 6.5 + EFW mini 20 + adapters). Get the spacing wrong and you will not reach focus. Discontinued; ZWO succession was ASI1600MM-COOL -> ASI1600MM Pro (adds a 256 MB buffer) -> replaced by the ASI2600MM Pro. Keep the desiccant plug dry - the sealed chamber relies on it. FLAG: whether this revision has an anti-dew window heater is NOT CONFIRMED.

RE-READ AFTER THE SETUP CORRECTION. On a 1064-excited, 1550-emitting PL bench this is THE EMISSION FILTER, and the single most important filter on the setup. It sits in front of the detector and does the one job PL detection depends on: block the excitation, pass the emission. It passes 1550 nm PL while rejecting the 1064 nm pump, and the pump is typically many orders of magnitude stronger than the signal, so the depth of that rejection sets your noise floor. Pair it with FBP-011 on the excitation side and you have the standard two-filter PL architecture: clean the pump going in, block the pump coming out. NOTE: FLP-009 (Thorlabs FEL1500) is a second 1500 nm longpass held as spare - if you ever need to stack two for deeper pump rejection, that is the one to reach for.

RE-READ AFTER THE SETUP CORRECTION. This bench is NIR PHOTOLUMINESCENCE, not polarisation, and that changes this filter from 'the odd one out' into the most sensible item of the four: on a PL setup a narrow line filter at the pump wavelength is the EXCITATION CLEAN-UP filter. It passes the 1064 nm pump and strips the diode/lamp sidebands and any residual fluorescence from the excitation optics before the light ever reaches the sample - which matters, because anything the excitation arm leaks in the detection band is indistinguishable from real PL. The Thorlabs CP02T cage plate hand-labelled '1064NM' seen on the same bench supports that reading directly. Its 25 nm FWHM is the deliberate choice for this job: wide enough to pass a diode pump that drifts with temperature, where FBP-004 (4 nm FWHM) would clip it. Use FBP-004 only when the source is truly on 1064.

Unbranded / unmarked

Wavelength
UNKNOWN. Absorptive ND glass is usually specified over a stated band (Thorlabs' NE-A series is 400-650 nm, the NENIR series 1050-1700 nm) and these carry no marking at all - so do NOT assume they are neutral at 1550 nm.

Four filters, four different densities by eye, and not one of them says what it is. TWO REASONS THAT MATTERS MORE THAN IT SOUNDS. First, ND glass is only neutral over the band it was designed for - outside it the transmission curve is not flat, so an unmarked filter used at 1550 nm may attenuate by a completely different factor than the same filter at 633 nm. Second, ABSORPTIVE means the rejected power turns into heat in the glass rather than being reflected away; that is good for stray light and bad for high power, where the filter can heat, distort the wavefront and eventually crack. MEASURING THE OD TAKES MINUTES with kit you already own: put each one in front of the HeNe (LSR-004), read the power on the PM16-121 (MTR-004) with and without, and OD = log10(P_without / P_with). Write the number on the edge. For anything quantitative at 1550 nm, use FND-002 instead - it is the only ND here with a known density and a known band.

REFLECTIVE AND ABSORPTIVE ND ARE NOT INTERCHANGEABLE, and choosing wrong causes two very specific problems. FIRST, A REFLECTIVE ND SENDS YOUR REJECTED LIGHT SOMEWHERE. It does not absorb the beam, it bounces it - so an ND 3 at normal incidence throws 99.9% of a 4 W supercontinuum straight back up the beam path toward the source. Tilt reflective NDs a few degrees and dump the reflection deliberately, or you get ghost beams, etalon fringes between the ND and the next surface, and in the worst case feedback into a laser. SECOND, THAT IS ALSO WHY THEY SURVIVE HIGH POWER. Because they reflect rather than absorb, they do not heat up and crack the way absorptive glass does. For LSR-005 (4 W) or LSR-001 (200 mW) a reflective ND is the correct choice and an absorptive one is a thermal-shock risk. COMPARE WITH FND-001 and FND-002 in this catalogue, which are ABSORPTIVE - those are the ones to use where a stray reflection matters more than heat. NOTE ON THE NUMBERING: you described photo 4 as the absorptive set and photo 5 as reflective. I have recorded them the other way round, because these three are metallic mirror-finish plates and the larger stack is varied grey and clear glass. If I have that backwards, say so and I will swap the two rows - but check a plate against a lamp first: a reflective ND looks like a dim mirror from the front, an absorptive one looks like grey glass. 'CAL-DET' most likely means this specific plate is the calibrated one used in front of a detector - if so it is the one whose OD somebody actually measured, and it should not be mixed in with the others.

MEASURING THE OD TAKES ONE SETUP AND ABOUT TEN MINUTES: put a stable source through each filter in turn and read the transmitted power on MTR-005 with the 818-SL (MTR-006). OD = log10(P_in / P_out). Write the number on the sleeve in permanent marker. An unmarked ND is nearly useless because the whole point of an ND is that you know the factor. DO IT AT THE WAVELENGTH YOU ACTUALLY USE. Absorptive ND glass is only approximately neutral, and the deviation is worst in the NIR - a filter that reads OD 2.0 at 633 nm can be OD 1.4 at 900 nm. Measuring at one wavelength and using at another is the classic way to get a factor-of-four error into a power budget. THE GREEN/BLUE ONE IS PROBABLY NOT AN ND. A coloured coating on an otherwise-grey stack usually means a dichroic, a hot mirror or a bandpass that has been filed in the wrong place. Check it separately. WHY ABSORPTIVE, NOT REFLECTIVE, IS THE RIGHT CHOICE SOMETIMES: absorptive glass does not throw a strong specular reflection back up the beam path, so it is the safer option in an interferometer or anywhere feedback matters. Thorlabs

Wavelength
Passive connector interface - no passband of its own. The fibre and the collimating optic set the wavelength.

Key spec
FC/APC receptacle - the 8-degree ANGLED ferrule variant, not flat-polish FC/PC.

APC IS THE WHOLE POINT HERE, and it is the right call for this bench. An angled physical contact ferrule reflects the Fresnel return out of the fibre core instead of back down it: return loss better than -60 dB, against roughly -14 dB for a flat FC/PC. That matters enormously with LSR-002, the Pure Photonics PPCL500 - a 10-15 kHz linewidth laser is exactly the kind of source that back-reflection destabilises, broadening the line or driving mode hops. THE MISTAKE TO AVOID: an FC/PC patch cable will thread on and appear to mate. It will not work properly - the flat ferrule cannot contact the angled one, you get a large air gap, huge loss and a strong reflection - and forcing it damages the angled ferrule end face. Use APC cables only; they are the ones with GREEN connector bodies. The kinematic mount with cage bores makes this a fibre launch: the two adjusters walk the fibre tip onto the axis of whatever collimating optic sits downstream on the cage rods.

THESE TWO ARE THE BUTTERFLY-LASER CONTROLLER PAIR, but you cannot connect them to a 14-pin butterfly package directly. A butterfly diode brings the laser, its monitor photodiode, a TEC and a thermistor out on ONE 14-pin package, and a BUTTERFLY MOUNT is what breaks those into separate connectors: laser plus monitor PD to the driver, TEC plus thermistor to the temperature controller. NO BUTTERFLY MOUNT IS ANYWHERE IN THIS CATALOGUE. Without one these two are just a driver and a TEC controller with nothing to plug into. The period-correct Newport part is the 744 14-pin butterfly mount; the current one is the LDM-4984T (+/-6 A TEC, 10 kohm NTC thermistor, DB9 to the TEC controller via a CC505S cable). IF YOU WANT TO USE THE MODULATION INPUT ON THE 5005, you need the bias-T version of the mount, not the plain one. WHY THE TEC CONTROLLER MATTERS AS MUCH AS THE DRIVER: a semiconductor laser's wavelength shifts roughly 0.1 nm per degree C for a Fabry-Perot diode and about 0.08 nm/C for a DFB. If you want a stable line you must stabilise the temperature, not just the current - and that is what this box is for. It is also what protects the diode: run a butterfly package hard with the TEC off and you cook it. THE THREE MODES ARE NOT INTERCHANGEABLE. Constant-T is what you want in normal operation. Constant-R servos on the raw thermistor resistance and is useful when you do not trust the temperature calibration. Constant-ITE drives a fixed TEC current with NO feedback loop - it will happily freeze or cook your device, so use it only for diagnostics. GPIB PLUS RS-232 MEANS IT IS SCRIPTABLE, which matters if you want automated wavelength tuning by temperature. REPLACEMENT IF IT DIES: nothing is a drop-in. Newport's current 4 A class is the LDT-5500B / LDT-5525B family; the 350B and 3150 are the other siblings. Budget for new cables too - the connector pinouts changed.

THESE TWO ARE THE BUTTERFLY-LASER CONTROLLER PAIR, but you cannot connect them to a 14-pin butterfly package directly. A butterfly diode brings the laser, its monitor photodiode, a TEC and a thermistor out on ONE 14-pin package, and a BUTTERFLY MOUNT is what breaks those into separate connectors: laser plus monitor PD to the driver, TEC plus thermistor to the temperature controller. NO BUTTERFLY MOUNT IS ANYWHERE IN THIS CATALOGUE. Without one these two are just a driver and a TEC controller with nothing to plug into. A laser diode is destroyed by a current overshoot lasting microseconds - far faster than you can react, and faster than most meters register. GREEN MEANS APC. That colour convention is an industry standard, not a habit: green boot or body = APC (8 degree angled endface), blue = UPC single mode, beige or black = multimode or older PC. It is the fastest way to avoid mismating, and it is worth trusting. THE RETURN LOSS ON THE LABEL IS BAD FOR AN APC. Typical targets are about 40 dB for PC, 50 dB for UPC and 60 dB for APC. 36.1 dB is worse than a plain PC spec and roughly 24 dB - a factor of 250 in reflected power - short of what an 8 degree endface should deliver. TWO EXPLANATIONS, and it matters which: either the number on a cheap consumer label is generic boilerplate rather than a measurement of this cable, or the connector really is poorly polished or contaminated. MEASURE IT if back-reflection matters to you - and it does, because reflection into a laser diode causes mode hopping, RIN and linewidth broadening. That is the whole reason APC exists and the whole reason you have a 1550 nm narrow-linewidth source. NEVER MATE APC TO PC OR UPC. Two things go wrong at once. PHYSICALLY, an angled ferrule cannot make full contact with a flat or domed one - they meet at an edge, the spring force concentrates on that edge, and you can permanently scratch or chip BOTH endfaces, including the one on an instrument bulkhead you cannot easily replace. OPTICALLY, refracting out of the 8 degree face bends the beam by about 3.7 degrees, which costs roughly 2 dB, plus the air gap adds a strongly reflective interface at about -14 dB - defeating the entire point of APC. GREEN MATES ONLY TO GREEN. Your ACC-002 (SM1FCA2) is APC, so this is the cable that goes with it - not ACC-012.

WHY THAT MATTERS MORE THAN USUAL ON THIS BENCH: LSR-002 is a narrow-linewidth C-band source, and back-reflection into it causes mode hopping and linewidth broadening. An FC/PC interface reflects at roughly -40 dB against about -60 dB for APC. If you see the PPCL500 misbehaving after inserting this coupler, that is the first thing to suspect. PART NUMBER DECODED: T = coupler, W = WIDEBAND single-mode (N = narrowband, M = multimode), 1550 = centre wavelength, R5 = 50:50 ratio (R1 = 99:1, R2 = 90:10, R3 = 75:25), F1 = FC/PC-terminated 1x2 (A1 = FC/APC 1x2, F2 = FC/PC 2x2). IT IS STILL IN THE FACTORY CARTON WITH THE FIBRE PROPERLY COILED. Keep it that way when it is not in use - the card inserts hold the bend radius, and a single-mode fibre kinked below about 30 mm radius loses light at 1550 nm faster than at any shorter wavelength.

POLARIZATION-MAINTAINING fibre coupler, 2x2, 1310 nm, 50:50 - WITH FACTORY TEST REPORT

Thorlabs
Test report: 'Polarization Maintaining Fiber Coupler Optical Test Report', dated Aug.03.2013, S/N L130250278, P/N PC1310-50-APC-1, description '1310 PMC 50/50', tested by Ying Liu, PASSED. PART NUMBER DECODED: PC = Thorlabs' 2x2 PM fused coupler prefix (PMC is the 1x2 family); 1310 = centre wavelength, +/-15 nm bandwidth; 50 = 50:50 split; APC = FC/APC connectors; trailing -1 = 1 m pigtails. STILL A CURRENT THORLABS PRODUCT.
Wavelength
1310 +/- 15 nm - NARROWBAND, and NOT your 1550 nm band. This is the O-band, not the C-band.
Size
2x2: four FC/APC legs. Input 1 = BLACK lead, Input 2 = BLUE lead, Out 1, Out 2 = blue. Package Ø3.0 +/- 0.1 mm x 70 +/- 0.5 mm steel splice-protection tube. Fibre is Fujikura SM13-PR-U25A-H PANDA PM: MFD 9.0 um at 1310 nm, beat length 3.8-5.6 mm, cutoff 1.13-1.27 um, 125 um cladding, 245 um coating, 2% proof test.
Key spec
MEASURED ON THIS UNIT - I1->O1: 51.0%, IL 3.35 dB, PER 26.18 dB. I1->O2: 49.0%, 3.53 dB, 21.50 dB. I2->O1: 49.9%, 3.80 dB, 20.41 dB. I2->O2: 50.1%, 3.79 dB, 18.55 dB. Directivity >=55 dB. Catalogue spec is >=18 dB PER.

THE SECOND ITEM IN THIS CATALOGUE WITH ITS OWN MEASURED TEST DATA (after ACC-015). Keep the sheet with the part. WHAT MAKES THIS DIFFERENT FROM YOUR OTHER COUPLERS: it is POLARIZATION-MAINTAINING. ACC-011 and ACC-016 scramble polarisation; this one preserves it along a defined birefringent axis. That matters for anything where the polarisation state carries information - polarisation-encoded qubits, PM interferometry, or feeding a polarisation-sensitive modulator. PER IS THE SPEC THAT DEFINES A PM COUPLER. Launch light on one axis, measure the aligned and crossed power at the output; PER = 10log10(aligned/crossed). 20 dB means 1% of your power has leaked into the wrong polarisation. I READ THE FOUR NUMBERS AND THEY TELL A STORY: Input 1 gives 26.2 and 21.5 dB; Input 2 gives 20.4 and 18.6 dB. Input 2 drags BOTH of its outputs down, which points at Input 2's launch splice or connector being the weakest joint in the device. THE INSERTION LOSSES SAY THE SAME THING. Against the ideal for each measured split, the excess loss is 0.43 dB from Input 1 and 0.78 dB from Input 2 - I checked it by summing the output powers, and both sums are self-consistent. Same weak port. SO: USE INPUT 1. It is measurably the better side on both PER and loss, and there is no reason to leave that on the table. IS 18-20 dB GOOD? It is ordinary commercial grade and it is at the spec floor - Thorlabs quotes >=18 dB for this part. A good PM patch cable does 25-30 dB. If you need better, the current PN1310R5A2 is specified >=20 dB. THE REAL CATCH: THIS IS A 1310 nm PART AND YOUR BENCH IS 1550 nm. At 1550 the split ratio, loss and PER are all unspecified and the +/-15 nm bandwidth is long gone. Do not press it into service on the C-band. The direct sibling you would want is the PC1550-50-APC. IT IS FC/APC, so it mates with ACC-002 (SM1FCA2) and ACC-013 - and NOT with ACC-012, ACC-016 or ACC-021, which are all FC/PC.

Thorlabs CFS series - PIGTAILED ASPHERIC COLLIMATORS, single-mode fibre (NOT PM). The number in the part name is the nominal focal length in mm; -APC means the pigtail is FC/APC terminated. A collimator this simple has one job: turn the diverging cone out of a fibre into a defined free-space beam, with the focus set at the factory so you cannot lose it. THE SHORT ONE - AND THAT IS A DELIBERATE CHOICE, NOT A LESSER VERSION. A 0.39 mm beam is small enough to pass through tight apertures, small optics and narrow-bore hardware, which is exactly what you want for compact fibre-to-fibre links or launching into a small modulator. BUT IT IS ONLY 'COLLIMATED' OVER A FEW CENTIMETRES. Rayleigh range about 75 mm means the beam has visibly grown by the time it has crossed 15 cm of table. If you need to send light any real distance, use ACC-019 instead. That is the whole difference between the two. COUNT NOT VERIFIED - the clamshell has two wells and I can see fibre in both, but only one connector clearly. Count them when you open it. IT IS FC/APC, which is the right polarity for ACC-002 and ACC-013 and the wrong one for your FC/PC parts.

Key spec
OUTPUT BEAM, CALCULATED as above: 1/e2 diameter 3.56 mm; full-angle divergence 0.55 mrad, about 0.032 degrees; RAYLEIGH RANGE ABOUT 6.4 METRES.

Thorlabs CFS series - PIGTAILED ASPHERIC COLLIMATORS, single-mode fibre (NOT PM). The number in the part name is the nominal focal length in mm; -APC means the pigtail is FC/APC terminated. A collimator this simple has one job: turn the diverging cone out of a fibre into a defined free-space beam, with the focus set at the factory so you cannot lose it. THE LONG-RANGE ONE, AND THE MORE USEFUL OF THE PAIR FOR MOST BENCH WORK. A 3.6 mm beam with 0.55 mrad divergence stays collimated across an entire optical table - the Rayleigh range is 6.4 m against 75 mm for ACC-018. WHY BIGGER IS BETTER HERE: divergence scales as 1/D, so a nine-times-larger beam diverges nine times less. It is also a better match to your O1 inch optics - a 3.6 mm beam sits comfortably inside a 25 mm aperture with room for pointing error, whereas a 0.39 mm beam wastes almost all of it. PAIRS DIRECTLY WITH YOUR 1550 nm HARDWARE: it is the natural way to get light out of LSR-002 (the PPCL500) into free space, through your C-coated optics (LEN-013, LEN-018, LEN-024, LEN-029, LEN-030), and back into fibre at the far end. COUNT: THE PACKING LABEL LISTS FOUR INSPECTION NUMBERS - 1256, 1378, 1602, 1616 - which normally means FOUR UNITS were packed and inspected. The tray shows two wells. COUNT THEM; if there really are four, this is the most numerous single optical component in the catalogue after the mirrors. Recorded as 4 pending a physical count. FOUR MATCHED COLLIMATORS WOULD BE WORTH KNOWING ABOUT - that is enough to build a full free-space link with a fibre in and a fibre out at both ends of an experiment, or a fibre Mach-Zehnder with free-space arms.

ACC-020

TAPERED LENSED FIBRE, 630 nm, PM, 1.2 um spot

Nanonics Imaging Ltd (Jerusalem, Israel)
Label: 'NANONICS / For 630 nm PM / Tapered Lensed Fiber with FC/PC/PM connector / Working distance 6 +/- 1 um / Spot diameter 1.2 +/- 0.2 um'. In a hinged clear case with the fibre coiled and the connector foam-blocked.
Wavelength
630 nm, POLARIZATION MAINTAINING. FC/PC/PM connector - a keyed PM connector, so the fibre axis is defined relative to the key.
Size
Working distance 6 +/- 1 um. Spot diameter 1.2 +/- 0.2 um. The fibre END IS THE LENS - the tip is drawn to a taper and rounded into a microlens; there is no separate optic.
Key spec
EFFECTIVE NA, CALCULATED from the Gaussian output (w0 = 0.6 um, lambda = 0.63 um): theta = lambda/(pi*w0) = 0.334 rad = 19.1 deg, so NA is about 0.33 - roughly three times the NA of the bare fibre. RAYLEIGH RANGE z = pi*w0^2/lambda = 1.8 um, so the usable depth of focus is only about 3.6 um.

THE MOST DELICATE OPTIC IN THIS ENTIRE CATALOGUE, and the numbers on the label are the reason. A 6 MICRON WORKING DISTANCE IS SMALLER THAN A RED BLOOD CELL. The tip must sit 6 um from the target, aligned to well under a micron laterally, with only +/-1.8 um of axial latitude before the spot blows up. That is not a manual-stage job - it needs a three-axis nanopositioner and live power feedback. AND THERE IS NO CRASH MARGIN. A stage slip, a vibration, or a sample that is not flat drives a drawn glass point into the surface. The taper has no protective coating and is mechanically weak in bending. Keep the tip guarded whenever it is not in use, and never move an axis toward the sample without watching. WHAT IT IS FOR: edge-coupling into a photonic waveguide (a 1.2 um spot matches a SiN or Si waveguide mode or an inverse-taper spot-size converter), coupling to a laser-diode facet, near-field and NSOM-adjacent work, microresonator and single-emitter excitation. Nanonics' core business is NSOM and multiprobe SPM, which is where this came from. 630 nm IS THE ODD PART FOR YOUR LAB. It is not 810 and it is not 1550 - it is HeNe territory, and LSR-004 is your 632.8 nm HeNe. If this fibre was bought for a visible-band photonics or NSOM experiment, that laser is its natural source. Ask what it was for; a lensed fibre is a specific tool bought for a specific job. IT IS PM, so the polarisation axis is fixed relative to the connector key - which is what you want for anything polarisation-sensitive and what makes it non-trivial to substitute with an ordinary lensed fibre. COMPARE WITH A GRIN-LENSED FIBRE, which gives millimetre working distances and loose alignment tolerance at the cost of a much larger spot. If your application does not strictly need 1.2 um, a GRIN version would be far easier to live with.

Two ruled 600 g/mm gratings on a motorised turret (see GRT-002). Reciprocal dispersion 11 nm/mm (G1) and 10.6 nm/mm (G2). Wavelength accuracy +/-0.5 nm, repeatability +/-0.15 nm. Stray light 0.03%. Micrometer slits, continuously adjustable ~4 um to 3 mm wide, 2-12 mm high, repeatability +/-10 um. USB 2.0 (USBTMC) AND RS-232 standard.

NOW FULLY IDENTIFIED from the rear nameplate - this was previously flagged as "model 130 vs 260 NOT CONFIRMED". It is a CS130B-3-MC, made October 2022, and it is the NEWER of the two monochromators here (INS-013 is the older 74000-series Cornerstone). MODEL STRING DECODED, and one part of it is commonly misread: "CS130B" = Cornerstone 130B, 1/8 m. "-3" = EXTENDED RANGE grating set - two ruled 600 g/mm gratings blazed at 400 nm and 1000 nm, giving 300-2200 nm. CONFIRMED against Newport configuration data. "-MC" = MICROMETER-DRIVEN CONTINUOUSLY ADJUSTABLE SLITS. It does NOT mean "motorised" - every CS130B is motorised in wavelength and grating selection regardless of suffix. The alternative suffix is -FH (fixed slit holders). WHY THE -3 CONFIGURATION MATTERS HERE: 300-2200 nm in one instrument spans essentially everything this lab works with - from the 405 nm violet line right through 800 nm Ti:Sapphire, 1064 nm and the whole 1550 nm telecom band. The other grating sets do not: -1 High Resolution is 280-1200 nm, -2 Holographic 280-1000 nm, -4 Near-IR 600-2200 nm. You have the broadest of the four. THE TRADE-OFF, so nobody is surprised: broad range is bought with LOW DISPERSION. At ~11 nm/mm, a 100 um slit gives about 1.1 nm of bandpass. That is fine for photoluminescence and lamp characterisation and far too coarse for laser linewidth work - use the HP 70951A OSA (MAJ-014) for anything narrow. CALIBRATION: the sticker reads calibrated 20 APR 24 but THE DUE DATE WAS NEVER FILLED IN. Treat the wavelength axis as approximately right and verify against a known line (a HeNe at 632.8 nm, LSR-004, is the easy in-house check) before trusting absolute numbers. One inconsistency worth knowing: Newport own web spec table lists 150 mm focal length on this product page while their datasheet and manual both say 130 mm. 130 mm is the credible figure.

Sample holder for the MTI tube furnace (MAJ-016) - carries powder, chips or wafers into and out of the hot zone. Two units, both unopened. HANDLING - THIS MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS: (1) ALWAYS WEAR GLOVES. Bare-hand contact deposits enough alkali from perspiration to leave fingerprints that show up as DEVITRIFICATION - the surface silica crystallises to cristobalite, goes white and frosted and porous, and the piece then shatters on cooling. Standing water droplets do the same. (2) Alkali-metal precursors (Li, Na, K salts) attack quartz at temperature - use alumina boats for those, not these. (3) Cool at 10 C/min or slower and never set a hot boat on a cold metal surface. (4) Clean with DI water; a light etch (<=7% ammonium bifluoride 10 min, or <=10% HF 5 min) removes contamination if needed. Note the boat rating and the furnace rating happen to match at ~1100 C, so the quartz TUBE, not the boat, is usually the limiting part.

THE correct way to clean the fibre connector endfaces in this lab (see the warning on MAJ-022 - do NOT ultrasonically clean connectors). The cloth sits over a resilient rubber pad so the ceramic ferrule presses against compliant backing and is not scratched; a sliding cover keeps the exposed section clean between uses. THE FIGURE-8 MOTION PRINTED ON THE LID IS NOT ARBITRARY: crossing strokes sweep the endface from multiple directions so debris pushed aside by the first stroke is picked up by the second instead of being smeared back across the core; the curved path continuously presents FRESH cloth instead of re-dragging the same contaminated patch; and the continuous motion avoids the stop-start pressure spikes that scratch a polished endface. One or two figure-8s, then ADVANCE THE REEL and inspect with a fibre scope. Never re-use a cloth section, and never wipe twice on dirty cloth. The lid instruction allows six connectors per exposed section. This matters more than it sounds: a single 5 um particle on a 9 um single-mode core is most of the light path. FLAG: cleanings per reel NOT CONFIRMED for the Thorlabs part (comparable cassettes are rated ~400 applications).

BULK UNTERMINATED FIBRE - a coil you cut and connectorise yourself, not a ready-made patch cord. 900 um tight-buffered means the coating is bonded directly to the fibre (rather than loose-tube), which is what you want for indoor patch cords and pigtails because it is easy to strip and terminate. 62.5/125 is the older OM1 multimode standard - large core, easy to couple into, but high modal dispersion, so it is fine for short runs and light delivery and poor for anything fast or long. FIBRE CONNECTOR INSPECTION MICROSCOPE, handheld, with adapter set and soft case

Unbranded (generic OEM handheld fibre scope)
No part number or magnification marked

Key spec

THIS FILLS A REAL GAP. Under TLS-049 I noted that the USB digital microscope is NOT usable as a fibre inspection scope - this is the proper tool. Given how much fibre is in this catalogue (roughly thirty patch cables, couplers and collimators), and that contamination is the single largest cause of insertion-loss and return-loss failures, this should be in routine use. THE WORKFLOW IS: INSPECT -> CLEAN (with the FCC-7020 cassette, TOO-004) -> RE-INSPECT -> CONNECT. Never mate a connector you have not looked at. A single 5 um particle sitting on a 9 um single-mode core is most of the light path, and mating a dirty connector transfers the dirt onto the good one and can pit both ferrules under optical power. WHAT TO LOOK FOR - the IEC 61300-3-35 zones, by diameter: A = core, 0-25 um; B = cladding, 25-115 um; C = adhesive, 115-135 um; D = contact, 135-250 um. For single-mode PC the rule of thumb is NOTHING at all in zone A - no scratches, no defects - and in zone B, defects under 2 um unlimited, 2-5 um at most five, nothing over 5 um. (Edition 3 of the standard dropped zones C and D from pass/fail and gives measured optical performance precedence over a failed visual.) READ THE WARNING LABEL SERIOUSLY - IT IS NOT BOILERPLATE. "Do not use this microscope to look at the active optical fiber." Three compounding reasons: (1) 1310 and 1550 nm are INVISIBLE, so there is no blink reflex and no aversion response - you get no warning at all that you are being exposed; (2) the powers on this bench are not small - the two EDFAs (MAJ-005, MAJ-010) run to hundreds of mW; (3) THE MICROSCOPE MAKES IT WORSE, NOT BETTER: a bare fibre end is largely self-limiting because the output diverges at NA ~0.14 and spreads within centimetres, but this objective COLLECTS THE WHOLE CONE and delivers it into your eye. The optic removes exactly the protection that divergence gives you. RULE: confirm the fibre is dark with a power meter (MTR-008) or a visual fault locator BEFORE putting a connector into this scope, and never inspect a port on a live system. A video probe puts a camera at the image plane instead of your retina and is the safer tool if you are ever unsure. FLAG: brand, magnification and the exact adapter complement are not recorded - check what is actually in the case.

AUTOMATED FILTER SWITCHING, and it is what turns the cooled mono camera (CAM-008) into a real multi-band imaging system. Load five filters, then in an acquisition script you loop "move to position 3, expose 30 s, move to position 4, expose" without opening the enclosure, touching the setup, or re-registering the image. WHY THAT BEATS A MANUAL SLIDER: repeatable positioning so frames across filters stay co-registered; no vibration or bump of the optical train mid-sequence; no room light let in; unattended overnight runs; and machine-recorded metadata of which filter took which frame. Obvious uses here are multi-band PL mapping of 2D flakes, ND steps for a detector-linearity check, and switching excitation-blocking filters. IT PLUGS INTO THE CAMERA. The USB cable goes to one of the ASI1600 USB 2.0 OUT hub ports (see CAM-008) - that is exactly what those ports are for, and it means one cable back to the PC. SOFTWARE: ZWO ASIStudio, plus a full ASCOM driver so NINA, SharpCap, SGP and MaxIm DL all drive it; INDI on Linux; and a C SDK if you want it in your own acquisition code or in Python. MIND THE 20 mm OF BACKFOCUS it adds - it has to be budgeted into the 55 mm stack. A BUILDING BLOCK OF THE 60 mm CAGE SYSTEM. Four precision bores at the corners slide onto four rigid cage rods that define a common optical axis; the central SM2 bore holds a Ø2 inch optic (with retaining rings) or an SM2 lens tube, concentric with that axis to tight tolerance. WHY THAT MATTERS: a cage train is SELF-ALIGNING. You thread optics on at whatever spacing you like along the rods and each one is automatically centred and perpendicular to the beam - no iterative tip/tilt/centring for every element, and no separate post per optic. The 30 mm cage handles Ø1 inch / SM1 optics; the 60 mm cage (Thorlabs LCP series) handles Ø2 inch / SM2 optics and larger beams, which is what wide-field microscopy paths need. NOTE THE SIZE - 60 mm CAGE AND SM2, NOT 30 mm AND SM1. Most of the cage hardware in this lab is likely the 30 mm/SM1 kind, and the two systems do not interoperate without adapters. Check before planning around it. FLAG: LCPY2 belongs to Thorlabs 60 mm Cage Plates for Microscopy group. Its sibling LCPY1 is specifically an Olympus BX/IX trans-illumination port adapter with a male D2Y dovetail - which is interesting here given the lab has two Olympus uprights (INS-011 and MAJ-001). Whether LCPY2 is a plain SM2 cage plate or carries a dovetail is NOT CONFIRMED from the photo; if it does have a microscope dovetail, it belongs with the Olympus hardware.

NOT CONFIRMED: the backing material and thickness are not stated by Thorlabs (these are 3M-type lapping films, so polyester backing is likely but unverified), and there is NO published Thorlabs colour-to-grit table - 'Blue' is simply what this box says, so do not infer other grits from colour. Store flat and keep them clean: a single coarse particle on a finishing sheet puts a scratch straight through a finished endface.
