THE RIGHT WAY TO CLEAN A DELICATE OR SOFT-COATED OPTIC, and far safer than solvent and lens tissue. You paint the liquid polymer on, let it dry to a film, and PEEL IT OFF - the film takes the dust and the molecular contamination with it. Nothing touches the surface, so there is no wiping and no risk of dragging a particle across a coating. USE IT ON: the things you would otherwise be afraid to clean - first-surface metal mirrors, soft coatings, gratings, laser optics with burn-sensitive coatings. Lay an applicator string into the film before it dries so you have something to pull. DO NOT USE IT ON: anything with an accessible cemented edge or an exposed adhesive joint, and never on a mounted optic where the film can creep behind the element and lift it. ALSO USEFUL as a temporary protective coat on a finished surface during a dirty operation. STILL SEALED. Note this is the RED formulation; the strippable film is the same idea as the white glue in MSC-006 but is designed to come off cleanly, which that one is not.

THE CLEAVER IS THE PART THAT MATTERS. A fusion splice is only as good as the cleave: the FC-6S is a precision cleaver that scores the bare fibre and snaps it to a flat, perpendicular endface, and a bad cleave angle shows up directly as splice loss. TWO RULES. First, THE BLADE IS CONSUMABLE - it has a finite number of cleaves per blade position and must be rotated to a fresh position when cleaves start going bad; a dull blade is the usual reason splices suddenly get worse. Second, COLLECT THE OFFCUTS. The fibre scraps a cleaver produces are short, invisible, needle-sharp glass splinters that embed in skin and do not show on an X-ray. There should be an offcut bin in the kit - use it, and never brush the bench with your hand. NOT RECORDED: whether there is a FUSION SPLICER to go with this. A cleaver and consumables alone are only useful with a splicer or for mechanical splices and bare-fibre adaptors - find out which the lab has and note it here. Also not itemised: the full contents of the case, and whether the cleaver blade is still good.

Ruled diffraction grating, 600 lines/mm, 1600 nm blaze

Blazed at 1600 nm - peak efficiency sits essentially on your 1550 nm PL band. Ruled gratings are efficient near the blaze and fall away from it; this one is chosen for the NIR, not the visible.

THIS PLUS THE SLIT IS A NIR SPECTROMETER, and the rest of the parts are already in this catalogue. Here is the arithmetic that shows it works. At 600 g/mm, d = 1/600 mm = 1667 nm. At 1550 nm in Littrow (incident and diffracted along the same path), 2 d sin(theta) = lambda gives theta = 27.7 degrees. The angular dispersion there is dbeta/dlambda = 1/(d cos beta) = 6.8e-4 rad per nm. Put a 150 mm camera lens after it - you own AC254-150-C (LEN-029), C-coated for exactly this band - and the linear dispersion at the detector is 150 mm x 6.8e-4 = about 100 um per nm. On a 10 um pixel that is roughly 0.1 nm per pixel: a properly sampled NIR spectrum. The 1600 nm blaze is the reason this works well rather than merely working - efficiency peaks right where your PL sits. HANDLING: a ruled grating's surface is a soft replica and CANNOT be cleaned. Never touch it, never wipe it, never blow canned air at it. Handle by the edges and keep it in the case.

PIN-001

Precision pinhole, 2 um

Maker not marked (in a labelled plastic case)
No part number - case marked '2 Microns' only.
Wavelength
N/A - a mechanical aperture, wavelength-independent, though DIFFRACTION from it is strongly wavelength-dependent (see notes).
Size
2 um aperture in a small metal foil disc, in a plastic storage case
Key spec
2 um diameter - by far the smallest aperture in the collection.

THE SPATIAL FILTER. A pinhole this small is used at the focus of a beam to strip everything but the fundamental spatial mode: the clean central part of the focused spot passes, the aberrated wings do not, and what emerges is a near-perfect Gaussian regardless of how ugly the input was. THE SIZE HAS TO MATCH THE FOCUS, which is where the wavelength comes in: the Airy disc diameter is about 2.44 x lambda x f/D. At 633 nm through a 4.5 mm objective at NA 0.47 (LEN-037/038) the spot is of order 1.6 um, so a 2 um pinhole is well matched. At 1550 nm the same optics give a spot roughly 2.4x larger and this pinhole would clip badly - pick a bigger one, or a longer focal length. ALIGNMENT IS THE HARD PART at 2 um: expect to spend real time walking the focus onto it, and use a low-power beam while you do, because a mis-aligned focused beam will happily burn the foil.

R1DF50 | box reads '50um/1mm Annular Dark-field precision pinhole' | Thorlabs' own product name: 'Annular Obstruction Target, epsilon = 0.05, Ø50 um Obstruction'

IMPORTANT CORRECTION, because the box's own wording is misleading. It says 'precision pinhole', but Thorlabs catalogues this as an ANNULAR OBSTRUCTION TARGET, and it does the opposite of what a pinhole does: instead of passing a small central spot and blocking the surround, it BLOCKS a Ø50 um central spot and passes the ring around it. Grab it expecting a spatial filter and you will get essentially zero on-axis transmission and a very confusing ten minutes. WHAT IT IS ACTUALLY FOR: dark-field. Placing an obstruction in a conjugate plane removes the directly-transmitted beam, so only light that has been SCATTERED by the sample reaches the detector - a weakly scattering feature that would be invisible against a bright background becomes a bright spot on a black one. The obstruction ratio epsilon = 0.05 means the blocked disc is 5% of the aperture, which is the small-obstruction regime: high throughput for the scattered light, at the cost of less complete rejection of the direct beam. STORE IT AWAY FROM PIN-001 AND PIN-003 so nobody grabs it as a pinhole.

THE ENTRANCE SLIT of the spectrometer that GRT-001 makes possible - and the component that sets its resolution. In a grating spectrometer the slit width, not the grating, usually decides how fine a spectral feature you can resolve: the detector sees an image of the slit, so a narrow slit gives sharp lines and little light, a wide slit gives bright, blurred ones. Working the numbers from GRT-001: at roughly 100 um per nm at the detector with a 150 mm camera lens, a 100 um slit maps to about 1 nm of spectral width, a 50 um slit to about 0.5 nm. That is the whole trade in one line, and having a MICROMETER drive rather than fixed slits is what lets you tune it during a measurement instead of committing up front. The micrometer also makes the setting repeatable and recordable - write the drum reading in your notes alongside the spectrum, because a spectrum without its slit width is not reproducible.

Newport Corporation
White label reads 'Newport Corporation'. No catalogue number is visible on the plate. Newport's glass USAF target is RES-1 - LIKELY but NOT CONFIRMED (see notes).
Wavelength
N/A - a chrome-on-glass amplitude pattern, not a spectral component. It works at any wavelength the substrate transmits; the glass sets that, roughly 380-2100 nm if it is standard optical glass.
Size
50 x 50 x 1.5 mm (2 x 2 in) plate - matches Newport's RES-1 geometry. Fits a Newport FH-2 / FH-2S filter holder. Surface shows scratches and handling marks; the chrome is soft, so treat the patterned face as the delicate side.
Key spec
Groups roughly -2 through 7, elements 1-6 - so about 0.25 to 228 line pairs per mm. Newport publishes RES-1 as groups 0-7 (1.00-228.10 lp/mm); the low negative groups on this plate are NOT in that published range, which is one reason the part number is unconfirmed.

WAS NOT PREVIOUSLY IN THE CATALOGUE - this is a new entry. The only thing close was PIN-002 (R1DF50), which is an annular obstruction target and a completely different object. HOW TO READ IT: spatial frequency in line pairs per mm is 2^(G + (E-1)/6), where G is the group number and E the element. Bar width in micrometres is 500 divided by that. Group 7 element 6 = 228.1 lp/mm = 2.19 um bars; group 6 element 1 = 64 lp/mm = 7.81 um; group 0 element 1 = 1 lp/mm = 500 um. Six elements is exactly one octave, each step a factor of 2^(1/6) = 1.1225. WHAT IT IS FOR IN YOUR LAB: this is how you measure the ACTUAL resolution of an imaging path rather than trusting the objective's NA. Image the target, find the finest group where the three bars are still separately visible, and read off the lp/mm. Compare against the Rayleigh limit 0.61*lambda/NA: your OBJ-002 (60x, NA 0.75) should reach about 2200 lp/mm at 550 nm, far beyond this target - so at 2 um minimum bar width this plate CANNOT characterise your high-NA objectives. It is well matched to low-NA work: OBJ-007 (5x, NA 0.12) resolves about 350 lp/mm, and camera-lens or relay testing sits comfortably inside its range. PIXEL-LIMITED, NOT OPTICS-LIMITED, IS THE USUAL ANSWER: with 2.4 um pixels (CAM-001/002/003) you need at least two pixels per line pair, so the sensor caps you near 200 lp/mm at the sensor plane no matter how good the optics are. That is almost exactly this target's top group, which makes it a good match to your cameras. POSITIVE OR NEGATIVE IS NOT DETERMINED, AND IT MATTERS. Newport's RES-1 is a NEGATIVE: clear bars in an opaque chrome field, for back-lit transmission. If your plate is chrome bars on clear glass it is a POSITIVE and it is NOT an RES-1 - Newport does not currently list a positive glass USAF target. THE TEST TAKES FIVE SECONDS: hold it up to a lamp. If most of the plate blocks the light and the bars glow through, it is negative. If most of it transmits and the bars are dark, it is positive. EQUIVALENTS IF YOU NEED A SECOND ONE: Edmund #38-256 (2 x 2 in negative) and #38-255 (positive) are the same geometry and substrate; Thorlabs R1DS1N / R1DS1P are the O1 in versions, groups 2-7.

THESE ARE NOT LOOSE OPTICS - they live inside INS-014 and are selected by motor, so they are catalogued here only so the instrument capability is searchable. Do not go looking for them in a drawer. WHY TWO GRATINGS WITH THE SAME LINE DENSITY: the groove density sets the DISPERSION and the blaze sets where the EFFICIENCY PEAKS. Both are 600 g/mm so both disperse the same, but G1 peaks in the near-UV/blue and G2 peaks in the near-infrared. You switch gratings not to change resolution but to stay near peak efficiency - using the 400 nm grating out at 1600 nm would work geometrically and throw away most of your light. RULE OF THUMB: a blazed grating is usefully efficient roughly from 2/3 to 2x its blaze wavelength. So G1 covers about 270-800 nm and G2 about 670-2000 nm, which is exactly how the 300-2200 nm system figure is built. Crossover is around 700-800 nm - if you scan across that region, check which grating is selected. WATCH FOR SECOND ORDER: at 600 g/mm, light at 800 nm appears in first order at the same angle as 400 nm in second order. When measuring above roughly 800 nm with a broadband source you need an order-sorting longpass filter in front of the entrance slit or you will record a phantom peak. This catalogue has suitable filters - FLP-016 (700 nm cut-on), FLP-017 (550 nm), FLP-011 (900 nm) and FLP-015 (1500 nm). SEPARATE FROM GRT-001, which is a loose Thorlabs GR25-0616 (600 g/mm, 1600 nm blaze) you can build with.

RECORDED AS UNIDENTIFIED rather than guessed. WHAT THE PHOTO ACTUALLY SHOWS: an optic with a violet-reflecting coating, mounted in a graduated ROTATION mount fitted with a vernier index - and that last detail is the most informative thing here. YOU DO NOT PUT AN OPTIC IN A GRADUATED ROTATION MOUNT UNLESS ITS ORIENTATION ABOUT THE BEAM AXIS MATTERS. That rules out plain lenses, windows, mirrors and most filters, and points at a POLARIZER or a WAVEPLATE. The vernier suggests someone cared about setting the angle to better than a degree, which leans toward a waveplate (where you set a specific angle relative to the fast axis) rather than a polarizer used as a simple on/off. HOW TO SETTLE IT IN TWO MINUTES: put it between two crossed polarizers (POL-001/002 are Glan-Taylors) and rotate it. A POLARIZER will null completely twice per revolution. A HALF-WAVE PLATE will pass light with four nulls per revolution as it rotates the polarisation. A QUARTER-WAVE PLATE will never fully null once you are off the axes. A plain window or filter will do nothing at all. Then check transmission at 633 nm versus 1550 nm to pin the band. Once identified, this row should be re-filed under Polarizers or Waveplates and given a proper label with the printer (TLS-024).

MSC-005needs check

FREE-SPACE FARADAY OPTICAL ISOLATOR, 780 nm, Ø5 mm - SEALED, NEW

Thorlabs
IO-5-780-VLP | S/N TP04169155-2
Wavelength
Centre 780 nm; full range 740-820 nm; tuning range 760-800 nm (rotate the analyser to recover peak isolation)
Size
5 mm clear aperture, Ø4.7 mm max beam; cylindrical housing, 0.18 kg
Key spec
ISOLATION 35 dB typical at centre; transmission ~90% (NOT CONFIRMED); max power 1.7 W; power density limits 25 W/cm2 blocking, 100 W/cm2 transmission. POLARIZATION-DEPENDENT design

A ONE-WAY VALVE FOR LIGHT - high transmission forward, about 35 dB attenuation backward. This protects a laser from its own back-reflections, and it is not a luxury: diode lasers and ECDLs at 780 nm are acutely sensitive to feedback. As little as 1e-4 of the output returning into the cavity causes MODE HOPPING, linewidth broadening, frequency pulling, excess amplitude noise, and at worse levels chaotic coherence collapse or physical damage to the diode facet. Every downstream surface - fibre tips, cell windows, AOMs, even a detector face - sends something back. HOW IT WORKS, because the non-reciprocity is the whole trick: input polarizer, then a Faraday rotator (magneto-optic crystal in a permanent axial magnetic field) that rotates the polarisation 45 degrees, then an analyser set at 45 degrees which passes it. The rotation direction is set by the MAGNETIC FIELD, not by the propagation direction - so returning light gets another +45 degrees in the same absolute sense rather than having it undone, arrives at the input polarizer at 90 degrees, and is rejected. A waveplate cannot do this: a waveplate is reciprocal and simply undoes itself on the return trip. THREE PRACTICAL POINTS: (1) IT HAS A DIRECTION. There is an arrow on the housing and the beam must go that way. Installed backwards it still transmits, but you get NO isolation in the direction you care about - you have fitted an expensive pair of polarizers. (2) THE INPUT MUST BE LINEARLY POLARISED AND ALIGNED to the input polarizer. Rotate the isolator body, or put a half-wave plate in front (the FR600HM, MSC-006, would do it). Misalignment costs transmission as cos-squared - it does not cost isolation, so you can quietly throw away most of your power without noticing. (3) RESPECT THE 1.7 W AND THE POWER-DENSITY LIMITS - thermal lensing and depolarisation in the rotator degrade isolation well before anything is damaged. PART NUMBER: IO = free-space optical isolator, 5 = 5 mm aperture, 780 = centre wavelength, VLP = Very Low Power polarizer type (siblings are LP and HP). Still sealed in its bag with hex keys.

FLAG - DO NOT ASSUME THIS IS A LENS. From the photograph the central element looks like a RING with an open hole through it, which would make it an APERTURE or a spacer, not a lens; but a small lens seen at an angle can look the same. THE TEST IS TEN SECONDS: hold it up to a distant window. If you see an inverted image, it is a positive lens - then measure the focal length by projecting that window onto a wall. If you just see a bright hole with no image, it is an aperture and what matters is the hole diameter, so measure it with calipers. If you can see a curved surface but no image forms, it is negative. WRITE THE ANSWER INTO THIS ENTRY. ABOUT THE GLUE, which matters more than the identification: the white fillet is untidy, has run onto the face, and is NOT how a commercial optic is mounted - a factory optic is held by a threaded retaining ring, not adhesive. So this is a lab-made assembly. TWO CONSEQUENCES. First, DO NOT PUT IT IN SOLVENT to clean it - if the adhesive is Crystalbond (TLS-039) it dissolves in acetone, and if it is a UV glue (TLS-036) acetone will attack the joint over time; either way the element falls out and whatever alignment it had is gone. Clean the optical surface only, with lens tissue, and keep solvent off the fillet. Second, the glue is a THERMAL and OUTGASSING liability - do not use it near a hotplate, and do not put it in the vacuum desiccator (MAJ-020) or any pumped setup. PROVENANCE: photographed in the same batch as the two K10CR1 rotation mounts (STG-023, STG-024) and the PRISM3 assembly (PRI-014), all on the same bench. It is plausible that this threads into one of the K10CR1 SM1 bores and belongs to that same setup - but that is INFERENCE from the photographs, not something anyone told me. Ask whoever owns the prism setup.

This is the electronics for two nanoindentation options, and it is an OEM-badged DSP lock-in underneath. CSM = Continuous Stiffness Measurement: a small sinusoidal oscillation is superimposed on the indenter load and the lock-in recovers the contact stiffness, so hardness and modulus come out CONTINUOUSLY versus depth from a single indent instead of one value per indent. The Axiophot is the PHOTOMICROSCOPE member of the Axioplan family: same universal research stand, but with the integrated photomicrographic system (camera port with automatic exposure metering electronics). Supports brightfield, darkfield, phase contrast, polarisation, Nomarski DIC and epifluorescence. OBJECTIVES FITTED (read off the nosepiece): Zeiss Epiplan-NEOFLUAR 5x/0.15 HD (cat. 44 23 24, red ring), a Zeiss Epiplan-Neofluar 100x, and a Zeiss EC Epiplan-Neofluar 10x (yellow ring). "Epiplan" = flat-field objective computed for REFLECTED (incident) light and used WITHOUT a coverslip - correct for chips, wafers and bare samples. "NEOFLUAR" = fluorite / semi-apochromat correction class. "HD" = Hellfeld/Dunkelfeld (brightfield AND darkfield, the German equivalent of "BD") - these carry the outer illuminating annulus, so darkfield works on them; non-HD Epiplan-Neofluars are brightfield/DIC only. MAGNIFICATION WARNING: Zeiss ICS uses a 164.5 mm tube lens, NOT the 200 mm of Thorlabs/Mitutoyo or the 180 mm of Olympus. If you move a Zeiss objective onto another brand of tube lens the actual magnification becomes M x (f_tube_actual / 164.5) - e.g. a Zeiss 100x behind a 200 mm tube lens gives 122x, not 100x. The reverse applies to the Olympus objectives (OBJ-020) on this stand. Two INDEPENDENT functions with separate ON/OFF buttons: the heater (SET C target vs ACTUAL C live tank reading, thermostatic closed loop) and the ultrasound (Minute/Second countdown, default 5 min). So you can pre-heat without cavitation, or sonicate cold. NEVER run either with a dry tank - dry-firing kills the heater and the transducers. Practical note: the 110 C setpoint range is a controller limit, not an achievable water temperature; VEVOR recommends 50-60 C. CAUTIONS THAT MATTER IN THIS LAB: (1) NEVER ultrasonically clean CEMENTED optics - achromatic doublets, triplets, cemented beamsplitter cubes. Cavitation plus heat attacks the cement line and delaminates them; this is the classic way to destroy a doublet. Same for anything epoxied into a cell. (2) Bare-metal coatings (Al, Ag, Au) and soft dielectric stacks can be pitted or lifted - test on a sacrificial part, lowest power, shortest time, and never rest a part on the tank floor above a transducer. (3) DO NOT use it on FIBRE CONNECTORS - ultrasonics loosen the ferrule epoxy and drive contaminated water into the connector body. Use the FCC-7020 cassette cleaner (TOO-004) instead. Bare ferrules, adapters and metal hardware are fine. (4) NEVER pour flammable solvent into the tank (acetone, IPA, methanol, toluene, hexane) - cavitation aerosolises it and the heater and transducer wiring are ignition sources. If you need solvent, suspend a GLASS OR PTFE BEAKER of it in a plain-water bath. Also keep chlorides and bleach out - they pit 304 stainless. STIR AND HEAT - the top plate heats and a magnet underneath spins the PTFE stir bar in the vessel. THE REASON THE LAB WANTS ONE is dissolving the transfer polymers: PPC in anisole (CHM-003 + CHM-001) and especially PC in chloroform (CHM-013 + CHM-012) take hours of stirring to go into solution properly, and a hand-shaken bottle gives you lumps and an inconsistent wt%, which changes the film thickness and the transfer yield. SAFETY, AND THIS IS NOT OPTIONAL FOR THE CHLOROFORM RECIPE: chloroform boils at 61 C and is toxic by inhalation with an OSHA CEILING of 50 ppm. DO NOT HEAT CHLOROFORM ON THIS, AND DO NOT USE IT OUTSIDE A FUME HOOD. Stir the PC solution COLD, in a capped bottle, in the hood. Heat is for the anisole route and for aqueous work. TWO GENERAL WARNINGS. The HEAT indicator tells you the heater is drawing power, NOT that the plate is cool when it is off - the plate stays dangerously hot for a long time after switching off, and there is no temperature readout on this unit at all, so you cannot know the plate temperature without an IR thermometer or a surface probe. And an uncalibrated knob-only hotplate can overshoot badly; if a protocol needs a specific temperature (the PC pickup at 60-90 C, release at 150 C), measure it, do not trust the dial. NOT CONFIRMED: maximum plate temperature, stir speed range and heater wattage - no model number was visible to look them up. Read the rear or underside label and add them here.

RACK POWER DISTRIBUTION PANEL with sequenced outlet banks and remote control

Optima EPS (Optima Enclosures - an Elma Electronic company, Tucker GA)
PDS-115-60
Wavelength

Key spec
Eight SWITCHED outlets in two banks of four (SWITCHED 1 / SWITCHED 2) plus four UNSWITCHED; front ON/OFF paddle, large breaker knob, LOCAL/REMOTE selector, and three 3-terminal barrier blocks labelled REMOTE I/O and SEQUENCED

Powers the instrument rack. THE POINT OF THE SEQUENCING: the two SWITCHED banks energise in order, a fraction of a second apart, rather than all at once. That does two things - it keeps aggregate INRUSH CURRENT from tripping the upstream breaker when a rack full of switching supplies starts together, and it enforces a TURN-ON ORDER (and the reverse on shutdown) so sources come up before amplifiers. The UNSWITCHED bank is always live off the breaker - that is where anything that must never be power-cycled belongs. LOCAL/REMOTE selects whether the front paddle or an external contact closure has control; the three-terminal blocks are the dry-contact interface, and a group of three is consistent with daisy-chaining trigger-in / trigger-out / common to another panel. FLAG - DO NOT ASSUME A CURRENT RATING: no datasheet, catalogue page or manual for PDS-115-60 exists in any accessible source, so the "115-60" decode is NOT CONFIRMED (115 V / 60 Hz is the more plausible reading than 60 A, since a 60 A panel would not use standard 5-15 duplex outlets). READ THE BREAKER KNOB AND THE NAMEPLATE before loading it, and check terminal polarity/voltage before wiring anything to the REMOTE I/O. Note also a naming collision: Marway Power Solutions sells an unrelated PDU line also branded "Optima".

RECORDED AS ONE LOT rather than separately - these are consumables, not instruments. THE PASTE is lead-free, no-clean, low-temperature, in a syringe with a fine needle, which is the form you want for hand-placing SMD parts and for BGA rework. TWO THINGS TO KNOW: solder paste has a SHELF LIFE and should be refrigerated - unrefrigerated paste separates and the flux goes off, and old paste gives cold joints and solder balls. Check the date before trusting it on anything that matters. And 'no-clean' means the residue is designed to be left, but it is still slightly hygroscopic, so wash it off anything carrying high impedance or sitting in a humid environment. THE WICK (desoldering braid) is flux-impregnated copper braid: lay it on the joint, press with the iron, and capillary action pulls the molten solder into the braid. Cut off and discard the used length - a saturated end will not wick. 2.5 mm is a general-purpose width, good for through-hole and most SMD pads. NOT RECORDED: paste alloy composition and exact melting point, and the manufacture date. Both are on the syringe body - read them before use.

THREE THINGS TO FLAG BEFORE ANYONE PLUGS IT IN. (1) IT IS 2.4 GHz ONLY - it will not join a 5 GHz-only network, which trips people up on modern campus WiFi. (2) IT IS A CLOUD CAMERA. The box advertises a cloud service, meaning video from inside the lab goes to a third-party server, usually in China, on an unbranded OEM app. DO NOT POINT IT AT ANYTHING YOU WOULD NOT POST PUBLICLY - whiteboards, screens, sample labels, unpublished data - and check with MIT IS&T before putting it on a campus network at all. (3) It has motion detection, which is genuinely useful for an alarm on an experiment, but it is motion in the IMAGE, not a real sensor. POSSIBLE DUPLICATE - FLAG: two box photographs were taken ('Small Size Big Eyes' side and 'Mini Camera' face). They are almost certainly the SAME box photographed twice, and are recorded as one unit; if there are in fact two cameras, correct the quantity. UNOPENED.

You said you did not know what it is called, and I cannot confirm it from the photo either - it is one of two things, and they are used differently: (a) CLOTH HARNESS TAPE (also called fabric or friction tape) - an adhesive-backed woven tape used to wrap cable bundles. It is quiet, does not go sticky and gummy the way PVC tape does in heat, and is the standard automotive/instrument way to dress a loom. Test: it will have adhesive on one face. (b) BRAIDED EXPANDABLE SLEEVING - a woven PET tube that slides over a bundle and expands; no adhesive, and the weave opens out when you compress it lengthwise. CHECK WHICH IT IS by feeling for adhesive on one side and trying to push the ends together. Both do the same job of tidying and protecting cable runs; the sleeving needs the cable ends free to thread it on, the tape does not.

THIS ONE IS NOT JUST OFFICE TAPE - it is the tape most commonly named in published 2D-material method sections for MECHANICAL EXFOLIATION of graphene, hBN and TMDs. That makes it a research consumable in this lab, feeding the flake-finder microscope (MAJ-001) and the PPC/PDMS transfer chain (CHM-010 / CHM-003 / CHM-001). A CORRECTION TO SOMETHING I WROTE EARLIER: I said under TLS-020 that ordinary clear tape is not exfoliation tape. THE REAL TRADE-OFF, WHICH IS PUBLISHED AND NOT SOLVED: Magic tape leaves acrylic polymer RESIDUE on the substrate, and it gets worse with slow peels and higher anneal temperatures. There is no reliable solvent-free way to remove heavy tape residue without damaging flakes. So: peel reasonably fast, keep anneals modest, and where the final interface must be clean, exfoliate onto a sacrificial chip and pick the flake up with an hBN or polymer stamp so the tape adhesive never touches the device interface. Historical note for the students: the Geim and Novoselov work is usually told as "the Scotch tape method", but the 2004 paper names no tape, in Manchester it was Sellotape, and their 2005 paper describes rubbing one crystal against almost any solid surface. No particular tape brand was ever load-bearing in the discovery.

Almost certainly DIAMOND-TIPPED SCRIBER PENS - the knurled handle plus a fine point under a clear press-on cap is the standard form, and eight identical units in a bin is how a lab stocks them. A tungsten-carbide scriber looks nearly identical; the difference shows up in use, since carbide dulls on silicon and sapphire and diamond does not. FLAG: tip material NOT CONFIRMED from the photo. WHAT THEY ARE FOR: scoring an initiation flaw so silicon, glass, sapphire or a III-V substrate cleaves along its crystal plane - the standard way to break the wafers in this catalogue (WFR-001 to WFR-004) down into working pieces. HOW TO CLEAVE SILICON PROPERLY, because doing it wrong wastes wafers: (1) On a standard (100) wafer the primary flat is a {110} plane, and the cleavage planes run PARALLEL and PERPENDICULAR to that flat - never scribe at 45 degrees to it. (2) Work on a clean flat surface over a lint-free wipe, polished side up, gloves and safety glasses on. (3) Make a SHORT NICK AT THE WAFER EDGE ONLY, about 1-3 mm, aligned to the flat - do NOT drag a scribe across the face. A shallow narrow nick beats a deep one: a heavy scribe seeds microcracks that steer the fracture off-plane and sheds particles across your device area. (4) Break with an even three-point load - cleaving pliers close to the edge, or lay the wafer over a thin rod placed under the scribe line and press evenly on both sides. The crack follows the plane by itself. (5) Halves to quarters, every scribe parallel or perpendicular to the flat. Keep the scribed face away from the device side. CAP THE TOOL IMMEDIATELY AFTER USE - a chipped diamond tip is scrap. Note (111) wafers and III-Vs cleave on different planes.

Nitrile or butyl gloves and safety glasses every time; sensitisation is cumulative and permanent. It also smells strongly of mercaptan. (2) UNDER-CURING IS THE COMMON FAILURE. Thiol-ene is oxygen-inhibited at the free surface, so an under-dosed joint keeps a tacky skin, outgasses unreacted monomer, and drifts in index and dimension. Give it the full 2 J/cm2 measured at 365 nm, cure under a cover slip or nitrogen where you can, and POST-BAKE 12 h at 50 C - full adhesion only develops after that (or a week at room temperature). (3) DO NOT PUT IT IN A UV OR BLUE BEAM PATH. It absorbs 320-380 nm by design, so continued UV - and blue around 405-450 nm to a lesser degree - drives photo-oxidation and yellowing. It also fluoresces, which matters near Raman or single-molecule work. Bond at the edge or annulus, outside the clear aperture, and keep it out of high-intensity beams generally - Norland publishes no laser damage threshold. (4) FOR VACUUM, NOA 81 IS NOT THE LOW-OUTGASSING GRADE. That is NOA 88 (ASTM E595 rated). Fully cured and post-baked NOA 81 is widely used in chambers, but for UHV or anything with cold optics use NOA 88 or an E595-rated epoxy. STORAGE: 5-25 C, DARK, in the original bottle - no refrigeration, do not freeze, keep below 65 C or it can self-polymerise. Shelf life 8 months from manufacture; the bottles are marked EXP 13 Mar 2027. TREAT THIS AS THE MOST DANGEROUS SMALL ITEM IN THE CATALOGUE, and that is not an exaggeration - it is more likely to cause an eye injury than any of the bench lasers, because it has no interlock, no key, no shutter and no beam enclosure, and it fits in a pocket. WHY: an unmarked "high power" green pointer is typically 50-500 mW at 532 nm. Anything above 5 mW is Class 3B - capable of causing permanent retinal damage FASTER THAN THE BLINK REFLEX, and the eye focuses 532 nm efficiently onto the retina, so the hazard is far worse than the raw number suggests. It is also a specular-reflection hazard: a glance off any mounted optic, a watch face or a wrench is enough. A SECOND, LESS OBVIOUS HAZARD: cheap DPSS green pointers frequently leak large amounts of UNCONVERTED 1064 nm INFRARED, because the IR filter is omitted to cut cost. That light is invisible, is not blocked by ordinary green-attenuating eyewear unless the eyewear is rated for 1064 nm, and can be several times the visible power. Do not assume the danger is only what you can see. RULES: never point it at a person or an aircraft; never use it on the optical tables without the beam terminated in a dump; wear eyewear rated for 532 nm AND 1064 nm; and get it labelled with its actual measured output - the Newport 1830-R (MTR-008) or the thermopile head (MTR-007) can measure it. EYEWEAR CHECK: SAF-006 in this catalogue covers 405 and 532 nm. Confirm before use, and confirm whether anything in the eyewear stock also covers 1064 nm. FLAG: output power, class and whether an IR filter is fitted are all NOT CONFIRMED - nothing is marked on the body. Measuring it should be a priority.

FIRST-STAGE AIR PREPARATION. It does two jobs at once: a swirl vane flings LIQUID WATER AND OIL AEROSOL out against the bowl wall, and the sintered bronze element traps PARTICULATE - pipe scale, rust, PTFE tape shreds, compressor debris. The drain screw at the bottom bleeds the collected condensate, and on a MANUAL drain like this someone actually has to open it periodically or the bowl fills and the separated water gets carried back into the outlet. WHERE IT GOES: always FIRST in the chain - filter, then regulator, then (only if a tool needs oil) lubricator. Filter first so the regulator seat never sees grit or slugs of water. DO NOT PUT A LUBRICATOR ANYWHERE UPSTREAM OF THE SPIN COATER OR ANYTHING OPTICAL - oil mist is precisely the contaminant you are trying to keep off samples. WHY THIS LAB NEEDS IT: the Laurell spin coater (MAJ-021) requires N2 or clean dry air at 60-70 psi for its SEAL PURGE, and Laurell manual is explicit that the gas must be MOISTURE FREE, recommending a point-of-use filter of 1 um or less after the regulator. That purge keeps solvent vapour and resist out of the motor bearing - it is what makes the machine last. It also matters for blow-off drying after acetone/IPA, where a single 5 um particle blown onto a 10 um flake ruins the sample. SAFETY - THE POLYCARBONATE BOWL IS THE REAL HAZARD HERE, AND IT IS A DOCUMENTED FAILURE MODE, NOT A THEORETICAL ONE. Polycarbonate suffers environmental stress cracking from acetone, MEK, toluene, chlorinated solvents, ammonia, methanol and some synthetic compressor oils. A cracked bowl at 8 bar does not fail gracefully - IT SHATTERS AND THROWS FRAGMENTS. Rules: clean it with soapy water ONLY, never solvent; do not mount it next to the solvent bench or a fume hood plenum; depressurise before opening the drain or unscrewing the bowl; keep it out of sunlight (PC yellows and embrittles); and replace it at any sign of crazing or cloudiness. In a lab that handles acetone and IPA daily, a METAL-BOWL variant is the correct choice. FLAG: micron rating and whether the 1/4 inch port is BSPT or NPT are both unconfirmed - BSPT and NPT will start to thread together and then leak or crack the boss.

THE PICKUP POLYMER for van der Waals heterostructure assembly - this plus anisole (CHM-001) makes the PPC/PDMS stamp that builds stacks for the flake-finder microscope (MAJ-001). HOW IT IS USED: dissolve ~15 wt% PPC in anisole, spin onto a PDMS block at ~1500 rpm for a ~5 um film. PDMS gives the compliant mechanics; PPC gives the TEMPERATURE-TUNABLE ADHESION that PDMS alone cannot. Pick up the top flake (usually hBN) at ~40 C, just above Tg - softened PPC wets the flake and PPC-hBN adhesion beats hBN-SiO2. That hBN then picks up each subsequent layer at 40-60 C, building the stack top-down. RELEASE at ~90 C: PPC adhesion to the stack collapses (the crossover is around 70 C) and the film delaminates from the PDMS, depositing stack + PPC onto the target. Then strip the PPC in warm NMP (CHM-002) or anneal it away. STAY BELOW ~200 C during assembly or the PPC starts depolymerising. WHY IT LIVES IN THE FRIDGE (+2 to +8 C): because Tg is near ROOM TEMPERATURE. Warm pellets cold-flow and sinter into one solid mass, and the polycarbonate backbone slowly backbites to cyclic propylene carbonate, dropping Mn and degrading film quality. Keep it cold and dry, and LET THE BOTTLE WARM TO ROOM TEMPERATURE BEFORE OPENING so condensation does not get in. FLAG: the cold-storage rationale is the established literature mechanism, not a statement Sigma publishes.

General rinsing, solution make-up and glassware work. KNOW WHAT TYPE II ACTUALLY GUARANTEES - IT IS NOT MUCH. Type II is a DISTILLATION grade defined mainly by >=1 MOhm.cm; Type I is >=18 MOhm.cm and 5x tighter on Na and Cl. COUNTERINTUITIVE BUT REAL: Type III (>=4 MOhm.cm) actually has a HIGHER minimum resistivity than Type II - the ASTM types are not a clean purity ladder, so do not assume II beats III on ionic purity. The semiconductor standard is ASTM D5127, which demands 18.2 MOhm.cm, TOC 1-2 ppb (vs 50 ppb allowed here), metals at ppb-to-ppt and specified particle counts. At 5 ppb Na/Cl with no particle spec, Type II water leaves ionic and particulate residue when it dries. Use it for pre-cleans and glassware; get Type I / UPW for anything that touches a finished flake. WHY BOTTLED WATER HAS AN EXPIRY (4/7/31, a 5-year shelf life): high-purity water has no buffering capacity, so it absorbs atmospheric CO2 into carbonic acid and the resistivity falls - exposed Type I water drops from 16 to about 1 MOhm.cm in 48 hours, and HDPE is gas-permeable so even a sealed bottle equilibrates slowly. TOC also creeps up from bottle leaching. So a five-year-old bottle is likely sitting AT the 1 MOhm.cm limit rather than comfortably above it. The date is a specification-conformance date, not a safety date. The cost is that it is soft (flows at ~49 C), so it creeps under grinding load and frictional heating, and it absorbs humidity. 590 (brown) is the STRONGEST and the hottest - 150 C to flow - for dicing tall or high-aspect-ratio parts, or when the process runs hot enough to soften 509. Wax residue is exactly the contamination that kills carrier mobility in graphene devices, and it is not removable to monolayer cleanliness by a solvent rinse. Hot solvent plus ultrasonics will also tear flakes. USE CRYSTALBOND TO HOLD A CHIP OR WAFER DURING MECHANICAL WORK BEFORE FLAKES GO ON, NOT ON ANYTHING TOUCHING A FINISHED FLAKE. THE SOLVENT FOR THE PC TRANSFER RECIPE - pairs with the polycarbonate (CHM-013) to make the PC/PDMS stamp. See CHM-013 for the recipe. THIS IS THE MOST ACUTELY DANGEROUS CHEMICAL IN THE CATALOGUE. It is worse than NMP (CHM-002), and in a different way: NMP is a reproductive hazard you absorb through skin, chloroform is TOXIC BY INHALATION and a suspected carcinogen, and it evaporates fast (160 mmHg). EXPOSURE LIMITS, which are strikingly low: OSHA is a CEILING of 50 ppm - not a time-weighted average, a ceiling you must never exceed. ACGIH TLV is 10 ppm. NIOSH recommends 2 ppm and treats it as a potential occupational carcinogen. IARC Group 2B, NTP "reasonably anticipated to be a human carcinogen", California Prop 65 listed for BOTH cancer and reproductive toxicity. FUME HOOD, ALWAYS - there is no version of this that is fine on the open bench. NITRILE GLOVES GIVE ONLY MINUTES of breakthrough against chloroform: treat them as splash protection, change them immediately after any contact, and use laminate (Silver Shield / 4H) for real handling. THE PHOSGENE PROBLEM - THIS IS WHY THE LABEL SAYS "AMYLENES". Chloroform photo-oxidises: light and dissolved oxygen generate CCl3 radicals which react with O2 and collapse to PHOSGENE (COCl2) plus HCl. The reaction is autocatalytic, so it accelerates once started, and it runs faster in a bottle that has been opened (fresh oxygen) and faster in clear glass. Phosgene is a chemical-warfare agent. The 100-200 ppm of AMYLENE (2-methyl-2-butene) is a RADICAL SCAVENGER that stops the chain before phosgene forms. Note what that does NOT mean: amylene does not destroy phosgene once it exists, and it evaporates off (bp 38 C). So amylene-stabilised chloroform has a SHORTER safe life once opened than the ethanol-stabilised kind, which works instead by consuming phosgene at 0.5-1% ethanol. WHY THE AMYLENE GRADE IS NEVERTHELESS THE RIGHT ONE HERE: 1% ethanol is a real cosolvent and a non-solvent for polycarbonate - it hazes or skins a 6% PC dope and leaves residue at the van der Waals interface. At 100-200 ppm with a 38 C boiling point, amylene leaves nothing behind. This is why the 2D community specifies ethanol-free chloroform. STORAGE AND SHELF LIFE: amber container, tightly closed, DARK, cool, ventilated - never in sunlight or near a UV source. Keep away from strong bases, strong oxidisers and reactive metals (Na, K, Li, Mg, Al powder - potentially explosive). Unopened it keeps 1-2 years; ONCE OPENED treat it as good for about 6 months, and for critical film casting more like 1-3 months. WITH A 2.5 L CAN, ALIQUOT INTO A SMALL AMBER WORKING BOTTLE AND KEEP THE MOTHER CAN SEALED - repeatedly opening the big can is what kills it. Never decant used solvent back in. HOW TO TELL IT HAS GONE BAD: a sharp acrid pungent smell instead of the sweet chloroform odour; yellowing; ACIDITY - shake a little with water and test the aqueous layer with pH paper (phosgene hydrolyses to CO2 + 2 HCl). Also unexplained film defects or hazy substrates. Proper phosgene tests exist (filter paper wetted with 5% diphenylamine + 5% dimethylaminobenzaldehyde in ethanol turns yellow-orange in the vapour; commercial Draeger-type detector tubes). IF IT TESTS POSITIVE, DO NOT TRY TO RE-STABILISE IT - dispose of it as hazardous waste.

GLASS TRANSITION Tg = 150 C. Density 1.2 g/mL at 25 C; nD20 1.585. Thermal decomposition onset ~440-480 C. Soluble in CHLOROFORM (excellent), dichloromethane, THF, dioxane, NMP; NOT soluble in alcohols, water, aliphatics or acetone; and NOT soluble in ANISOLE

THE SECOND TRANSFER RECIPE. With the chloroform (CHM-012) this gives the lab a PC/PDMS stamp alongside the PPC/anisole one it already had (CHM-003 + CHM-001) - and the two are complementary, not redundant. THE PC RECIPE (Zomer et al., Appl. Phys. Lett. 105, 013101, 2014): 6 wt% PC in chloroform. DO NOT TRY TO SPIN-COAT IT - the original authors found spin coating difficult. Instead DRIP the solution onto a glass microscope slide, lay a second slide on top and immediately SLIDE IT OFF sideways, leaving a uniform film; air-dry about 15 minutes. Lift the dried film off with adhesive tape and drape it over the PDMS block, tape acting as the frame. PICK UP at 60-90 C, then switch the heater off and retract while cooling. RELEASE at about 150 C to melt the PC onto the target. Dissolve the PC off in chloroform, roughly 10 minutes. CRITICAL POINT ABOUT THE STAMP, AND IT EXPLAINS THE WHOLE ODD PROCEDURE: the PC film is cast on GLASS and only then transferred to the PDMS. THE CHLOROFORM MUST NEVER TOUCH THE PDMS. Chloroform swells PDMS by about 39% (Whitesides swelling ratio S = 1.39, among the worst solvents tested) - casting directly onto the stamp would destroy it. The PDMS here is purely a compliant mechanical backing, chemically isolated from the solvent. This is the opposite of the PPC recipe, where anisole IS spun straight onto the PDMS. WHICH RECIPE TO USE - the deciding factor is TEMPERATURE BUDGET: PC (Tg 150 C): pick up at 60-110 C, release at 150-180 C. Choose it for RELIABLE hBN PICKUP - PC grips hBN better and is the workhorse for hBN-encapsulated graphene; for MANY-LAYER STACKS where each pickup needs a robust film; when you want intermediate hot steps mid-stack; and for the cleanest final interface, since PC dissolves off more completely. PPC (Tg 35-40 C): pick up at ~40 C, release at ~90 C. Choose it for THERMALLY FRAGILE OR AIR-SENSITIVE MATERIALS - CrI3, black phosphorus, MnBi2Te4, thin superconductors, organics - because the whole cycle tops out at 90 C rather than 180 C; for release onto pre-patterned electrodes or flexible substrates; and for glovebox work. Rule of thumb: PC = high temperature, high yield, hBN-first, cleanest stacks. PPC = low temperature, delicate materials. WHY Mw ~45,000 SPECIFICALLY: it is the deliberate middle. At 45k a 6% chloroform dope is fluid enough to spread between two slides into a uniform micron film; a 100k+ PC at 6% is stringy and gels. It is also comfortably above the entanglement threshold so the film is self-supporting and does not tear on pickup, yet low enough to flow and detach cleanly at 150-180 C. Very high Mw makes release sluggish and drags the stack; very low Mw gives brittle films and oligomeric residue. This is the standard grade for the recipe. Note PC is AMORPHOUS - the "Tm 267 C" some datasheets list is a formality, there is no sharp melt. It softens through 150 C and melt-processes at 260-300 C. Keep the bottle out of direct sunlight as the label says.

WHAT THAT COMBINATION IS FOR: a 60 um device layer is far too thick for photonics or for 2D-material substrates and is the signature of MEMS / bulk micromachining - you etch all the way through the 60 um by DRIE and the 2 um buried oxide acts as the etch stop, releasing a suspended structure. The low resistivity means the silicon is being used as a conductor (electrodes, electrostatic actuators, through-silicon contacts), not as a low-loss optical or RF medium. If anyone is planning to use these as a photonics or RF substrate, that is a mistake: 0.001-0.005 ohm-cm silicon is lossy. IMPORTANT - THIS IS NOT THE 2D-MATERIAL SUBSTRATE. The oxide here is BURIED under 60 um of silicon, so it gives you NO optical contrast for finding flakes. For exfoliation you still need the 285 nm or 90 nm thermal-oxide wafers (see the other WFR entries). Do not let anyone grab these by mistake. KEEP THE BAG SEALED until needed - it is an ESD/moisture barrier bag and once opened the wafers start collecting particles. 150 mm is 6 inch, so check your chucks and carriers actually take 6 inch before planning around them.

FAB-001

GEL-PAK CARRIERS AND GEL-TRAYS for die and flake handling

Gel-Pak
GEL-TRAY BD-22CC-02-X4-P0041 (Lot 3909 4V/68821-1); AD-22T-00-X4 (Order 3016403-1-1, Qty 25, Ref 100510)
Wavelength
n/a
Size
One full drawer; several sealed multipacks
Key spec
Gel-based retention surfaces in hinged clear boxes and trays

THE STANDARD WAY TO STORE AND MOVE FRAGILE DIE AND EXFOLIATED SAMPLES. A Gel-Pak is a low-tack silicone gel layer in a clamshell: you press a chip, die or a flake-bearing piece onto the gel and it is held by conformal contact alone - no adhesive, so it lifts off cleanly with tweezers or a vacuum pen and leaves no residue to clean off afterwards. That is why they are used in place of tape or gel-free boxes for anything valuable. PRACTICAL POINTS: handle the gel surface only with the part you are placing - fingers and dust ruin the tack, and it does not come back. Keep the boxes closed. Gel retention weakens with contamination and with age, so if a part starts sliding around, retire that carrier. The GEL-TRAY versions are the multi-cavity ones for batches of die. Not itemised beyond the two part numbers read from the labels.

Blue tape of this kind has two jobs in a lab like this: as WAFER PROTECTIVE FILM, laid over a polished face to keep particles off during handling, cutting or storage; and as DICING/BACKING TAPE, holding a wafer flat and holding the pieces together while it is cut. It is NOT the same thing as the thin exfoliation tape used to cleave 2D crystals - if the aim is exfoliating graphene or a TMD, use proper exfoliation tape, not this. Test the tack on a scrap before putting it on a good wafer - a film that is too aggressive will leave residue on a polished surface.

FAB-004×2

PTFE / PFA BEAKERS - fluoropolymer, two units

Not marked
No part number
Wavelength
n/a
Size
Approximately 250-500 mL, translucent white fluoropolymer
Key spec
PTFE service temperature to about 260 C; chemically inert to essentially everything except molten alkali metals and elemental fluorine

THE ACID BEAKERS. This is why they exist: glass DISSOLVES in hydrofluoric acid and in hot strong bases, so any HF, buffered oxide etch (BOE), or hot KOH/TMAH work MUST be done in fluoropolymer, never glass. They are also metal-free, so they do not leach ions into a wafer clean. Use them for BOE and HF oxide etching, KOH/TMAH silicon etching, piranha and RCA cleans, and any solvent. Keep them dedicated to that job - do not use them as general beakers, and keep acid beakers and solvent beakers separate. PTFE is soft and scratches easily; scratched surfaces trap contamination. Rinse thoroughly with DI water (CHM-008) after every use.

The tools for getting wafers and samples INTO and OUT OF a chemical bath without putting your hand near it. The perforations let the liquid drain as you lift, so the piece comes out with minimal carry-over into the next bath - which is exactly what you want in a multi-stage clean (etch, rinse, rinse). The slotted carrier holds several pieces at once. Fluoropolymer throughout, so they are safe in HF, BOE and hot base along with the PTFE beakers (FAB-004). Metal tweezers ARE NOT - never put stainless tweezers into HF or hot base, both for the tool and for the contamination. Keep these dedicated to wet chemistry and rinse them well.

CLN-002

BORON SPUTTERING TARGET, 2 inch, indium-bonded to copper backing plate

Kurt J. Lesker Company
Part# EJUBXXX302A4; Lot# P22-056 / VR10-0045569
Wavelength
n/a
Size
Target 2.00 inch diameter x 0.125 inch thick; backing plate OFHC 101 copper, 2.00 inch dia x 0.125 inch thick
Key spec
Boron, 99.7-99.9% pure; density >55%; INDIUM BONDED to the copper backing plate

A sputtering target for depositing boron films. Two things about it are worth understanding: (1) BORON IS A POOR CONDUCTOR AND A POOR THERMAL CONDUCTOR, and this target is only >55% dense - that is why it is INDIUM BONDED to an oxygen-free copper backing plate. The indium bond carries heat out of the target into the cooled plate. Without it the target cracks. (2) THE INDIUM BOND SETS A HARD POWER LIMIT: indium melts at 157 C. Run too much power, or run it with poor cooling, and the bond melts, the target debonds and you lose both the target and possibly the gun. Ramp power gently and make sure cooling water is flowing before you start. Store it dry and flat; do not handle the target face.

CLN-003

GOLD STARTER SOURCE for electron-beam evaporation, 99.99% pure

Kurt J. Lesker Company
Part# EVMAU40.295; Lot# 20600 / VPU097112
Wavelength
n/a
Size
0.759 inch top OD x 0.601 inch bottom OD x 0.295 inch high - a truncated cone shaped to fit an EB-13M crucible liner
Key spec
Gold, 99.99% pure; shaped "starter source" for e-beam evaporation

HIGH-VALUE ITEM - this is bulk 99.99% gold. A "starter source" is pre-shaped to sit correctly in a specific crucible liner (here the EB-13M), so the electron beam couples into it properly from the first run instead of spitting. Gold is the standard contact and interconnect metal for the devices this lab makes: chemically inert, excellent conductor, and it bonds and probes well. NOTE it adheres poorly to oxides, which is why gold is almost always deposited over a thin chromium or titanium adhesion layer. TREAT AS VALUABLE AND TRACK IT. Keep it sealed and dry, handle with clean gloves only, and never let it touch the general workshop tools - gold picks up contamination readily and any transferred metal ruins the purity that is the whole point of paying for 4N material.

THE TWEEZER SET - the single most-used cleanroom tool, and worth knowing which is which because using the wrong one destroys samples. WHAT IS IN THE CASE: fine-point stainless for general small parts; FLAT/BLUNT and WAFER tips for picking up wafers and die WITHOUT scratching or point-loading them - always use these on a polished face, never a sharp point; ANGLED tips for working under a microscope; and two Excelta 159-RT with CARBON-FIBRE REPLACEABLE TIPS, which are non-marring, non-magnetic and chemically resistant - the right choice for delicate optics, coated surfaces and anything where a steel tip would scratch or transfer metal. ANTI-MAGNETIC matters when you are near a sensitive detector or handling magnetic samples; ANTI-ACID matters for wet-bench work - though for HF and hot base use the PTFE tools (FAB-005), not any metal tweezer. CARE: tweezer tips bend and misalign easily. Do not use them as pry bars, do not drop them, and keep them in the case with the tips in the foam. A tweezer whose tips no longer meet is scrap for precision work.
